Our central structural characterization explicitly constructs a single collection of mutually independent utilities, reproducing Mallows choice probabilities simultaneously for all offered sets. This exact choice equivalence connects pending Mallows-related challenges to the recent approximation framework of Bowers et al. (FOCS 2025) for assortment optimization under independent random utilities. We make this connection algorithmically feasible through a finite-support reduction that produces distributions of polynomial size while controlling revenue loss uniformly over all assortments. Fused together, these ingredients lead to an $O(n^{\tilde{O}(1/ε^2)})$-time approximation scheme for assortment optimization under the Mallows model, while allowing arbitrary product prices, concentration parameters, and modal rankings.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Bipartite Carrier Compression and Machine-Certified Bounds in Schönhage Trilinear Multiplication Tensors
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Under the conditional framework breaking the longstanding O(n log n) integer multiplication barrier (originating from OpenAI Preprint #109), the asymptotic time complexity exponent T(n) = O(n (log n)^{1-κ}) is governed by bounding the second moment E[X^2] < 1 of recursive branching processes over trilinear tensor carrier graphs. In this work, we present a constructive combinatorial optimization over the alternating carrier bipartite matching graphs of the Schönhage trilinear tensor decomposition at dimensions h=23 and h=25. Through an alternating augmenting path search, we uncover a non-trivial cluster-unlocking cascade that eliminates 185 carrier roles (95 roles in h=23 and 90 roles in h=25), reducing the global physical wire width by 377,890 wires from the reviewed baseline W = 177,284,805 down to W = 176,906,915. Evaluated over the exact 10^{-14} rational grid, this wire reduction certifies an improved second-moment coefficient AB = 5,164,059 / 125,000,000,000 and establishes the sharpened conditional exponent κ= 826,215,307 / 20,000,000,000,000 \approx 4.131076535 \times 10^{-5}, strictly surpassing the preceding record on this architecture (κ\approx 4.123864 \times 10^{-5}). All 47 polynomial constraints and 7 rational security margins are audited in exact Q-arithmetic with zero floating-point error, and the fundamental wire reduction identity is formally verified in the Lean 4 interactive theorem prover without unproven axioms.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: 5 pages, self-contained. Lean 4 formal proofs, standalone certificate verifier, and full experimental artifacts openly available at Zenodo: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23268580

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Many Scores Force Many Reads: An Optimality Proof for Score of Parentheses
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
LeetCode Problem 856, Score of Parentheses, admits a one-pass algorithm using $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ auxiliary registers. Its correctness follows from a local interpretation: every occurrence of () contributes a power of two determined by its nesting depth. The space bound is immediately optimal in the usual programming-challenge model, but the linear-time bound is less obvious. In particular, a direct adversary that forces an algorithm to inspect every character is difficult to maintain under the promise that the input is balanced.
  We instead prove a counting lower bound. For every $k$, we construct $2^k$ balanced parenthesis strings of the same length $4k+2$, all having distinct scores. The construction encodes each bit using one of two operations, changing a current score $v$ to either $2v+1$ or $2v+2$. Consequently, any deterministic character-query decision tree computing the score must have depth at least $k$. A two-character padding argument extends the result to every even input length, proving an $Ω(n)$ worst-case time lower bound. The one-pass algorithm is therefore asymptotically optimal in the unit-cost RAM model.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: A Framework for the Design of Efficient Diversification Algorithms for Packing and Covering Problems
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
There has been considerable recent interest in computing a diverse collection of solutions to a given optimization problem. Given a classical optimization problem $Π$ (e.g., minimum spanning tree, maximum independent set) with input size $n$ and an integer $k\geq 1$, the goal is to generate a collection of $k$ maximally diverse solutions to $Π$. This diverse-X paradigm not only allows the user to generate very different solutions, but also helps make systems more secure and robust by handling uncertainty and achieving energy efficiency.
  For several problems $Π$ solvable in polynomial time, there are efficient $\text{poly}(n,k)$-time exact or approximation algorithms available for their diverse-solution variants. In contrast, only FPT algorithms are known for NP-complete problems such as vertex covers and independent sets. In the worst case, these algorithms run in time $\exp((kn)^a)$ for some $a>0$.
  In this work, we address this gap and give a general framework for $\text{poly}(n,k)$-time \emph{bi-criteria} PTAS for the diverse variants of several NP-hard problems such as \textsc{Knapsack}, \textsc{Maximum Weight Independent Set} (MWIS) and \textsc{Minimum Weight Vertex Cover} (MWVC) in planar graphs. More precisely, given a maximization (or, minimization) problem $Π$, an integer $k \geq 1$, user-specified quality threshold $ c \in (0, 1) $, and user-controlled error parameters $δ,\varepsilon \in (0,1)$, our bi-approximation algorithm returns a collection of $k$ solutions $S_1,S_2,\ldots,S_k$ that are $(1-δ)c$-optimal and whose diversity is at least a $(1-\varepsilon)$-fraction of the maximum diversity achievable by any collection of $k$ $c$-optimal solutions.
  To complement our positive results, we prove that the diverse-solution variants of \KP and MWIS mentioned above do not admit standard single-criterion PTASs.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Attention via Black-Box Vector Search
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
Sparse attention mechanisms estimate attention over $n$ tokens using a small subset of keys. Many existing approaches use maximum inner product search (MIPS) to retrieve the heaviest keys, which motivates the following question: given black-box access to a MIPS oracle, how many keys must be retrieved to output an $\varepsilon$-accurate attention estimate?
  We answer this question by unifying prior approaches through the framework of priority sampling. With a single MIPS index, we show that $Θ(\sqrt{n}/\varepsilon)$ retrieved keys are both sufficient and necessary. With $Θ(\log n)$ indices, we give an algorithm that retrieves only $O(\log n+1/\varepsilon^2)$ keys and prove that this is near-optimal. More generally, we design algorithms that establish a smooth tradeoff between the number of MIPS indices and number of retrieved keys. We then show that if we allow augmentation of keys and queries, we can bypass the above lower bounds: there exists a simple priority-sampling estimator using a single MIPS index and $O(1/\varepsilon^2)$ retrieved keys. When integrated into LLM inference, our algorithms outperform top-$k$ and sampling approaches used in prior work and yield attention approximation that scales favorably to long contexts.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: An Evaluation of Vertex Elimination Strategies for Algorithmic Differentiation
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
The algorithmic differentiation (AD) of mathematical functions can be interpreted as a sequence of vertex eliminations in an underlying directed acyclic graph. The problem of determining a minimum-cost elimination ordering, which we call Optimal Vertex Elimination, is NP-complete, and much effort has been devoted to the design of heuristics. Many of these heuristics are widely believed to perform well in practice, but this hypothesis has so far been difficult to test due to the lack of scalable exact methods.
  We design and engineer new integer programming formulations for Optimal Vertex Elimination and for a related objective we call Minimum Edge Count. Our implementations scale to graphs one-to-two orders of magnitude larger than existing techniques, facilitating the assembly of a corpus of medium-sized graphs for which optimal solutions are known. We give a comprehensive evaluation of existing heuristics on this corpus.
  We also make several theoretical contributions, including a tight analysis of the forward and reverse modes of AD, a simple algorithm for Optimal Vertex Elimination with approximation ratio parameterized by the size of a minimum source-sink separator, and the first approximation lower bounds for both problems.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Algorithms with Smoothed Polynomial-Time Complexity for Deterministic Discounted-sum and Mean-payoff Games
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Turn-based deterministic games on graphs are two-player zero-sum games played on finite directed graphs, where the vertex set is partitioned between the Max and the adversarial Min Player. The respective player chooses outgoing edges from their vertices. We consider these games with the classical discounted-sum and mean-payoff objectives. The goal of the Max Player is to maximize the objective against the adversarial Min Player. These games lie in NP $\cap$ coNP and are among the rare combinatorial problems that belong to this complexity class, yet the existence of a polynomial-time algorithm is a major open question. All known deterministic algorithms require exponential time in the worst case, while the classical strategy iteration (policy iteration) algorithm is remarkably efficient in practice, which motivates the study of the smoothed complexity of these games. Previous results established a smoothed polynomial-time bound only for the restricted class of ergodic games and presented only a high-probability guarantee. Our main result is a new analysis technique for a variant of the strategy iteration algorithm, and we show these algorithms achieve smoothed polynomial complexity for general game graphs with both high-probability and expected runtime guarantees. In particular, our result removes the ergodicity restriction of prior work and strengthens the high-probability guarantee to the stronger expected-runtime guarantee, thereby resolving the open question on the smoothed complexity of these games.

Graphics.title: Make It Flow: Animating Water in 3D Gaussian Splatting Scenes
Graphics.summary: Explicit 3D scene representations such as 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) have recently enabled high-quality, real-time novel view synthesis. However, these methods assume static scenes, limiting realism in the presence of dynamic phenomena ubiquitous in real-world environments. While coherent motion (e.g., humans or vehicles) can be captured and reconstructed, high-frequency effects such as flowing water remain intractable under casual capture conditions, where dense multi-view, high-speed acquisition is not feasible. We present a method to animate water in static 3DGS scenes, enabling visually plausible motion without requiring dynamic capture or physical simulation. Our approach estimates 2D optical flow from reference images or model renderings and lifts it into a consistent 3D Eulerian motion field. We propose a cinemagraph-inspired algorithm that applies this motion field to deform Gaussian primitives, producing temporally seamless looping animations. The resulting representation retains real-time rendering performance, significantly enhances perceptual realism, and preserves free-viewpoint navigation within the scene. We evaluate our method on a newly captured dataset of in-the-wild waterfall scenes and demonstrate clear improvements over prior work in dynamic Gaussian splatting and 3D cinemagraph generation in visual quality and computational efficiency.

Graphics.title: Efficient Confidence-Aware Densification for 3DGS
Graphics.summary: 3DGS-MCMC has replaced the gradient-driven density control of 3D Gaussian Splatting with opacity-based sampling and relocation, and is now the de facto standard for prior-free densification under a fixed primitive budget. Because opacity stays high where the scene is already well reconstructed, this sampling sends most new primitives to the foreground and leaves the background under-reconstructed. At low budgets, prior-based methods such as ConeGS and EDGS outperform it, at the cost of a pre-trained radiance field or dense image matches and a separate initialization stage. We argue for a comeback of error-driven densification within the fixed-budget MCMC framework. Our confidence-aware densification keeps the fixed budget and gradual growth of 3DGS-MCMC, but places primitives by the image error instead of the opacity. New primitives are drawn mostly where screen-space gradients are large. We favor primitives with a low learned confidence, which marks regions the reconstruction still explains poorly, and relocate the primitives that contribute least to the rendered images to these places. Averaged over 24 scenes, our method outperforms 3DGS-MCMC in PSNR, SSIM and LPIPS at every budget from 100k to 2M primitives. At 100k, without a prior or an initialization stage, it recovers 0.84dB of the 1.05dB PSNR by which ConeGS leads 3DGS-MCMC, and from 500k on, it has the highest PSNR and SSIM of all fixed-budget methods we compare with, including ConeGS and EDGS. While inherently prior-free, our densification can also exploit priors: from the ConeGS or EDGS initialization, it matches ConeGS in PSNR and SSIM at 100k and is best in all three metrics at 500k.

Graphics.title: SplatQ: Interaction-Aware Pruning of 3D Gaussian Splatting via Quadratic Selection
Graphics.summary: Existing 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) pruning methods primarily rely on global Top-K selection based on independent importance scores, lacking regional budget control and ignoring joint deletion effects. Consequently, they cannot ensure balanced reconstruction quality across a scene. We propose SplatQ, a combinatorial pruning algorithm that coordinates regional budget allocation and joint Gaussian selection under a fixed budget. SplatQ partitions Gaussians by spatial proximity and appearance similarity into size-limited blocks, decomposing global selection into subproblems of a specific size. It then smooths importance-based block retention quotas to prevent excessive budget concentration. Finally, it constructs a quadratic approximation of joint deletion effects using the responses of representative pixel colors to changes in Gaussian opacity. Individual responses, pairwise interactions, and quota penalties are incorporated into a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) objective, solved using simulated annealing (SA) or a coherent Ising machine (CIM) to jointly select Gaussians. Experiments on 5 benchmarks demonstrate that SplatQ outperforms state-of-the-art pruning methods in aggregate reconstruction quality, spatial quality balance, and rendering speed. Ablations confirm that budget smoothing improves local detail reconstruction, while interaction modeling improves Gaussian selection quality under a fixed budget.
Graphics.comment: Under review at ICLR 2027 (main paper 9 pages, 5 figures, 2 tables; appendix included)

Graphics.title: A Hybrid and Hierarchical Ray Tracing Method for Efficient 3D Gaussian Rendering
Graphics.summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) is a powerful representation for real-time neural reconstruction and rendering. While existing 3DGS systems rely on rasterization for efficiency, recent work explores ray tracing to enable secondary lighting, highly distorted cameras, and depth-of-field effects. However, compared with rasterization, ray-traced 3DGS introduces three major challenges: (1) the highly non-uniform spatial distribution of massive numbers of Gaussian primitives creates severe load imbalance; (2) neighboring pixels often generate rays with highly similar traversal paths, leading to substantial redundant traversal overhead; and (3) supporting both Gaussian and triangle primitives yields heterogeneous intersection workloads that are not well matched to existing GPU architectures. We present H2-Ray, a hybrid and hierarchical ray tracing architecture for efficient 3D Gaussian rendering. H2-Ray introduces three techniques. Load-Balanced Spatial BVH (LB-SBVH) partitions the scene into uniform grids and uses density-aware representations to convert an imbalanced global workload into balanced local traversal units. Ray-Cluster Path Reuse (RCPR) lets a proxy ray share traversal state with neighboring rays to amortize redundant traversal. The Unified Intersection Engine (UIE) supports mixed Gaussian and triangle intersections through a mode-multiplexed datapath that shares 40% of its floating-point units across both primitive types. Across 8 scenes, H2-Ray achieves a geometric-mean speedup of 3.77x and a maximum speedup of 9.26x over RaySplats on the NVIDIA RTX A5000, combining a cycle-accurate model of the modified RT Core with measured CUDA timings.

Graphics.title: Hierarchical Graph Neural Network for Probabilistic Power Flow with Grid Topology Contingencies
Graphics.summary: Data-driven surrogates reduce the nonlinear solves required for probabilistic power flow (PPF), but models tied to a fixed bus--branch graph often generalize poorly when outages change electrical coupling. This paper proposes a topology-decomposition-driven hierarchical bidirectional graph neural network (TDD--HBGNN) for PPF under unseen topologies. For each realized topology, the network is decomposed into fundamental topological units (FTUs), dynamically homogeneous voltage clusters (DHVCs), and a core backbone sub-grid (CBSG), with equivalent-admittance representations preserving electrical ports between units. A sensitivity-based linear prior captures the first-order voltage-magnitude and phase-angle response, while the HBGNN learns topology-dependent nonlinear residuals. Impedance- and uncertainty-aware bottom-up aggregation condenses local perturbations, while mode-modulated top-down broadcasting restores system context at buses. We evaluate our approach on the IEEE 118-bus and Polish 2746-bus systems under unseen N--1 and N--2 contingencies against six baseline methods. Compared with these methods, TDD--HBGNN achieves 2.47--4.20-fold lower all-bus phase-angle errors and lower phase-angle errors in every held-out event. Its voltage-magnitude advantage is concentrated near the outaged branches, where paired error ratios reach 1.75--2.58 on the IEEE system and 1.87--1.97 in Polish N--2 events. All system--contingency--baseline comparisons favor TDD--HBGNN in joint voltage--angle error. Moreover, shared hierarchical operators keep the model size at 0.658 million parameters across both grids and yield 0.161--1.793~ms forward latency per probabilistic case. These results demonstrate system-wide angular accuracy, outage-local voltage accuracy, and parameter-efficient scaling across unseen topologies.

Graphics.title: Sonic-AMG: Streaming Human Motion Generation from Spatial Audio
Graphics.summary: Modeling human reactions to spatial audio requires understanding both what is heard and where it comes from. Prior work generates motion offline from complete acoustic and spatial input sequences. Humans, however, react to sounds without knowing what they will hear next. We present Sonic-AMG, to our knowledge the first framework for streaming human motion generation from spatial audio. The model encodes acoustic content and body-relative source geometry as separate tokens. Conditioned on these tokens, a causal transformer with a flow head generates continuous motion latents, from which a causal decoder reconstructs motion segments. Standard teacher-forced training derives motion histories and body-relative source locations from ground-truth motion, whereas streaming inference relies on generated motion for both, resulting in a training-inference mismatch. To reduce this history discrepancy, we introduce rehearsal training, which combines full-sequence teacher-forced supervision with supervised prediction along short autoregressive self-rollouts. To keep spatial conditioning consistent with generated motion, we propose spatial feedback, which recomputes body-relative source locations from generated root poses during both rehearsal training and inference. On SAM, Sonic-AMG achieves state-of-the-art FID and R-precision. It further supports real-time online generation of coherent reactions across sound events and source locations. Project page: https://jingchengni.com/sonic-amg/.

Graphics.title: The Invisible Hand of Physics: When Video Diffusion Models Know More Than They Show
Graphics.summary: Modern video diffusion models generate increasingly realistic and temporally coherent videos, motivating their use as candidate world simulators. Yet it remains unclear whether these models internally encode physical structure, or merely reproduce motion patterns seen during training. We study this question by probing video diffusion models along latent trajectories corresponding to real videos with known physical plausibility. To obtain such trajectories, we approximately invert the deterministic sampling process by integrating the learned velocity field backward from a clean video latent to noise, giving access to the model's intermediate states and attention maps. Using these recovered trajectories, we show that physical plausibility is linearly decodable from diffusion transformer states across IntPhys and InfLevel, reaching around 81.27% average accuracy and outperforming dedicated representation-learning baselines such as V-JEPA and VideoMAE. Surprisingly, this signal is absent from the VAE latent input and emerges inside the denoising transformer itself, despite the model not being trained with a self-supervised predictive objective. These findings suggest that physically meaningful representations can arise as a byproduct of generative denoising.

Graphics.title: 3DRAG: 3D-Native Object Drag Editing with Generative Models
Graphics.summary: The rapid progress of 3D generative models has made 3D asset creation increasingly accessible. However, achieving intuitive, precise, and interactive user control, such as point-based drag editing, remains challenging. Existing 3D drag methods either rely on slow 2D diffusion priors, such as Score Distillation Sampling, or directly warp geometry, often causing multi-view inconsistency and topological artifacts. In this paper, we present 3DRAG, a training-free framework that executes precise drag editing natively within the explicit 3D latent space of large-scale generative models, without SDS-based optimization or iterative point tracking. To ensure geometrically plausible deformations, 3DRAG explicitly extends the drag displacement field into 3D space, incorporating an Occupancy-Aware Winner-Takes-All (OA-WTA) strategy to robustly handle sparse geometries. Furthermore, we introduce a generative editing pipeline that explicitly transforms latent representations via the 3D displacement field. By fully leveraging the model's generative capabilities, it achieves smooth geometric deformations while maintaining the object's identity. To further transfer original geometry and texture with high fidelity, we propose Logits-Level Token Fusion, which accurately injects source information into the destination region. To evaluate 3D point-based editing, we construct a novel dataset featuring diverse 3D assets and complex multi-point drag instructions. Quantitative and qualitative experiments demonstrate that 3DRAG achieves state-of-the-art performance, surpassing existing baselines in drag accuracy, geometric fidelity, and unedited region preservation.

Graphics.title: Spherical Geometrical Bases of Spherical Origami
Graphics.summary: This paper establishes a rigorous geometrical framework for spherical origami (origami using spherical sheets based on spherical geometry) in two settings: origami restricted to the unit sphere $\mathbb{S}^2$, and three-dimensional folding of spherical sheets in space. Three main results are proved. First, all seven Huzita--Justin axioms admit explicit constructions on $\mathbb{S}^2$, so spherical origami inherits the same one-fold axiom structure as Euclidean origami. Second, the Kawasaki--Justin theorem on flat-foldability extends to $\mathbb{S}^2$ by a local-tangent-plane argument, and the resulting vertex condition is equivalent to the angle-sum condition that characterizes Robertson's spherical $f$-tilings. Third, taking equidistant curves (small arcs) as fold curves yields a one-parameter family of isometric 3D folds, parametrized by the dihedral angle whose closed-form expression is derived, and recovers geodesic folds as the flat limit. The framework is illustrated by constructing computer graphics of spherical origami birds as a concrete example.
Graphics.comment: v3: corrected the account of prior work by T. Kawasaki (including his result that the spherical counterpart of Axiom 6 always has at least two solutions) and the attribution of the incircle condition to J. Justin; added references to preliminary abstracts (JCDCG^3 2024; Symposium of the Society for Science on Form 2024). 27 pages, 8 figures

Graphics.title: ARS-Avatar: Animatable and Relightable Surfel Avatars with Learnable Ambient Occlusion
Graphics.summary: Creating animatable and relightable human avatars from multi-view images remains challenging, as pose-dependent deformation, materials, and light visibility are tightly coupled in images. In this paper, we present ARS-Avatar, a novel method using surfel representation for high-quality, animatable, and relightable human avatars from multi-view images captured under unknown illumination. For faithful surfel estimation, we extract deformation displacement and body model deviation two priors from the mesh, which jointly capture local deformation complexity and serve as auxiliary. We employ deferred shading to estimate BRDF materials and further introduce a differentiable screen-space ambient occlusion formulation that enables gradient-based optimization of body-part specific occlusion radii through finite differences, providing an efficient approximation of light visibility that can be jointly optimized with the avatar. Extensive experiments show that ARS-Avatar achieves competitive or improved radiance reconstruction on multiple metrics and consistently outperforms the evaluated PBR relighting baselines, while enabling realistic animation and relighting under novel poses and illuminations.

Graphics.title: TopoPilot: Reliable Conversational Workflow Automation for Topological Data Analysis and Visualization
Graphics.summary: Recent agentic systems demonstrate that large language models can generate complex codebases from natural language prompts. Despite this progress, they present reliability concerns for scientific visualization due to invalid operations, subtle errors, and failure to resolve underspecified inputs. These challenges are compounded in real-world workflows that exceed the complexity of standard benchmarks. In this work, we introduce TopoPilot, a reliable and extensible agentic framework for automating complex scientific visualization workflows. We focus on topological data analysis and visualization as a primary use case, while designing the framework to generalize to broader visualization domains. TopoPilot employs a two-agent architecture: an orchestrator translates user prompts into workflows composed of atomic backend actions, while a verifier evaluates workflows prior to execution. Its modular design isolates components and supports new topological descriptors and domain-specific workflows without modifying the core system. It also employs numerous deterministic guardrails to ensure semantic consistency and accurate execution. To systematically improve reliability, we develop a taxonomy of failure modes and employ targeted safeguards for each class of error. Across 1,000 simulated multi-turn conversations spanning 100 prompts, including adversarial and infeasible requests, TopoPilot achieves a success rate exceeding 95%, compared with under 50% for a baseline without comprehensive guardrails and verification. We also show that TopoPilot outperforms Claude Code and Codex on similar prompts in terms of accuracy, completion time, and token usage.

Graphics.title: SliderEdit++: Improved Slider Trajectories in Instruction-Based Image Editing
Graphics.summary: Slider-based control aims to give users continuous, fine-grained control over the intensity of individual edits in instruction-based image editing. However, existing approaches fail to deliver reliable continuous controllability: traversing a slider can produce abrupt visual jumps and non-monotonic changes, while jointly controlled sliders can interfere with one another. To systematically study these limitations, we introduce SlideBench, a comprehensive benchmark for continuous image editing spanning diverse editing categories and equipped with a unified suite of metrics quantifying monotonic progression, perceptual continuity, and inter-slider disentanglement. Building on these observations, we propose SliderEdit++, which explicitly regularizes the intermediate editing trajectory rather than supervising only its endpoints. Our method combines velocity- and semantic-space trajectory regularization with spectral control to encourage smooth, predictable slider traversal, together with a disentanglement objective that reduces interference between independently controlled edits. On SlideBench, SliderEdit++ achieves state-of-the-art performance, improving the overall score by 18.5% relative to the strongest baseline. At the same time, using a few-step editing backbone makes our method approximately 3x to 20x faster than existing slider-based approaches, enabling substantially more responsive interactive editing.

Graphics.title: MeshRepair: Autoregressive Topology Repair for Generated Artisan Meshes
Graphics.summary: Recent artisan mesh generation methods produce meshes whose topology comes close to the preferences of human artists. But gaps to artist quality remain because generated meshes commonly contain holes, stray faces, and duplicated faces. Regenerating a mesh from scratch is costly, and a new draw may change the preferred topology entirely or introduce errors elsewhere. In this work we study artisan topology correction. The task is to correct the topology of a generated mesh (the draft) in place, toward the layout an artist would make. We propose a method for this task. It is a face-level correction network based on a prefix-LM. It reads the mesh bidirectionally and emits an edit sequence autoregressively. The sequence consists of a deletion phase followed by an addition phase. We propose the novel formulation of the deletion head which picks faces to delete autoregressively and the addition head that selects vertices to form a face to add. The addition head also adds vertices when needed. Untouched faces pass through unchanged, so the corrected mesh keeps the vertices and the layout of the draft. The draft enters as a prefix and only the edits are generated. A correction therefore takes far fewer decoding steps than generating every face again with an autoregressive mesh generator. We benchmark our method against repair tools on scripted defects and on held-out drafts from two mesh generators. Across both scripted defects and generated drafts, our method improves the quad-equivalent face F1, removes non-manifold faces, and cleans up the topology.

Operating Systems.title: Towards Virtual Networking for a Time-Triggered Hypervisor
Operating Systems.summary: Virtualization enables mixed-criticality applications to run on shared hardware by isolating them within separate virtual machines (VMs). However, achieving end-to-end timing guarantees for critical tasks hosted on virtual CPUs (VCPUs) without relying on static partitioning is hard. A possible solution is a time-triggered hypervisor that dispatches VMs' VCPUs to processor cores according to a predetermined global schedule. A global schedule includes the computation, the network, and the virtualization layer to provide end-to-end timing guarantees across hosts and VMs during design time. In this work, we propose a VirtIO-based virtual network that realizes IEEE 802.1Qbv quasi-compliant inter-VM communication, providing predictable timing for critical messages exchanged between time-triggered VMs. We present our VirtIO-based virtual network architecture and derive network-level scheduling constraints that emerge from the properties of the proposed solution. We implement the proposed design in the ACRN hypervisor and evaluate the end-to-end latency of critical traffic in a loaded network, demonstrating that our time-triggered VirtIO-net prototype provides predictable end-to-end latency under load.
Operating Systems.comment: Published at RTNS 2025. This is the author's version of the work

Hardware Architecture.title: HILO: Enabling Low-power, Dual-Band Communication using Tunnel Diode Oscillators
Hardware Architecture.summary: Wireless communication remains the most power-consuming operation in embedded systems. Low-power transmitters such as backscatter achieve microwatt-scale operation but produce weak signals susceptible to in-band interference and frequency-selective fading, particularly in non-line-of-sight settings. Multi-band transmission can mitigate these effects through spectral-domain redundancy rather than temporal-domain redundancy, improving reliability without sacrificing bitrate or latency. However, conventional multi-band radio transceivers require duplicated RF chains or power-hungry synthesizers. We introduce HILO, a tunnel diode-based frontend that enables dual-band operation from a single circuit. HILO inverts the conventional paradigm: rather than suppressing the harmonics inherent to tunnel diode nonlinearity, it harnesses them. An external device injection-locks the oscillator to a fundamental frequency, simultaneously stabilizing a higher harmonic and yielding two injection-locked carriers without a second oscillator or frequency multiplier. In transmit mode, HILO exploits self-oscillating mixing to modulate both carriers simultaneously; in receive mode, it uses autodyne downconversion at both frequencies. By turning an inherent nonlinearity into a feature, HILO achieves dual-band links while consuming under 210 $μ$W.
Hardware Architecture.comment: 6 pages, 12 figures. Accepted at the 2026 IEEE International Conference on RFID (IEEE RFID 2026)

Hardware Architecture.title: HULK: An Efficient Algorithm for Enabling Fast Bulk Bitwise Operations on Homomorphically Encrypted Data
Hardware Architecture.summary: A wide range of important cloud applications, e.g., database analytics, graph analytics, and genome analysis, spend a considerable amount of time performing bulk bitwise operations (e.g., AND, OR, XOR). These applications often operate on highly sensitive data, making data privacy a critical concern. Homomorphic encryption (HE) enables secure computation on encrypted data without requiring decryption, ensuring privacy in untrusted and shared environments. We analyze 13 end-to-end applications across three domains (healthcare, graph, and database analytics) and observe that bulk bitwise operations take 62-100% of the execution time of the healthcare and graph workloads. The key problem is that existing HE approaches perform them with high-latency homomorphic operations (e.g., multiplication or lookup tables) and significantly increase the data size. Our goal is to enable fast bulk bitwise operations on homomorphically encrypted data by designing an efficient HE algorithm that reduces the use of these costly operations. To this end, we propose HULK, which performs two key steps: (1) it constructs bulk bitwise operations using low-cost homomorphic additions, which compute the Hamming weight of the encrypted operand bits in every slot of a packed ciphertext without any homomorphic multiplication, and (2) it decodes the result of an AND, OR, or XOR from the Hamming weight with a single indicator polynomial, keeping the result in the standard encoding. Across 13 end-to-end applications in healthcare, graph, and database analytics, HULK improves performance over the arithmetic approach used by prior works by up to 7.26x (CPU) and 6.65x (GPU), and on average by 2.32x/1.78x/1.45x (CPU) and 2.08x/1.70x/1.51x (GPU) for healthcare/graph/database analytics. When we increase the reduction depth in a representative application, HULK's speedup grows to 10.10x over the state-of-the-art GPU baseline.
Hardware Architecture.comment: 24 pages, 10 figures, 3 tables. Code: https://github.com/CMU-SAFARI/HULK

Hardware Architecture.title: FPGA Based Design And Implementation of Neural Network Compensators for Nanocrystalline MEMS Pressure Sensor
Hardware Architecture.summary: In this paper the effects of nonlinearity and temperature of nanocrystalline MEMS pressure sensor have been compensated using neural network algorithm which has been implemented on a FPGA chip. The neural network employs back propagation algorithm to train the multilayer perceptron feed forward network that causes an error reduction due to temperature upto the level of 98%. It is realized on FPGA with pipelined architecture for parallel and fast sensing operation. The pressure sensor along with the FPGA based compensation results in an intelligent sensor system capable of high speed and accurate pressure measurement which has been tested for a typical biomedical application.
Hardware Architecture.comment: 6 pages

Hardware Architecture.title: PDAGENT-BENCH: Characterizing, Grounding, and Architecting LLM/VLM Agents for VLSI Physical Design
Hardware Architecture.summary: Large Language Models and vision-language models have shown remarkable success in the front-end design of Very Large-Scale Integrated Circuits, yet their capabilities for VLSI physical design remain significantly underexplored. The primary cause is the lack of standardized benchmarks for evaluating agentic physical design workflows that require high-dimensional, multi-stage optimization under strict design constraints, coordinated interaction with diverse Electronic Design Automation tools, and iterative refinement. This work introduces PDAGENT-BENCH, a comprehensive and multi-dimensional benchmark for evaluating LLM/VLM-based agents across the physical design stack. PDAGENT-BENCH integrates both task-level assessment and workflow-level execution. The benchmark suite contains 353 curated problems that combine conceptual questions with real-world industrial artifacts, with expert-validated references and executable solutions. In addition, the benchmark provides a unified, human-aligned agentic physical design workflow framework that enables closed-loop evaluation of holistic physical design in realistic EDA environments. Experiments on 11 state-of-the-art models reveal that while modern LLMs/VLMs perform competitively on conceptual tasks, they remain substantially limited in tool-centric execution (e.g., 42.2% on Innovus script generation) and long-horizon, multi-stage reasoning. Our studies further show that human-skill-enhanced agentic workflows significantly improve end-to-end physical design performance. PDAGENT-BENCH establishes a standardized, reproducible, and realistic evaluation framework for advancing LLM/VLM-driven holistic physical design automation. To ensure full reproducibility, we release \textsc{PDAgent-Bench} at https://github.com/fenggev56/PDAGENT-BENCH.

Hardware Architecture.title: TALU: A Reconfigurable Tiled-ALU Grid for RISC-V
Hardware Architecture.summary: Lane-based RISC-V vector processors exploit data parallelism well but pay a recurring cost for two common patterns: reductions, which require a separate tree pass, and deep dependent expression chains, which cannot be fused and are issued as serial vector instructions. We present TALU, a 5-stage RISC-V core whose execute stage is an NxN grid of registered ALU tiles instead of a single ALU. The grid is a reconfigurable, feed-forward spatial fabric: tiles route operands only from non-backward neighbours, and added diagonal forwarding lets a reduction collapse spatially. A minimal custom extension configures the per-tile operation, routing, and per-tile constants, and streams operands through the array. On a single fabric, TALU runs ordinary scalar code, single deep-path expressions, and multi-lane vector kernels. On the benchmark suite of the RISC-V2 vector processor, TALU is 1.8-5.5x faster than RISC-V2 and 4.5-15.5x faster than Vicuna at equal lane count, with a reduction cost (dot÷add) of 1.05x versus 1.96x and 1.26x for the vector cores. A retimed implementation places and routes at 1.03 GHz in 45 nm in 0.30 mm2, half the area of RISC-V2.
Hardware Architecture.comment: Submitted to the 2027 IEEE International Symposium on Circuits and Systems (ISCAS)

Hardware Architecture.title: AMAX: Accuracy-Aware Multi-Loop Asymmetric Perforation for Heterogeneous Architectures
Hardware Architecture.summary: Thermal constraints in heterogeneous multi-core systems can significantly degrade performance, as conventional techniques such as dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS) and task migration introduce overhead under high utilization. Approximate computing, particularly loop perforation, can mitigate this overhead by reducing computation at the cost of accuracy loss. However, existing approaches typically apply a uniform perforation rate across all loops, ignoring loop-specific sensitivity. We propose AMAX, an accuracy-aware multi-loop asymmetric perforation framework that reduces the combinational design space through loop-wise profiling and multi-objective configuration selection, and dynamically adapts the resulting configurations at runtime according to performance requirements. Experiments on PARSEC benchmarks show that {\em AMAX} achieves up to 0.85 improvement in normalized accuracy over symmetric perforation for the same performance targets.
Hardware Architecture.comment: To appear in the Proceedings of the IEEE Nordic Circuits and Systems Conference (NorCAS), Tampere, Finland, 2026

Hardware Architecture.title: CacheSmith: Accurate RAG Serving under Latency SLOs with Adaptive KV Reuse
Hardware Architecture.summary: This paper presents CacheSmith, a KV cache reuse system for RAG prefill that maximizes quality-gated SLO attainment. While context caching lowers prefill latency by reusing precomputed KV states for retrieved chunks, it misses cross-chunk attention that a full prefill would compute over concatenated inputs. Prior selective recomputation schemes tackle this problem but enforce static, one-size-fits-all configurations that fail to effectively handle request heterogeneity or dynamic latency budgets. CacheSmith decomposes selective recomputation into a three-phase workflow of WarmUp, Probe, and Patch that can be dynamically configured to exploit a wide range of cost-accuracy trade-offs. At serving time, an SLO-aware scheduler in CacheSmith forms batches to mitigate inter-request interference during layer-by-layer prefill, while a budget-aware planner configures recomputation phases across the batch to maximize the number of requests satisfying both generation quality and latency targets. Both components make fast, solver-free decisions over profiled cost-accuracy bands. On four benchmarks across varying arrival rates and burstiness levels, CacheSmith improves quality-gated SLO attainment by up to 27.5%, over four state-of-the-art baselines.

Programming Languages.title: FlowBook: Enforcing Reproducibility in Computational Notebooks
Programming Languages.summary:
Computational notebooks interleave code cells with their outputs and let users edit and execute cells in arbitrary order. This flexibility supports interactive exploration, but it also allows outputs to become inconsistent with the notebook's current code and data. Such inconsistencies can lead users to draw invalid scientific conclusions. We argue that notebooks should always be output consistent: every output should match what a top-to-bottom execution of the current code would produce. Forcing a top-to-bottom execution after each edit would guarantee this, but at prohibitive cost: such an execution can take minutes to hours.
  We present FlowBook, a dynamic analysis for Python notebooks that enforces output consistency without giving up out-of-order execution. FlowBook does this by enforcing a stronger property, rerun consistency: no location read by a cell may be written by any cell below it. Rerun consistency guarantees that rerunning a cell later, in any order, reproduces its current output. FlowBook tracks each cell's read and write sets at cell boundaries, blocks updates that would violate rerun consistency, and marks as stale any cell whose inputs may have changed. We prove that a notebook with no stale cells is both rerun and output consistent. Users remain free to execute cells in arbitrary order; the only restriction is that recorded outputs may not silently depend on the order in which cells were executed.
  Across 61 real-world notebooks, FlowBook flagged 203 rerun-inconsistent cells. Rerunning 62% led to output inconsistencies. A further 21% change notebook state with no visible output, which can affect the results of later edits and reruns; only 5% are false positives of FlowBook's conservative analysis. FlowBook's AI repair agent repaired all 203 cells with local edits and no human intervention. FlowBook's median overhead is only 26 ms per cell execution.

Programming Languages.title: Soliduzz: Finding Miscompilations in Smart-Contract Compilers with Assertion-Driven Equivalence Oracles
Programming Languages.summary:
Smart contracts compiled to the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) can manage high-value assets and are difficult to patch after deployment. Compiler miscompilations are therefore especially dangerous: compilation succeeds, but the generated bytecode does not preserve the semantics of the source program. Existing smart-contract compiler fuzzers either focus on robustness failures or rely on differential oracles that compare compiler configurations.
  We present Soliduzz, an approach for finding miscompilations in EVM smart-contract compilers using assertion-driven equivalence oracles. Soliduzz uses product programs to encode semantic equivalence as executable assertions. The key shift is to compile these self-checking programs and let off-the-shelf fuzzers and symbolic execution engines explore the resulting bytecode for assertion violations, without requiring compiler-specific support from the analyzer.
  Soliduzz instantiates this idea with two complementary families of metamorphic transformations. The first starts from equivalent expressions and lifts them into smart-contract code that deliberately exercises EVM-specific features such as storage, data locations, control flow, contract interactions, and inline assembly. The second generalizes Equivalence Modulo Inputs (EMI) from fixed concrete inputs to symbolic input spaces. Our symbolic EMI records coverage in the original computation and uses it to guard mutations in the transformed computation. Together, these transformations produce product programs that assert that paired computations yield the same outputs.
  We evaluate Soliduzz on three EVM smart-contract compilers (solc, solx, and vyper) using several analysis tools. Overall, Soliduzz exposes 29 bugs. Of these, 24 are compiler bugs: 6 miscompilations, 17 internal compiler errors, and 1 hang. The remaining 5 are bugs in the analysis tools.

Programming Languages.title: OpenMQPI: An MLIR-based Pipeline to Offload Quantum Circuits via OpenMP
Programming Languages.summary: Quantum computing introduces specialized software stacks and programming interfaces that are often tightly coupled to specific ecosystems and hardware backends, limiting interoperability and software reuse. For HPCQC application developers, this complicates the integration of quantum accelerators into existing applications. Existing quantum frameworks also use ecosystem-specific circuit representations and compilation pipelines, hindering integration with established heterogeneous compiler infrastructures. We propose OpenMQPI, an MLIR-based OpenMP extension for quantum programming that leverages OpenMP's standardized target offloading infrastructure to integrate quantum resources into HPC applications. OpenMQPI introduces QPIR, a lightweight MLIR dialect for representing quantum circuits within OpenMP target regions, and a compiler pipeline that performs quantum-specific optimizations and lowers circuits to executables compatible with OpenMP offloading. At runtime, an MQSS plugin enables the generated executable to offload quantum circuits to quantum hardware through the OpenMP target offloading model. We evaluate OpenMQPI using the VQE, QFT, and Deutsch-Jozsa algorithms with 5, 10, 15, and 20 qubits, comparing execution times against Qiskit and CUDA Quantum. OpenMQPI achieves the lowest average VQE execution time across all tested qubit configurations. At 20 qubits, it requires 5.18 s, compared with 5.83 s for Qiskit and 7.39 s for CUDA Quantum. For QFT and Deutsch-Jozsa, OpenMQPI achieves execution times comparable to Qiskit and lower than those of CUDA Quantum.

Programming Languages.title: From Rocq to Metal: A Pipeline for Formally Verified Microcontroller Firmware
Programming Languages.summary: Enforcing invariants in safety-critical firmware is increasingly urgent as generated code becomes widespread, but standard extraction targets for proof assistants require runtimes too large for many embedded devices. We present a pipeline for running formally verified Rocq firmware logic on Cortex-M microcontrollers. The pipeline extracts Gallina to Scheme, compiles it with Encore!, a bare-metal Continuation-Passing Style (CPS) bytecode virtual machine, and embeds the result in no_std Rust firmware. We structure applications as pure state-transition functions, so the business logic is proved in Rocq while the event/effect boundary, host callbacks, compiler, and VM remain explicit trusted components: no proof yet relates bytecode execution to Gallina semantics. On eight firmware workloads, from APDU parsing to a credential store, Encore! runs unmodified Rocq-extracted code within the 50 KiB RAM budget of ST33-class targets on every input size, where CertiRocq's generated code runs out of memory on the larger ones, at the price of up to 10 times more executed instructions than CertiRocq; a transaction-signing application is validated on physical Ledger Flex hardware.
Programming Languages.comment: Preprint: Accepted to the 19th International Conference on Verification and Evaluation of Computer and Communication Systems (VECoS 2026)

Programming Languages.title: Stdlib or Third-Party? Empirical Performance and Correctness of LLM-Assisted Zero-Dependency Python Libraries
Programming Languages.summary:
Third-party Python libraries introduce dependency-management overhead, supply-chain risk, and deployment friction. We study when eliminating a dependency preserves enough correctness and performance to justify the gains in footprint, deployability, and trust surface. Our testbed is zerodep, 44 single-file, stdlib-only Python modules spanning 12 categories, each benchmarked against its reference library.
  Three performance regimes emerge. Stdlib-only implementations achieve parity (within 2x) in the majority of cases; many outperform their references by 5x-115x where architectural overhead dominates; and a clear cliff appears for C-extension-backed computation (image processing, binary serialization, low-level crypto), confirmed by PyPy JIT and profiling experiments. Beyond speed, stdlib modules reduce installed footprint by orders of magnitude (median 31 KB vs. 700 KB), import 2.2x faster, and eliminate 88 transitive dependencies maintained by 128 distinct PyPI accounts.
  Analysis of the LLM-assisted development process across all 44 modules shows that specification completeness, not model capability, is a strong predictor of generation success, and that contract-linked review reduces review volume by 5x while eliminating compatibility regressions. Together, these results turn dependency elimination from an anecdotal coding style into an evidence-based engineering tradeoff.

Programming Languages.title: Compositional Information Geometry of Probabilistic Programs
Programming Languages.summary: We study the compositional, intensional information geometry of probabilistic programs. For a first-order probabilistic programming language with finite random variables, we construct a contravariant lax monoidal functor that, for a program of type $X \to Y$, pulls back a (degenerate) Riemannian metric on $Y$ to $X$. It specialises to the Fisher metric in the case of standard statistical models and to ordinary pullback in the case of deterministic programs. We further justify this construction in two ways. First, we show that this functor arises as a pullback of geometry from a universal space of programs over a type $Y$ with a fixed trace space. Second, we show that it is a special case of a more general pullback construction over weighted measures. Our compositional geometry depends on the presentation of the program, and we study how it relates to the (non-compositional) geometry of the realised measures by establishing a three-level inequality relating our score-velocity metric for the program, the program's corresponding output-conditioned metric, and the standard Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao metric of the realised family. Finally, we show how the theory can be extended to accommodate continuous random variables using diffeological quasi-Borel spaces. We also discuss several concrete directions for future work.

Programming Languages.title: QEDIA: Quantum Program Verification in Lean
Programming Languages.summary:
Practical quantum programs interleave quantum and classical computation: classical data shape the quantum operations that are performed, and measurement outcomes shape the classical computation that follows. Formal verification of such programs in a proof assistant requires mechanizing a program logic that handles this interplay consistently at every level, from the mathematics of quantum mechanics, through program syntax and semantics, to specifications and proof rules. Such mechanizations, along with the program proofs built on them, typically require substantial manual effort.
  We present QEDIA, a framework for verifying quantum programs with classical variables in Lean 4. At its foundation is an open library that formalizes the quantum Hoare logic QHL+ across all these levels and proves the logic sound for both partial and total correctness. We construct the library and the program proofs, under human supervision, using an LLM-based prover agent, whose general-purpose core we extend for quantum program verification. We illustrate QEDIA with verified programs including the quantum Fourier transform, phase estimation, repeat-until-success circuits, and Hamiltonian simulation.

Programming Languages.title: LLMON: An LLM-native Markup Language to Leverage Structure and Semantics at the LLM Interface
Programming Languages.summary:
Textual Large Language Models (LLMs) provide a simple and familiar interface: a string of text is used for both input and output. However, the information conveyed to an LLM often has a richer structure and semantics, which is not conveyed in a string. For example, most prompts contain both instructions ("Summarize this paper into a paragraph") and data (the paper to summarize), but these are usually not distinguished when passed to the model. This can lead to model confusion and security risks, such as prompt injection attacks.
  This work addresses this shortcoming by introducing an LLM-native mark-up language, LLMON (LLM Object Notation, pronounced "Lemon"), that enables the structure and semantic metadata of the text to be communicated in a natural way to an LLM. This information can then be used during model training, model prompting, and inference implementation, leading to improvements in model accuracy, safety, and security. This is analogous to how programming language types can be used for many purposes, such as static checking, code generation, dynamic checking, and IDE highlighting.
  We discuss the general design requirements of an LLM-native markup language, introduce the LLMON markup language and show how it meets these design requirements, describe how the information contained in a LLMON artifact can benefit model training and inference implementation, and provide some preliminary empirical evidence of its value for both of these use cases. We also discuss broader issues and research opportunities that are enabled with an LLM-native approach.

Programming Languages.title: LLMs program using Reusable and Composable Abstract Representations
Programming Languages.summary: When writing code, the same computation can be expressed in different programming languages and through different implementation strategies. We show that the activations of LLMs capture this shared structure in reusable and composable abstract representations when they generate code. These representations emerge in the middle layers, are reusable across programming languages, and afford the model an impressive amount of generalization ability when generating code under various interventions. Using activation steering, we show that function, programming language, and implementation strategy can be independently manipulated. The independent interventions on language and function can be flexibly composed to control code generation, even in cases when the prompt contains no information about language and function. We additionally find that finetuning on examples of arbitrarily defined functions in one programming language transfers to other languages, consistent with the models reusing abstract features of code generation that are shared across different examples. Finally, to study how such abstract representations come to be, we implement a minimal model of shared, reusable, and composable structure in a synthetic setting, and show that transformers trained on such data learn representations that reuse these parts flexibly across contexts.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Settling the Approximability of Submodular Facility Location
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: In submodular facility location (SFL), introduced by Svitkina and Tardos (SODA 2006), clients $\cal C$ in a metric space are assigned to facilities $\cal F$. A facility serving a set $S \subseteq \cal C$ of clients incurs cost $g(S)$, where $g$ is a monotone submodular function common to all facilities. The best known approximation factor for SFL is $O(\log\log|\cal C|)$, due to Abbasi, Adamczyk, Bosch-Calvo, Byrka, Grandoni, Sornat, and Tinguely (ICALP 2024), improving on the $O(\log|\cal C|)$-approximation of Svitkina and Tardos. We show that this is best possible up to a constant factor in the value-oracle model by showing that there exists no algorithm with only polynomially many queries to $g$ with approximation ratio $o(\log\log|\cal C|)$. This bound holds for algorithms with unlimited computation time, and when $g$ is restricted to matroid rank functions. We also show that the natural linear programming relaxation has an integrality gap of $Θ(\log\log|\cal C|)$. Our lower bound follows by constructing an extension of Vondrák's symmetry-gap approach (FOCS 2009) for matroid rank functions.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: An initial proof of a constant-factor lower bound was obtained using ChatGPT 6.1 Astra. The stronger result shown in the paper was obtained in conversations with Claude Opus 5.5 and ChatGPT 6.1 Astra. The authors have improved the presentation and simplified the arguments. 25 pages, 2 figures

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Bipartite Matching with Few Rounds of Demand Queries
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We study the randomised and deterministic demand-query complexity of approximate bipartite matching with few query rounds. The demand-query model, introduced in [Blumrosen and Nisan SICOMP 2009; Nisan SODA 2021], is inspired by combinatorial auctions and welfare maximisation, where an oracle returns the first neighbouring vertex (item) of a vertex u (agent) according to a given permutation pi (preference ordering of the agent over the items).
  For randomised algorithms, our main result gives a trade-off between the number of rounds k, the per-round query budget q=n^{1+δ}, and the achievable approximation ratio. Let 1 <= k <= log n, and -1 <= delta <= 1/k. Every k-round randomised algorithm using O(q) demand queries per round has a worst-case expected-size approximation factor of Omega(n^{1/2k-delta/2}/k). Conversely, we give a randomised algorithm achieving approximation factor O(n^{(1-k*delta)/(k+1)}/k) in expectation.
  For deterministic algorithms, for k*q >= n, we show that the optimal deterministic approximation factor is ~Theta(n^2/(q*k^2)), thereby improving the previous lower bound of [Nisan SODA 2021] by a polynomial factor over a wide range of parameters. In particular, for q=Theta(n), we improve the deterministic round-complexity lower bound for constant-factor approximation from ~Omega(n^{1/3}) to ~Omega(sqrt n). Our algorithms produce matching and vertex-cover certificates; the deterministic trade-off also extends to minimum vertex cover and maximum fractional matching.
  We extend the randomised upper bounds to the weaker Demand-OR model [Nisan 2021]. We prove a non-adaptive simulation of uniform random-neighbour queries using known techniques, avoiding the O(log n)-round penalty of the trivial binary-search simulation. Consequently, our upper bounds yield the same k-round approximation guarantees using O(q * log^2 n) Demand-OR queries per round.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Two Holes Make a Difference: Deterministic Paging with Delay and Deadlines
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
In this paper, we study online paging with delay or deadlines. In online paging with delay, an online algorithm manages a cache of size $k$ and needs to serve incoming requests by adding the requested pages to the cache. In addition, it has the option to delay serving incoming requests at a cost that depends on the delay. We propose a new online algorithm, which combines a threshold rule with first-in, first-out (FIFO) replacement, and show that it is $(2k+2)$-competitive for cache size $k$. This result corrects a previously published claim that the competitive ratio is exactly $2k+1$ regardless of the number of holes (pages outside the cache). However, in the case of one hole, we show that the FIFO rule with a different threshold is indeed $(2k+1)$-competitive, giving a tight result.
  In the case of deadlines, the same analysis gives a deadline-triggered algorithm that is $(k+1)$-competitive in general and $k$-competitive if there is only one hole. Moreover, we show that the second hole makes paging with deadlines strictly harder than classical paging, where the competitive ratio is independent of the number of holes. For paging with deadlines, we prove a deterministic lower bound of $k+\tfrac12$, already for two holes. We show that, as a consequence, no threshold-triggered algorithm can achieve a competitive ratio less than $2k+\frac32$ in general.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Policy Iteration Is Not Strongly Polynomial for Deterministic Markov Decision Processes: The Price of Algorithmic Anarchy
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We establish exponential iteration lower bounds in the number of states for Howard's policy iteration on deterministic discounted and average-reward Markov decision processes (MDPs), with a constant number of actions per state. This rules out strong polynomiality of Howard's policy iteration in both settings. We further prove that a Dantzig counterpart of Howard's policy iteration runs in strongly polynomial time on deterministic average-reward MDPs. Together with the known strongly polynomial bound for Dantzig's rule on deterministic discounted MDPs, these results establish an exponential separation between the two algorithms in both settings. This separation between Howard's decentralized and simultaneous selfish improvements and Dantzig's coordinated selection of a single action with the largest improvement across all states reveals a ``price'' of algorithmic anarchy.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: Added results on average-reward MDPs and extended the discounted lower bounds to constant-bit integer rewards

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Selecting the 7th Smallest of 16 Elements Takes Exactly 28 Comparisons
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Let $V_i(n)$ denote the minimum worst-case number of comparisons needed to find the $i$-th smallest of $n$ distinct elements. We construct algorithms showing $V_7(16)\le28$ and $V_8(16)\le29$, improving the previously reported upper bounds of 30 and 31. Together with known lower bounds, these results establish $V_7(16)=28$ and leave $V_8(16)\in\{28,29\}$. For 17 elements, we establish $V_5(17)=27$ and improve the upper bounds for ranks 6 through 9 to 29, 30, 31, and 31, respectively. Every new upper bound has an explicit decision-graph certificate verified by a static checker developed independently of the search. We also derive a lower bound for selection from a partially ordered state by combining the Fussenegger-Gabow weight with its order-reversed counterpart. All new upper bounds and this lower bound are formally verified in Lean 4. For $V_8(16)$, we show that a lower bound based solely on the total number of decision-tree leaves cannot establish $V_8(16)\ge29$. The algorithms were found using fixed-budget search, information-guided comparison ordering, and proof-number search. Proof-number search was decisive in finding the 28-comparison algorithm; in our experiments, refuting a comparison budget remained substantially more expensive than finding an algorithm within it.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: 11 pages, 1 figure, 4 tables. Code, certificates and Lean proofs: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23346948

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Optimal Support Size Testing
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We present an optimal tester for support size that determines whether an unknown probability distribution is supported on $n$ elements or $\varepsilon$-far away (in total variation distance) with sample complexity $Θ(\frac{n}{\varepsilon\log(n)})$, improving the prior best $O(\frac{n}{\varepsilon\log(n)} \log(\min\{\frac{1}{\varepsilon}, n\}))$ due to Ferreira Pinto Jr. and Harms (STOC 2025). As a generalization, we provide a pretty good lower bound on support size.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Exploring Minimal Blocking Sets for Kernelization Lower Bounds for $\mathcal{F}$-Minor Deletion
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
For Vertex Cover, a minimal blocking set of a graph $G$ is an inclusion-wise minimal vertex set contained in no minimum vertex cover of $G$. Bougeret et al. [SIDMA 2022] showed that, for all minor-closed graph classes $\mathcal{G}$, Vertex Cover has a polynomial kernel parameterized by the distance to $\mathcal{G}$ if and only if $\mathcal{G}$ has bounded minimal blocking sets.
  In this work, we explore how far this connection between minimal blocking sets and kernelization extends to $\mathcal{F}$-Minor Deletion parameterized by the deletion distance to $\mathcal{G}$. A minimal $\mathcal{F}$-blocking set of $G$ is a minimal vertex set not contained in any optimal $\mathcal{F}$-Minor Deletion solution of $G$. For connected families $\mathcal{F}$, we show that if some graph class $\mathcal{G}$ closed under disjoint union has unbounded minimal $\mathcal{F}$-blocking sets, then $\mathcal{F}$-Minor Deletion parameterized by the deletion distance to $\mathcal{G}$ has no polynomial kernel. This generalizes a result of Hols et al. [SIDMA 2022] for Vertex Cover. We then show that this criterion does not capture all kernelization lower bounds for $\mathcal{F}$-Minor Deletion, even for minor-closed graph classes. Motivated by the work of Dekker and Jansen [Discrete Appl. Math. 2024], we study the more general notion of extended $\mathcal{F}$-blocking sets and the kernelization lower bounds they yield.
  For every fixed integer $η\geq 1$, Pw-$η$ Deletion is the problem of deleting at most $k$ vertices to reduce the pathwidth to at most $η$. We show that it has no polynomial kernel parameterized by the distance to graphs with pathwidth at most $η+1$. Moreover, for connected families $\mathcal{F}$, we show that $\mathcal{F}$-Minor Deletion parameterized by the distance to graphs with pathwidth at most $\max_{F\in\mathcal{F}} pw(F)+1$ has no polynomial kernel.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: Full version of an IPEC 2026 contribution. Abstract has been shortened for arXiv

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Semi-Streaming Estimation of the Held--Karp Bound and Graph-Metric TSP Cost
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
The Held--Karp bound is a linear-programming lower bound for the metric traveling salesperson problem (TSP). We approximate this bound in the multi-pass insertion-only streaming model for metrics induced by connected positive-weight graphs. For an $n$-vertex, $m$-edge graph and $0<\eps\le1/2$, the algorithm returns a $(1+\eps)$ upper approximation with high probability, using $\wtO(\eps^{-4})$ passes, $\wtO(n\eps^{-2})$ words, and $\wtO(m\eps^{-4})$ arithmetic operations per pass.
  We replace the changing edge-weight vector by a short history of multiplicative-weights (MWU) updates. After initialization, updates repeat until a column is removed. We store each repeated update once, with its repetition count. The record length depends on the number of columns, not updates; the argument applies to any fixed nonnegative matrix. For Held--Karp, tree-path queries recover edge weights from these records. Separate search and update thresholds allow fresh sparsifiers at successive search stages. Controlled rounding gives a bounded-precision implementation.
  The estimate yields a $(3/2+\eps)$ graph-metric TSP value estimate and a $(7/5+\eps)$ estimate when the input graph is unweighted. Conversely, in weighted graph streams, every one-pass $(1+η)$ upper approximation to Held--Karp, for fixed $0\leη<1$, requires quadratic space. The algorithms estimate values; they do not construct tours within these bounds.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Sublinear-Time and Semi-Streaming Algorithms for Path Cover and TSP
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We give improved sublinear-time and semi-streaming approximation algorithms for maximum path cover, $(1,2)$-TSP, and Max-TSP. For each fixed $\eps>0$, our distance-query algorithm estimates the optimum cost of an $n$-vertex $(1,2)$-TSP instance from above within factor $2-\cstar+\eps=1.413184\ldots+\eps$, with high probability, in $n^{2-Ω_\eps(1)}$ time, where $\cstar=2(\sec1-\tan1)$. This improves the $3/2+\eps$ factor of direct matching estimation in this subquadratic regime~\cite{BhattacharyaKissSaranurak2023} and of the faster near-linear estimator~\cite{BehnezhadEtAl2024}. A single random vertex order defines an implicit bipartite graph whose matchings project to path covers. An alternating-permutation analysis shows that its expected maximum matching size is at least $\cstar$ times the optimum path-cover size. On long paths, even the best of polynomially many uniform orders retains only a $\cstar+o(1)$ fraction with high probability.
  In semi-streaming, we construct deterministic $(5/7-\eps)$-approximate unweighted path covers and $(9/7+\eps+5/(7n))$-approximate $(1,2)$-TSP tours, improving the respective $2/3-\eps$ and $4/3+\eps+1/n$ guarantees in~\cite{AlipourFarokhnejadMoemke2025}. For nonnegative weights, we obtain $2/3-\eps$ for path cover and Max-TSP, improving the earlier asymptotic $7/12-\eps$ Max-TSP bound. These algorithms use $\poly(1/\eps)$ passes independent of $n$ and $O(n\log(n/\eps)\poly(1/\eps))$ words. We compute two approximate matchings separated by edge deletion. A cycle-compensation lemma accounts for the weight removed when breaking their cycles. For unweighted graphs, a third approximate matching on a simple auxiliary graph with at most $2n$ vertices chooses component connections; a Tutte--Berge count proves the stronger bound.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: A Randomized Approximation Algorithm for Doubly Free-Boundary Macdonald Processes
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We construct an approximate sampler for finite doubly free-boundary Macdonald rail-yard processes with Macdonald, boundary, and edge parameters in $(0,1)$. The construction allows arbitrary finite sequences of additions and removals of horizontal or vertical strips and all four boundary types. It reverses a finite commutation--reflection history from a partition sequence whose entries are equal, with the common partition weighted by both boundaries. We derive local reconstruction kernels from the skew Cauchy, Littlewood, and branching identities. Bulk and boundary updates combine integer increments with conditional shape sampling at a prescribed size; same-sign swaps use finite conditional resampling.
  For $K$ reflection periods and an initial partition-size cutoff $M$, the algorithm terminates almost surely and samples the resulting approximating law exactly. We prove total variation convergence to the target process as $K,M\to\infty$ and give explicit bounds for both truncation errors, decaying geometrically in the cutoffs for fixed input parameters. Under fixed parameter bounds, we also bound the expected operation count of direct enumeration in a unit-cost model.
  We further construct an exact rejection sampler for the initial partition law without a size cutoff or evaluation of its normalizing constant. Using this sampler removes the size-truncation error, leaving only the error from the finite reflection history.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Subgaussian Vector Balancing by an Ising Model
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We show that the guaranties of the Gram-Schmidt Walk Algorithm of Bansal, Dadush, Garg, and Lovett can be achieved by an Ising model. Given vectors $v_1, \ldots, v_n$ of norm less than 1, we give a closed form for a centrally symmetric distribution on a vector $σ\in \{\pm 1 \}^n$ so that the signed sum $\sum_j σ(j) v_j$ is $1$-subgaussian. We show that the Glauber dynamics for this model mix rapidly provided that the norms of the input vectors are bounded below 1 by an inverse-polynomial.
  The proofs employ the theory of Lorentzian polynomials, and we use these techniques to show fast mixing bounds for other spin systems.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Adding an Edge in a $P_4$-sparse Graph
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
For a graph family~${\cal F}$, the minimum ${\cal F}$-completion problem asks for the minimum number of non-edges to be added to a given graph~$G$ so that the resulting graph belongs to the family~${\cal F}$. This problem is NP-complete for many subclasses of perfect graphs, while polynomial solutions are available for minimal completion sets or restricted input.
  We study the minimum $P_4$-sparse completion problem that arises after adding a prescribed non-edge to a \(P_4\)-sparse graph \(G\), with the resulting graph required to remain \(P_4\)-sparse. For the case in which $G$ consists of two connected components, each containing one endpoint of the added non-edge, we characterize the possible forms of an optimal solution. Combining this characterization with the solution of the other cases identified by the structural decomposition of \(P_4\)-sparse graphs, we obtain an algorithm for the general problem that runs in $O(n^2)$ time and $O(n)$ space.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Solving SAT via Treewidth Backdoors in Linear Time: Beyond Sparsity
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
The Boolean Satisfiability (SAT) problem is a remarkably expressive computational problem, serving both as a cornerstone of complexity theory and as a unifying language for a wide range of search and reasoning tasks. While $\mathrm{NP}$-complete in general, SAT is well known to be linear-time solvable on instances with bounded treewidth. This motivates the search for "hidden" tree-like structures in formulas---for instance by detecting so-called weak $t$-treewidth backdoors. Such backdoors are sets of $k$ variables that can be assigned in such a way that the remaining instance has treewidth at most $t$ and is satisfiable whenever the original instance is.
  Ever since Gaspers and Szeider [ICALP 2012] showed that finding a weak $t$-treewidth backdoor for a SAT formula is $\mathrm{W}[2]$-hard with respect to $k$, tractability results have been restricted to structurally sparse formulas---most notably, a linear-time algorithm for $d$-SAT (bounded clause-length SAT) by Fomin, Lokshtanov, Misra, Ramanujan, and Saurabh [SODA 2015] and a non-uniform polynomial-time algorithm when the incidence graph of the input formula belongs to a nowhere-dense graph class (or more generally is $K_{d,d}$-free) by Lokshtanov, Panolan, and Ramanujan [ICALP 2022].
  In this paper, we push the tractability boundaries of finding weak $t$-treewidth backdoors beyond sparsity and into the regime of "well-behaved" dense formulas. Aiming towards relaxing structural input restrictions from nowhere-dense to edge-stable graph classes, as featured in the theory of beyond sparsity for FO model checking, or to bounded VC-dimension set systems, we identify signed semi-ladder-freeness as the correct dense structural restriction that establishes the boundary between tractability and intractability along this line.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Stochastic Network Speed Scaling with Competitive Ratios Independent of the Network
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: In network speed scaling, jobs arrive over time at a network of servers whose speeds can be tuned, every job must be processed by the servers along one of its allowed routes, and the goal is to minimize the total flow time plus the total energy. For stochastic arrivals, the competitive ratio of Vaze and Nair depends on the network, through the lengths of the routes it uses. We show that this dependence can be removed: we give an algorithm, which routes the jobs by solving a convex program and runs every server at a fixed speed, whose competitive ratio depends only on the power functions; for $P(s)=s^2$, it is at most the golden ratio $\varphi\approx1.618$. The key idea is a lower bound on the optimal cost which, like the cost of our algorithm, is a sum over the servers of a function of each server's load, so the analysis reduces to a single server. We also show that the routing rule of Vaze and Nair can be a factor $Ω(L)$ away from optimal, where $L$ is the length of the longest route.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Almost Optimal Relative Error Streaming Quantiles with Full Mergeability
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
Quantile summaries provide a scalable way to estimate the distribution of individual attributes in large datasets that are often distributed across multiple machines or generated by sensor networks.
