The state-of-the-art summaries with \emph{relative error guarantees} of $\pm \varepsilon\cdot \mathrm{rank}$, offering increasingly higher accuracy towards the distribution's tails, are ReqSketch (Cormode et al., JACM 2023) and the recent streaming algorithm by Gribelyuk et al. (SODA 2025). For inputs of size $N$ and probability $δ$ of exceeding the error bound, ReqSketch achieves space of $O(\varepsilon^{-1}\cdot \log^{1.5}(\varepsilon N)\cdot \sqrt{\log δ^{-1}})$ memory words, and offers \emph{full mergeability}, allowing distributed or parallel processing of datasets. In contrast, the latter algorithm exceeds the lower bound of $Ω(\varepsilon^{-1}\cdot \log(\varepsilon N)\cdot \log\logδ^{-1})$ from (Cormode \& Veselý, PODS 2020) only by a factor of $O(\log\varepsilon^{-1}\cdot (\log \varepsilon^{-1} + \log\log N)\cdot\log^2\logδ^{-1})$, but it lacks the mergeability property, is substantially more involved than ReqSketch, and has unclear practical performance. Both of these data structures consist of relative compactors from ReqSketch that subsample the stream in a structured way and work well in the streaming setting but are difficult to analyze under mergeability.
  We design a new relative-error quantile summary that achieves full mergeability and also improves the state-of-the-art streaming space bound to $$O(\varepsilon^{-1}\cdot \log(\varepsilon N) \cdot\log \log δ^{-1} \cdot (\log \varepsilon^{-1} + \log \log(\varepsilon N) + \log \log δ^{-1})),$$ which is substantially closer to the lower bound. At the same time, our data structure is simpler than the algorithm from (Gribelyuk et al., SODA 2025) and therefore more suitable for implementation.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: To appear in SODA 2027; this paper is reuses some parts of the earlier manuscript at arXiv:2511.17396

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: A Deterministic Near-Linear Time Approximation Algorithm for Restricted Shortest Paths in Directed Graphs
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
In the restricted shortest paths problem, we are given an $n$-vertex $m$-edge directed graph $G$ whose edges are assigned two non-negative weights (or resources) called lengths and costs, a source vertex $s$, and a cost threshold $C$. The goal is to find, for each target vertex $t$, the length of the shortest $(s,t)$-path whose total cost is at most $C$.
  Ashvinkumar, Bernstein, and Karczmarz (SODA 2025) gave the first randomized bicriteria $(1+\varepsilon,1+\varepsilon)$-approximate algorithm on directed graphs running in sub-$mn$ time, answering a problem posed by Bernstein (SODA 2012). We substantially improve this on two fronts, supplying a deterministic bicriteria $(1+\varepsilon,1+\varepsilon)$-approximate algorithm running in near-linear time.
  Our approach straightforwardly generalizes to more than two resources. For $k$ resources, a deterministic $(1+\varepsilon_1,\ldots,1+\varepsilon_k)$-approximate algorithm running in near-linear time is possible, with $\varepsilon_1=\ldots=\varepsilon_k=\varepsilon$.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: A Practical Combinatorial Interior Point Method for Minimum-Cost Flow
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: In a recent breakthrough, Chen, Kyng, Liu, Peng, Probst Gutenberg, and Sachdeva (arXiv:2203.00671) designed the first almost-linear-time algorithm for minimum-cost flow. Their approach uses an Interior Point Method (IPM) to achieve complexity $m^{1+o(1)}\log U \log C$. However, the $m^{1+o(1)}$ factor hides intricate recursive data structures, large constants and multiple log factors. In this paper, we give an implementation following the core ideas of their IPM with practical data structures and empirically obtained decision rules. We compare our solver with the cost scaling and network simplex solvers of LEMON on the instance families of the DIMACS Flow Challenge 2.0 core benchmark. Our implementation scales competitively on five of twelve families and better on two. On grid_wide we observe close to linear scaling: $m^{1.04}$ against $m^{1.48}$ for LEMON. We read these results as first evidence that the almost-linear-time framework can be relevant in practice, discuss our insights gained during the implementation process, and motivate where future work should focus to bridge the theory-practice gap.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: Submitted to the 13th DIMACS Implementation Challenge: Network Flows 2.0

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: The Complexity of Hamiltonian Cycles and Paths with Prescribed Walk Lengths
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Fix a set $S$ of positive integers. An $S$-Hamiltonian cycle is a cyclic ordering of all vertices of a graph such that each consecutive pair is joined by a walk whose length belongs to $S$. We study the complexity of deciding whether an input graph admits such an ordering, together with the corresponding path variants with prescribed or unrestricted endpoints. We complete the complexity classification for undirected graphs. In particular, we prove NP-completeness for every finite nonempty set of odd lengths, resolving an open problem posed by Amarilli, Lombardo, and Monet (WG 2026). For digraphs, all three problems are NP-complete for every fixed finite nonempty $S$ and admit linear-time algorithms when $S$ is cofinite. For other fixed infinite sets $S$, we establish NP-complete and undecidable cases, with undecidability occurring even when $S$ is recursive.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: No Truly Sublogarithmic-Round Algorithm for Distributed MIS in the LOCAL Model
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We prove that $o(\frac{\log n}{\log\log n})$-round randomized LOCAL algorithms find a maximal independent set (MIS) with subconstant probability on some input. This shows that the 40-year-old $O(\log n)$-round randomized CONGEST algorithm of Luby and Alon, Babai, and Itai is nearly optimal. Our lower bound improves upon the $Ω(\sqrt{\log n})$-round lower bound of Khoury and Schild and nearly closes the 20+ year-old gap between the $O(\log n)$-round algorithm and the $Ω(\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{\log\log n}})$-round lower bound of Kuhn, Moscibroda, and Wattenhofer.
  To close this gap, one must show a lower bound for a graph that is not locally treelike. We do this by starting with a $D$-regular, $Θ(\log_D n)$-girth graph, with $D = Θ(\log n)$. Crucially, this is not our final graph. We obtain our hard instance by \emph{replacing} each vertex of this treelike graph with a clique on $n^c$ vertices for some constant $c \in (0,1)$. We then replace each edge with a bipartite Erdős--Rényi graph between the corresponding cliques, with each edge present independently with probability $1/2$.
  We analyze arbitrary LOCAL algorithms on our non-treelike hard instance with a novel round elimination approach. We describe algorithms that output a set of vertices in this graph using two metrics: their \emph{occupancy probability} and their \emph{conflict probability}. Our round elimination framework takes an $r$-round algorithm and produces an $(r-1)$-round algorithm where occupancy and conflict probabilities collectively slightly degrade, but individually can significantly improve or degrade. This round elimination result is obtained by exploiting the lack of large biclique complements in dense bipartite Erdős--Rényi graphs, which in turn allows us to bound the entropy of the output distribution for any independent set algorithm.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: 34 pages, 2 figures. Abstract shortened due to arXiv requirements

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: A Better-than-2 Approximation for k-Median Part I: The Power of General Bids
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
The Greedy algorithm of Jain, Mahdian, Markakis, Saberi, and Vazirani was the best Lagrangian-multiplier-preserving (LMP) approximation algorithm for facility location, and thus the engine behind the best $k$-median guarantees, for over two decades. Its $2$-LMP guarantee was only recently broken by a small amount ($(2-η)$-LMP where $η\approx 2.25 \cdot 10^{-7}$) through local-search post-processing. That analysis relies on the structure of worst-case instances, and it appears difficult to obtain substantial further improvements along those lines.
  We take a different approach and change the algorithm itself: we introduce general bidding functions, replacing the classical linear bid with a richer family of rules and prove a polynomial-time $1.95$-LMP approximation, a large improvement over the long-standing factor of~$2$.
  We further show that these generalized bidding rules can be made smooth (log-adaptive), building on the recent framework developed for the classical Greedy algorithm by Cohen-Addad, Grandoni, Lee, Schwiegelshohn, and Svensson. This yields a polynomial-time $1.95$-approximation that opens $k+O_\varepsilon(\log n)$ centers. Combined with a $(1.89+\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithm for stable instances in our companion work \cite{stableinstances}, we achieve a better-than-2 approximation for the $k$-median problem in polynomial-time.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: On the Parameterized Complexity of Capacitated Stack and Queue Layouts with Colored Edges
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Stack and queue layouts are two extensively studied and complementary linear representations of graphs. A stack (queue) layout $\langle \prec, σ\rangle$ of a graph $G$ consists of a total ordering $\prec$ of its vertices and of a partitioning $σ$ of its edges into pages, such that no two independent edges on the same page cross (nest). We propose a generalized model with colored edges (one color per edge) and capacitated pages. Namely, the input graph is equipped with colored edges and a prescribed budget for each page-color pair $(p,c)$ - this budget determines the maximum number of edges of color $c$ that page $p$ can accept. This model is motivated by fair allocation scenarios where budgets can be used to control the share of monochromatic edges on each page. Unfortunately, it is known that deciding whether a stack (queue) layout exists is NP-hard already with two (one) pages. Thus, we focus on the fixed-order setting - where the linear order $\prec$ is part of the input - for which an ordinary 2-page stack or $\ell$-page queue layout can be computed in polynomial time. Despite the restrictive setting, we show that both capacitated problems are NP-complete already for two pages. Furthermore, we study the complexity of the problems when parameterized by the number of pages, colors, and/or the structure of the edge conflict graph with respect to the fixed linear order $\prec$. Our analysis paints a detailed complexity landscape and uncovers a surprisingly intricate interplay between the considered parameters.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Inclusion-wise extremal knapsack problems are (mostly) hard to approximate
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We study two inclusion-wise extremal variants of the 0-1 Knapsack Problem (KP). Given $n$ items with integer weights and nonnegative costs or profits, the Minimum-Cost Maximal Knapsack Packing Problem seeks a minimum-cost packing for capacity $c$ to which no item can be added, while the Maximum-Profit Minimal Knapsack Cover Problem seeks a maximum-profit cover for threshold $d$ from which no item can be removed. Both problems are weakly $\mathrm{NP}$-hard and pseudo-polynomially solvable, as is the classical KP, but their approximability is fundamentally different: unless $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}$, with positive values neither problem admits a polynomial-time $2^{p(n)}$-approximation for any polynomial $p$; allowing zero values rules out every multiplicative factor. Even with unit costs for packing and unit profits for covering, neither admits an $n^{1-\varepsilon}$-approximation for any fixed $\varepsilon>0$, whereas a trivial $n$-approximation exists. We identify restrictions that restore approximability. If every item weighs at least a fixed fraction of the capacity, respectively of the threshold, both problems can be solved exactly in polynomial time. For the cover problem, if each weight $w_i$ satisfies $w_i-1\geδ(d-1)$, we give an approximation scheme for arbitrary profits whose running time is polynomial in $n$, $1/\varepsilon$, and $1/δ$. If values equal weights, a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme (FPTAS) was already known for the packing problem; we give an FPTAS for the cover problem, improving on the previously known factor $2$. If value-to-weight ratios differ by at most a factor $κ$, we obtain a $(1+\varepsilon)κ$-approximation for both problems.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Exact power indices for plurality-voting ensembles
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Plurality-voting ensembles aggregate the predictions of multiple base classifiers and output the most voted class, with ties typically broken at random. Despite the simple aggregation rule, attributing the impact of each base classifier to the ensemble's predictions is far from straightforward. That is, a single base classifier's impact depends on how it interacts with the votes of all other classifiers in the ensemble, for example, in resolving ties, and not only on its own predictions. We address the attribution problem using established tools from cooperative game theory, studying the Banzhaf and Shapley power indices for new games modeling plurality voting and random tie-breaking, for binary and multiclass classification settings. Computing power indices is, in general, intractable. Surprisingly, our methods, collectively named ENPOWER, enable the exact computation of Banzhaf and Shapley values in linear time for the binary classification setting and in low-degree polynomial time for the multiclass setting. The algorithms in ENPOWER rely on new combinatorial formulations of the Banzhaf and Shapley indices, yielding closed-form solutions for the binary case and ordinary generating function representations for the multiclass case. We validate empirically the methods in ENPOWER demonstrating their high applicability, providing attribution values not captured by existing methods. We apply the attribution of ENPOWER to: ensemble pruning and prompt-based ensembling of vision-language models.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: Extended version of a work accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 59 pages, 9 figures, 11 tables

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Mining Correlated Motifs with Wildcards in PPI Networks: Exact and Optimal
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
A protein-protein interaction (PPI) network is a graph whose nodes are protein sequences and whose edges represent physical interactions between proteins. Correlated Motif Mining (CMM) seeks pairs of sequence motifs whose co-occurrence in interacting proteins reveals binding sites and interaction mechanisms. Formally, in the $(\ell,d)$-CMM problem, we are given a graph $G=(V,E)$, with $V\subseteqΣ^*$ for an alphabet $Σ$, and integers $0\leq d<\ell$, and we seek a pair $\{X,Y\}$ of motifs, each of length $\ell$ and containing $d$ wildcards, that maximizes a support measure $f(G,\{X,Y\})$; e.g., the count $f_E$ of edges $\{u,v\}\in E$ such that $X$ matches a substring of $u$ and $Y$ matches a substring of $v$, or vice versa. Although existing approaches have produced biologically meaningful results, they are either inefficient or heuristic-based, as the underlying optimization problem is NP-hard.
  Here, we revisit $(\ell,d)$-CMM. For $d=0$, we give an exact $\mathcal{O}(N^2)$-time and $\mathcal{O}(N)$-space algorithm, where $N$ is the total length of the node strings, and prove that this time is conditionally optimal under the Strong Exponential-Time Hypothesis. For any $d>0$, we give an exact $\mathcal{O}\!\left(\binom{\ell}{d}^2N^2\right)$-time and $\mathcal{O}(N)$-space algorithm, and observe that the problem is W[1]-hard parameterized by $d$. The latter algorithm improves the state of the art by exponentially large factors in both time and space. We further demonstrate experimentally that our algorithms are practical on real-world PPI networks and find significantly higher-scoring motif pairs than the state of the art. Moreover, we show that our algorithms find many top-scoring motif pairs that the state of the art misses entirely. Taken together, our results suggest that exact CMM with wildcards is more tractable in practice than previously assumed.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Jumbled Simon's Equivalence and Embeddings
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: \emph{Jumbled scattered factors} are a generalisation of scattered factors (or subsequences) where a jumbled scattered factor is obtained from another word by deleting and rearranging letters. For limiting the number of rearrangements, we distinguish $\ell$-jumbled scattered factors where $\ell$ limits the number of letters that may occur rearranged. For instance, $\mathtt{car}$, $\mathtt{start}$, $\mathtt{rat}, \mathtt{cat}$ are jumbled scattered factors of $\mathtt{abstract}$ even though $\mathtt{car}$, $\mathtt{start}$ and $\mathtt{cat}$ are no scattered factors and each need one jumble. An example for a jumbled scattered factor with $2$ jumbles is $\mathtt{tatar}$. In this work, we investigate two problems on jumbled scattered factors from an algorithmic perspective. First, we give algorithms for testing jumbled Simon's equivalence where two words are equivalent if they share the same $\ell$-jumbled scattered factors up to length $k$. Second, we investigate how to count the possible occurrences of a jumbled scattered factor -- the jumbled binomial coefficient. After defining the jumbled binomial coefficient, we study jumbled embeddings and factorisations of such as well.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: PHastR: Faster Minimal Perfect Hashing with Rotated Layouts
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We present PHastR, a minimal perfect hash function of the PHast family. Like PHast+, the fast-to-build variant of PHast, PHastR finds feasible seeds with bit-parallel operations: its seeds move keys along rings of slots, and to evaluate the seeds of a bucket it cyclically shifts, for each key, a word recording which slots of its ring are used. Unlike PHast+, however, it avoids self-collisions, which make two keys of a bucket collide for (almost) all its seeds: more than a third of the buckets bumped by PHast+ with wrapping and multiplier 3 contain one. With 8-bit seeds, PHastR uses $1.94$ bits per key, the same space as the best variant of PHast+ with wrapping, but it is built in $37\%$ of the time, and its queries are $28\%$ faster on $10^9$ keys, as it bumps $0.5\%$ of the keys instead of $3.9\%$; they are faster also than those of PHast, which takes eleven times as long to build, and about as fast as those of PtrHash, which uses more than one bit per key more. With a larger expected bucket size PHastR comes within $0.02$ bits per key of the space of PHast, using $1.90$ bits per key, and still has faster queries. Its construction also scales better with the number of threads: with all the threads of a 48-core machine it is almost three times faster than that of PHast+. Finally, we argue that when each key can be placed only within a range of $W$ slots, every placement of $n$ random keys on $n$ slots, however found, must bump on large key sets a constant fraction of the keys: we derive a lower bound of about $0.1/W$ on this fraction, and we estimate that the best placement bumps about $1/2W$ of the keys, which is about on tenth of the keys bumped by PHastR.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Optimal Extrapolation Bounds for Sparse Fourier Sums
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We prove a sharp extrapolation bound for $k$-sparse Fourier sums with arbitrary real frequencies and no separation assumption. For every $g(t)=\sum_{j=1}^k v_je^{iλ_jt}$ with $λ_j\in\mathbb{R}$ and every $x\geq 1$, \begin{align*}
  |g(x)|\le k\exp(O(k\operatorname{arcosh} x))\|g\|_{L^2[-1,1]}. \end{align*} Near the endpoint at $x=1+δ$, this gives an exponential factor of $\exp(O(k\sqrtδ))$, improving on the $\exp(O(k^2\log k\cdotδ))$ estimate of Chen and Price (ICALP 2019), and the exponent is optimal up to a constant factor. Our theorem has algorithmic applications to recovering gapless Fourier-sparse signals: it improves the resolution of cluster-location algorithms and the sample complexity of Fourier interpolation algorithms. In addition, it gives sharp bounds on the error transfer of sparse Fourier models just outside the training interval.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: A Matroid Generalization of Weighted Popular Matching: Characterization and Algorithm
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We study a problem that unifies two major generalizations of popular matchings in the one-sided preference model. In a bipartite graph in which each vertex, or applicant, on one side has preferences over the adjacent vertices, a matching is called popular if it does not lose a head-to-head election against any other matching. Since the seminal work of Abraham, Irving, Kavitha, and Mehlhorn, who gave the first polynomial-time algorithm for finding a popular matching, numerous generalizations of the popular matching problem have been investigated. Two prominent directions are weighted popular matchings, in which each applicant is assigned a voting weight, and popularity problems under matroid constraints. The former admits a polynomial-time algorithm due to Mestre, while the most general form of the latter is the popular common independent set problem, for which a polynomial-time algorithm is given by Kavitha, Makino, Schlotter, and Yokoi.
  In this paper, we introduce the weighted popular common independent set problem, which simultaneously generalizes weighted popular matchings and popular common independent sets. Our main result is the first polynomial-time algorithm for this problem. A key ingredient of the algorithm is a solution-independent characterization of weighted popular common independent sets, which we establish in this paper. As consequences of our algorithmic result, we obtain polynomial-time algorithms for several previously unresolved problems, including weighted popular matchings with matroid constraints and weighted popular branchings.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Sampling from the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick Model up to Criticality
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We prove that the simulated annealing algorithm efficiently samples from the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model at inverse temperature $β< 1$ to an arbitrary inverse polynomial accuracy in total variation.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Fully Dynamic Random-Walk Quantities on Undirected Expanders and $κ$-Uniform Directed Graphs
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We study fully dynamic data structures for random-walk quantities on undirected expanders and fast-mixing directed graphs. For an unweighted graph whose normalized Laplacian has spectral gap at least $γ$, we give a $(1\pm\varepsilon)$ effective-resistance data structure with expected update time $O(γ^{-4}\varepsilon^{-2}\log n\log^4(n/\varepsilon))$ and expected $O(1)$ query time.
  For directed graphs, somewhat surprisingly, the OMv conjecture precludes a fast data structure based on rapid mixing conditions alone. To address this, we introduce the notion of $κ$-uniform directed graphs, which requires the stationary distribution to $κ$-approximate the uniform distribution, and show that in this setting, random walk based data structures with $\text{poly}(κ, \log{n}, \varepsilon^{-1})$ update/query times are possible.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Hitting Minors: Stronger Lower Bounds
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
For a fixed finite collection of graphs $\mathcal{F}$, the $\mathcal{F}$-Minor-Free Deletion problem asks, given a graph $G$ and an integer $k$, whether there is a set $S\subseteq V(G)$ with $|S|\leq k$ such that $G-S$ contains no graph of $\mathcal{F}$ as a minor. This generalizes Vertex Cover, Feedback Vertex Set, and Vertex Planarization, among many others. Baste, Sau, and Thilikos [JCSS 2020, SICOMP 2023] showed that, assuming the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH), there are collections $\mathcal{F}$ for which the problem cannot be solved in time $2^{o(\mathrm{tw}\log\mathrm{tw})}n^{O(1)}$ on $n$-vertex graphs of treewidth $\mathrm{tw}$, and gave a matching algorithm.
  We ask whether this super-exponential dependence persists under more restrictive structural parameters. First, we strengthen their lower bound. Assuming ETH, for every fixed $h\geq 6$, $\{P_h\}$-Minor-Free Deletion, where $P_h$ is the path on $h$ vertices, cannot be solved in time $2^{o(t\log t)}n^{O(1)}$, where $t=\mathrm{fvs}+\mathrm{td}$ is the sum of the feedback vertex set number and treedepth of the input graph. These two parameters are incomparable, but both individually upper bound the treewidth. Together with the $2^{O(\mathrm{tw}\log\mathrm{tw})}n^{O(1)}$-time algorithm of Baste, Sau, and Thilikos [SICOMP 2023], our lower bound is tight.
  In contrast, we show that asymptotically faster algorithms are possible when parameterized by the vertex cover number $\mathrm{vc}$. Specifically, for any finite family $\mathcal{F}$, $\mathcal{F}$-Minor-Free Deletion can be solved in time $2^{O(\mathrm{vc})}n^{O(1)}$. Taken together, our results show that the boundary between single-exponential and super-exponential complexity for this problem lies between the vertex cover number and the feedback vertex set number (plus treedepth).

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Nearly Optimal Quantum Sample Complexity of Learning Fourier-Sparse Boolean Functions
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We study the number of uniform quantum examples needed to exactly learn a Boolean function with at most $k$ nonzero Fourier coefficients. We give a learner with near-optimal $\widetilde{O}(k)$ sample complexity independent of the input length $n$. The learner uses only separate measurements of individual examples. This improves the previous $O(k^{3/2}\log^2 k)$ upper bound (Arunachalam, Chakraborty, Lee, Paraashar, and de Wolf, 2021). The main ingredient is a candidate set formed by symmetric differences of subsets from independent groups of Fourier samples. A multilinear majority polynomial combines unbiased random approximations into an accurate witness whose Fourier support lies in this set. Granularity then forces the set to contain the entire Fourier support, including subsets never directly sampled. For comparison, we derive the tight classical sample complexity $Θ(nk)$ by combining known sparse-recovery and lower-bound results.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Query Complexity of Densest Sub(hyper)graph Problems
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
Rubinstein et al. introduce the study of connectivity and minimum cut problems in the cut query model, where an algorithm can only access the edges of a graph through CUT queries. In this work, we examine the query complexity of densest subgraph problems. Our first contribution is to generalize the uniform sparsification approach for Densest Subgraph and other heavy subgraph problems to weighted graphs, achieving the following results.
  >A $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation for weighted Densest Subgraph in $O(n\log^2 n/\varepsilon^2)$ queries, roughly matching the $Ω(n/\log n)$ lower bound we prove for randomized algorithms.
  >A $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation for weighted Max Cut in $O(n\log^2 n/\varepsilon^2)$ queries. This improves upon the bound of $O(n\log^3 n(\log n+1/\varepsilon^2))$ queries achieved by Plevrakis et al., making significant progress towards their lower bound of $Ω(n/\log n)$ queries.
  In contrast, we rule out approximation schemes with truly subquadratic query complexity for Densest $k$-Subgraph and settle its exact query complexity in both the unweighted and deterministic settings.
  For hypergraphs, we show CUT queries alone cannot achieve $o(\sqrt{n})$-approximation for Densest Subhypergraph or $o(n)$-approximation for Densest $k$-Subhypergraph, regardless of the number of queries. Augmenting CUT queries with the EDGE oracle of Chen et al., we overcome this barrier for Densest Subhypergraph and obtain a $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation on rank-$r$ hypergraphs using $O(nr\log n/\varepsilon^2)$ queries. We also extend our Densest $k$-Subgraph hardness results to hypergraphs and prove exponential query lower bounds for exact Densest $k$-Subhypergraph. Lastly, confirming a conjecture of Chakrabarty and Liao, we show that simulating an ADD query using CUT and IS-EDGE$^?$ queries requires exponentially-many queries.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Certifying Capacity and Gaps of the Rank-Dependent Gain-Sharing Framework for Ranking
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
The randomized primal-dual framework of Devanur, Jain, and Kleinberg (SODA 2013) splits each unit matching gain between endpoint dual variables according to the matched offline rank. The gain-sharing function affects the certificate but not Ranking's decisions. Keeping the splitting rule and expected edgewise feasibility criterion fixed, we define certifying capacity as the strongest uniform guarantee obtainable by functional optimization over a prescribed function class. Its shortfall from Ranking's actual competitiveness is the certifying gap.
  We study unweighted online bipartite matching under adversarial arrivals on graphs with online degree at most $d$ and on $d$-regular graphs. The optimized protocol is tight on both degree-one classes and in the unrestricted setting, but has a strictly positive gap on both degree-two classes, even over all measurable nonnegative complementary splits. In both degree-two settings, we determine Ranking's exact competitiveness and the exact certifying capacity over nondecreasing gain-sharing functions. For general $d$, we optimize over nondecreasing, right-continuous functions $f:[0,1]\to[0,1]$ with $f(1)=1$, using their probability-measure representation. Both the certifying capacity and actual competitiveness converge to $1-1/e$ in both instance families as $d\to\infty$. The resulting gap is at most $1/(2ed)+O(d^{-2})$ for online degree at most $d$; on $d$-regular graphs, it vanishes but is at least $(1/(2e)-o(1))/d$. These results distinguish function-class restrictions from limitations of the fixed protocol and motivate tighter randomized primal-dual frameworks.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Improved Combinatorial Auctions with and without Samples
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We give new mechanisms for combinatorial auctions in the offline, secretary, and prophet-with-samples models. Specifically, we obtain the following guarantees for social welfare maximization with $m$ items and $n$ XOS buyers:
  * In the prophet-with-samples version, buyers arrive in adversarial order and draw their values from independent distributions. We give a universally truthful, polynomial-time $(2+\eps)$-approximation mechanism using $O(\log\!\log m)$ samples from each distribution. The approximation factor is tight even for a single item and without the incentive constraints, due to the classic prophet inequality. Compared to the previous state-of-the-art with the same guarantees [Dütting--Kesselheim--Lucier--Reiffenhäuser--Singla (FOCS 2024)], our running time is exponentially faster, and our sample complexity is doubly-exponentially lower, resolving two explicit open problems by Dütting et al.
  * Using the same techniques, we also obtain improved mechanisms in the secretary and offline versions, where the values are worst-case, and buyers are processed in either random order (secretary) or without any timing restrictions (offline). After a long line of works, the state of the art in both models is an $O((\log\!\log m)^2)$-approximation due to [Assadi--Kesselheim--Singla (SODA 2021)], who explicitly ask whether it can be improved to $O(\log\!\log m)$. We indeed obtain an $O(\log\!\log m)$-approximate universally truthful mechanism for the secretary and offline models.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: Abstract shortened to fit arXiv constraints

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: With Leverage, the Gambler is Not the One Who Gets Ruined
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: In this note we explore the following simple question: How does the classic \emph{gambler's ruin} phenomenon change if we allow the gambler \emph{financial leverage}? We show that, with a moderate amount of leverage, it is possible for an (idealized) gambler to sustain seemingly improbable profits over a remarkably long time horizon without ever going bankrupt, \emph{even} if the gambler makes only fair bets. With a leverage ratio of $L = 10$ (less than what Lehman Brothers Holdings had from 1995--2008), the probability of multiplying one's money by $1000\times$ without going bankrupt is roughly $50\%$. More generally, given $L$-fold leverage, and given the goal of multiplying one's money by a factor of $r > 1$, the optimal gambling strategy has probability roughly $r^{-1/L}$ of success. The results in this note are designed as part of the course development for the CMU randomized algorithms course.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Conjectured Bounds for 2-Local Hamiltonians via Token Graphs
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We explain how the maximum energy of the Quantum MaxCut, XY, and EPR Hamiltonians on a graph $G$ are related to the spectral radii of the token graphs of $G$. From numerical study, we conjecture new bounds for these spectral radii based on properties of $G$. We show how these conjectures tighten the analysis of existing algorithms, implying state-of-the-art approximation ratios for all three Hamiltonians. Our conjectures also provide simple combinatorial bounds on the ground state energy of the antiferromagnetic Heisenberg model, which we prove for bipartite graphs.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: 47 pages, 2 figures v2: updated with Basu et al's proof of conjectures and added separation oracle to convex relaxations v3: updated with refutation of Conjecture 7

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Online Tokenization with Optimal Delay in Linear Time
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
Tokenization is an essential preprocessing step in almost all large language models (LLMs). One of the most popular frameworks is BPE tokenization, which consists of special token segmentation, pretokenization, and byte-pair encoding (BPE). However, existing algorithms are sequential, with each stage only processing complete output from the previous stage. In order to reduce latency and memory footprints, recent works (Jiang and Gong, ICML 2026) (Li, Yang and Mamouras, ASPLOS 2026) (Mamouras, Li and Yang, PLDI 2026) have initiated the study of online algorithms for subroutines such as pretokenization and BPE with a goal of streaming input to output as the input arrives online. However, the search for efficient online tokenization remains open.
  In this work, we formalize and resolve online tokenization. We introduce the notion of delay for online tokenization which characterizes the extent to which the algorithm output lags behind the (possibly computationally intractable) optimum. We give a near-linear time algorithm with optimal delay (up to constant factors). We complement this algorithm with a conditional lower bound: unless $\mathbf{P} = \mathbf{NP}$, there is no polynomial time algorithm that beats the delay of our algorithm by more than a constant factor.
  We implement a practical variant for tokenizers from OpenAI's tiktoken and HuggingFace's tokenizers. We obtain a $7.9\times$-$34.8\times$ latency advantage (measured as time to first token) over tiktoken (as well as the recent gigatoken tokenizer) and our implementation maintains approximately constant memory usage independent of input size. Our implementation also achieves a $2.4\times$-$7.0\times$ improvement in throughput over tiktoken and $15.8\times$-$38.1\times$ over tokenizers.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Finding non-bisimplicial and triad-free minimal separators
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
A $u\hbox{-}v$ separator in $G$ is a set $S\subseteq V(G)\setminus\{u,v\}$ such that there is no $u\hbox{-}v$ path in $G\setminus S$. A minimal separator in $G$ is a set $S$ such that for some $u,v\in V(G)\setminus S$, $S$ is a $u\hbox{-}v$ separator in $G$ but no proper subset of $S$ is. A set $S$ is bisimplicial if it is the union of at most two cliques. Recognizing graphs in which every minimal separator is the union of at most $k$ cliques is polynomial-time solvable for $k=1$ and NP-hard for every fixed $k\geq 3$. We settle the remaining case $k=2$ by giving a polynomial-time algorithm to decide whether every minimal separator in a graph is bisimplicial.
  A set $S$ is triad-free if its independence number $α(S)$ is at most two. Given a graph $G$ and two vertices $u,v$, the problem of finding a $u\hbox{-}v$ separator $S$ with $α(S)\leq k$ had the same complexity gap: it was known to be polynomial-time solvable for $k=1$ and NP-hard for every fixed $k\geq 3$. We resolve the remaining case $k=2$ by giving a polynomial-time algorithm that finds a triad-free $u\hbox{-}v$ separator or determines that none exists.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Dijkstra Is NOT Greedy: A Global-to-Local Proof of Correctness
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Dijkstra's algorithm is traditionally classified as a greedy algorithm. We argue that this classification misrepresents the mechanism by which the algorithm determines shortest paths. We present a direct global-to-local proof of correctness. At each iteration, the algorithm identifies a shortest path over the entire set of paths whose endpoints remain unsolved. This global minimum is necessarily a shortest path to its own endpoint. More fundamentally, the algorithm uses already determined shortest paths to establish one additional shortest path at each iteration. We identify this progression as dynamic programming. A three-step exclusion proof shows how the full path space is reduced to frontier candidates, how relaxation removes inferior alternatives, and why minimum extraction yields the global minimum. The choice is thus determined by a global comparison, not by an optimistic local greedy choice. We conclude that the algorithm is more accurately characterized by dynamic programming and deterministic path exclusion than by the traditional greedy classification.

Graphics.title: Cepheid: Decoupling Scale from Structure for Cross-Family Motion Completion
Graphics.summary: Sparse-to-dense motion completion recovers dense mesh motion from sparse vertex displacements. Residual priors trained on one geometry family frequently fail to beat parameter-free harmonic extension off-family. Moreover, cross-family training meets a scaling barrier: residual amplitude varies by more than an order of magnitude across geometry families and collapses as observations become denser. Since this scale depends on unknown target motion, it cannot be measured directly at test time. We decouple residual structure from physical scale by learning a dimensionless prior, estimating amplitude from observables and a lightweight correction fitted only on training sources. Our unified model surpasses harmonic extension across all evaluated families, including unseen cloth and legged bodies, without skeletons, registration, or cross-mesh correspondence. The same prior applies without retraining to point-tracked animal video and a robot grasping a soft body. Project page: https://su-terry.github.io/cepheid-website/

Graphics.title: RoboSimStudio: An Interactive Toolkit for Rapid Real2Sim of Robot Manipulation Tasks
Graphics.summary: It is difficult to accurately model the physics of the interaction between a robot and the objects it manipulates, including contact mechanics, coupled contact dynamics, deformations, stiffness and friction. We present RoboSimStudio (RSS), an interactive toolkit that makes choices of solver, contact model, and physical parameters explicit and editable, allowing both humans and coding agents to iteratively refine simulations based on observed physical behavior. We implement RSS with the open Newton physics simulation system and describe experiments with human-guided real2sim using (1) visual evaluation, (2) force-feedback and (3) agentic Real2Sim2Real. Code, video and additional information can be found on the project website.
Graphics.comment: 13 pages, 7 figures, 1 table. Project website: https://robosimstudio.github.io

Graphics.title: Texture Interpolation as Texton Matching
Graphics.summary: Texture interpolation asks what should lie between two textures. Standard methods typically blend pixels or features at corresponding spatial locations, implicitly assuming that co-located elements should be mixed. For unrelated textures, however, this correspondence is arbitrary: a crack at one location has no particular relationship to a fiber at the same location in another image. We study whether this hidden pairing choice is itself a major determinant of interpolation quality. We represent textures as collections of local appearance vectors, or textons, and replace positional pairing with appearance-aware matching while keeping the encoder, representation, and decoder fixed. This isolates the effect of correspondence from changes in model capacity or training. Across texture pairs, appearance-aware matching consistently improves the distributional quality of interpolated midpoints over positional feature blending. Soft matching produces the strongest midpoint statistics, whereas one-to-one assignments yield more balanced transitions and closer agreement with the target endpoint. The same intervention also improves a second pretrained texture interpolator without retraining. These results identify correspondence as a first-class design choice in texture interpolation: meaningful transitions depend not only on how strongly two textures are mixed, but also on which local appearances are mixed with one another.

Graphics.title: Sivia: Learning to Draw, Learning to Learn
Graphics.summary: A paper's overview figure is often the first thing readers see: it must explain the method correctly and look polished. We present Sivia, an overview-figure system that reads the paper, plans its relations, adapts visual organization from recent top-conference papers, and composes a design for image generation. Sivia improves with use through human-guided recursive self-improvement (RSI) at two levels: learning to draw revises its drawing skill from feedback on accuracy and presentation, and learning to learn revises the updater that proposes those revisions. A personal profile adapts presentation to its user's aesthetic preferences while the scientific content stays fixed. A diagnostic study of 1,964 overviews for 445 papers (17,973 relation judgments) shows that most errors are omissions and that source-derived relation plans raise required-relation accuracy (RRA) by up to 19.85 points. On 48 test papers, learning both levels reaches 93.54\% RRA, 15.31, 9.38, and 8.33 points above the initial skill, the Fixed-updater, and the GEPA baselines, while readability and visual quality rise from 3.95 and 4.00 to 4.70 and 4.78 on five-point scales. Learned presentation profiles raise liking from 4.02 to 4.73 and adoption from 34 to 45 of 48 tasks. Code and released artifacts are available at https://github.com/exsinger-hub/Sivia

Graphics.title: Content-Edited Layout Generation for Graphic Design
Graphics.summary:
In this paper, we formulate a novel form of conditional layout generation
  for graphic design, termed content-edited layout generation(CELG).
  CELG extends conventional content-aware layout generation (CLG), which
  generates a foreground layout for a fixed background image. The key
  distinction is that CELG treats the input image as an editable visual asset
  and, conditioned on a textual design intention and a foreground requirement
  that may be empty, produces an adapted background together with its layout. To study
  this task, we introduce Search-Compare-Edit(SCE), a data construction
  framework that supplies the paired supervision missing from existing design
  datasets. Starting from professional design canvases and their layouts, SCE
  synthesizes plausible pre-edit source images and corresponding editing
  instructions, yielding InstructEdit, a dataset of aligned source
  images, target canvases, instructions, and layouts. Based on the generated
  data, we train a two-flow multimodal flow matching model that couples a
  pretrained image editor with a layout flow transformer, enabling background
  editing and layout generation simultaneously within a unified framework that
  more closely reflects real-world design workflows. Our experiments
  systematically demonstrate the value of CELG as a distinct task and the
  performance advantages of the proposed model.

Graphics.title: Construction of Simple Quadrangulations of the Sphere at Skeletal Joints
Graphics.summary: We present a method for constructing a simple quadrangulation of the sphere from an unordered set of $n$ direction vectors, with application to parametric volumetric models of skeletal joints. We first select a quadrangulation encoding the joint topology by exhaustively enumerating candidate dual graphs, prioritizing convexity and regularity of the resulting quads. We then realize this topology on the sphere without crossings by solving a conflict-constrained assignment problem with lazy cyclic-order separation, and recover the corresponding primal graph. Experiments on direction sets from spherical Fibonacci sampling of size $3$ to $20$ show that the method robustly produces valid, high-quality quadrangulations across a range of input configurations. The resulting primal graph is directly converted into exact rational Bézier shell and column volumes, yielding a compact and precise volumetric representation of the joint. The approach extends naturally to multi-joint assemblies, enabling the construction of truss-based lattice structures within 3D domains.

Graphics.title: TempFit: Panoptic Symbol Spotting via Template Fitting
Graphics.summary: In this paper, we introduce TempFit, a novel approach for the problem of Panoptic Symbol Spotting on CAD drawings. Existing methods treat symbol spotting as a per-primitive classification or mask-prediction task, with no explicit constraint enforcing that the primitives assigned to one instance form a spatially connected group. As a result, predictions may erroneously merge primitives from distant symbols into a single instance or fragment a coherent symbol across multiple predictions. Motivated by the professional "retrieve-and-transform" CAD design workflow, we reformulate this task as a Template Fitting problem, where each foreground instance is detected by retrieving and aligning a canonical template from a library, enforcing structural completeness by construction. Building on this formulation, we present an autoregressive transformer that unifies template retrieval and pose prediction within a single end-to-end pipeline. The framework treats the template library as an explicit geometric memory, parsing background regions in parallel via learnable background tokens and synthesizing foreground instances autoregressively while attending to template-specific geometry at each step. Experiments on FloorplanCAD and our newly collected IndustryCAD dataset, a more challenging benchmark with complex industrial symbols, heavy occlusion, and wide scale variation, demonstrate state-of-the-art performance with particularly large gains on IndustryCAD. Project page: https://tempfit-project.github.io/.

Graphics.title: Integrating 3D Posture Neutralization with Statistical Shape Modeling for Head-Neck-Shoulder Ergonomic Design
Graphics.summary: The design of ergonomic products and workspaces requires a deep understanding of human anatomy and posture. In particular, the head-neck-shoulder region is critical for many applications such as cervical orthoses, helmets, and other head-worn or neck-worn devices. This paper presents a framework that integrates posture neutralization with statistical shape modeling (SSM) for the head-neck-shoulder (HNS) region. We acquire a single three-dimensional (3D) scan of the head-neck-shoulder region from each of 200 Chinese adults in a natural posture for each subject. Every scan is then posture-neutralized before SSM. We fit a parametric head-neck model to each scan to separate cervical pose from anatomy, and reset the cervical pose to a common neutral configuration, so that the resulting model captures anatomical shape variation rather than posture-induced deformation. The resulting shape space yields a standardized template and population-wide modes of variation, providing baselines for parametric ergonomic design. We further discuss how the model supports population coverage analysis and the design of products that accommodate anatomical diversity while maintaining neutral cervical posture.

Graphics.title: MeshSplatBench: A Unified Benchmark for Triangle- and Mesh-Based Neural Rendering
Graphics.summary: Triangle- and mesh-based neural rendering seeks to bridge neural representations and graphics engines through triangle primitives compatible with standard rasterization. Yet existing methods were developed and evaluated under inconsistent settings, with few direct comparisons and little evaluation in graphics engines. We introduce MeshSuite, the first benchmark for systematic evaluation of engine deployment and Non-Engine Render in triangle- and mesh-based neural rendering. MeshSuite evaluates two deployment settings: Standard Deployment, using an opaque mesh pipeline with vertex colors and hardware Z-buffering; and Dedicated Deployment, using method-specific engine implementations to preserve appearance and compositing features. For mesh splatting, we also audit exported surfaces for topological and geometric integrity as downstream graphics assets. Our results show that engine deployment reduces image quality in both settings; among evaluated methods, MeshSplatting degrades least under Standard Deployment. Dedicated Deployment preserves most fidelity at roughly 5-33x the runtime of Standard Deployment across two deployment datasets. For mesh splatting, explicit connectivity and shared indexing remain limited: shared vertex indexing alone guarantees neither manifoldness nor global connectivity. These findings show that rasterizability is only part of graphics readiness and underscore the need to assess engine deployment. Project page: https://prinasi.github.io/MeshSuite.

Graphics.title: DiffGIPC: Differentiable Mixed-Coordinate Contact Dynamics on GPU
Graphics.summary: Contact-rich inverse problems require efficient gradients and reliable enforcement of non-penetration. Existing differentiable methods provide fast simulation and rigid-deformable coupling, but contact treatments based on penalties or velocity-level constraints can permit penetration or positional drift. Incremental Potential Contact (IPC) maintains non-penetration through geometric barriers and {continuous collision detection (CCD)}. However, repeated forward and backward evaluations remain costly in full-space finite-element (FEM) implementations, particularly when nearly rigid components retain many vertex {degrees of freedom (DoFs)}. We present DiffGIPC, a GPU-accelerated differentiable IPC framework for optimizing interacting deformable and nearly rigid bodies. Our affine-body derivatives enable {rest-shape} design, initial-state optimization, and articulated control while retaining only twelve motion DoFs per affine body. These gradients account for how changes in geometry, placement, and actuation affect other objects through collision and friction. We preserve these interactions in one coupled FEM-affine adjoint system per frame, reducing the backward-system size without discarding the dependencies that drive the inverse problem. GPU-optimized backward computation further reduces the cost of repeated gradient evaluations. A reusable PyTorch interface connects supported physical parameters to user-defined parameter maps and losses across design, identification, motion, placement, and articulated control. Experiments demonstrate peak speedups over DiffIPC of approximately 150.0x with full-space FEM and 4133.3x with affine bodies for combined forward simulation and backward differentiation.

Operating Systems.title: Extending concurrent separation logic to the hardware level to verify the xv6 OS kernel on RISC-V with AI agents
Operating Systems.summary:
MachCSL is a framework for verifying system software, such as an OS kernel, on top of low-level semantics of a RISC-V computer, based on the Sail RISC-V semantics. The key idea behind MachCSL is to adapt concurrent separation logic, based on Iris, to reasoning about low-level hardware execution at the sub-instruction level: page-table translation, TLB, privilege levels, configuration registers, instruction fetch/decode/execute, traps and interrupts, DMA, shared memory, power failures, etc. Reasoning at this level of detail ensures that the system software correctly manages all of the hardware details.
  Verifying software at this low level of abstraction is tedious, but LLM-based agents are capable of reasoning about such low-level details. As a case study, we verify the xv6 OS kernel (6,657 lines of C and assembly code), which provides a traditional Unix system call interface (processes, file system, file descriptors, and preemptive scheduling) and has substantial internal concurrency (multi-core support with fine-grained locking, shared memory, interrupts, DMA, etc.). In the verification process, we uncovered 11 bugs in the xv6 implementation, as well as one bug in the Sail RISC-V semantics, and one bug in Sail's Lean extraction. The verification effort took us 102 days, including the time to develop the MachCSL framework.
  On top of the verified xv6 kernel, we prove a theorem about console-level behavior: e.g., if the user types echo hello world as input on the UART console, the only output the system can produce is hello world (if there are no crashes or other errors). This theorem covers both the kernel and the init, sh, echo, cat, grep, sync, and seccomp binaries in the initial file system image.

Hardware Architecture.title: Formal-Verification-Guided Bayesian Optimization for Non-Intrusive Last-Mile Coverage Closure
Hardware Architecture.summary: Last-mile functional coverage closure for modern chip designs remains costly because a mature UVM environment exposes many controls while direct hits on the remaining bins are sparse. We present a non-intrusive workflow that closes pre-defined bins in an existing, human-authored functional coverage model; it does not synthesize verification objectives from the design specification. The workflow first uses abstract-syntax-tree (AST) parsing and cone-of-influence (COI) tracing to map each residual target to existing testbench knobs. Under a matched 20-simulation budget, Bayesian optimization (BO) is compared with continued constrained-random verification (CRV) and random search over the same AST/COI-reduced space. Formal reachability then removes only targets supported by complete unreachability proofs, after which retained targets are grouped by formal difficulty and processed by group-specific BO under a second matched 20-simulation budget. Cleanup and grouping never add numerator bins; only simulator coverage artifacts do. On OpenTitan AES, first-pass reduced-space BO reaches 241/271 bins; formal cleanup removes two denominator bins; the integrated post-cleanup stage - difficulty grouping, policy routing, and group-specific BO - adds 20 simulator-confirmed hits, yielding 261/271 raw coverage (96.31%) and 261/269 effective coverage (97.03%). On Entropy Source, first-pass reduced-space BO reaches 2117/2277 bins; formal cleanup removes ten denominator bins; the integrated post-cleanup stage - difficulty grouping, policy routing, and group-specific BO - adds 93 simulator-confirmed hits, yielding 2210/2277 raw coverage (97.06%) and 2210/2267 effective coverage (97.49%). These results characterize the integrated diagnosis-and-search workflow; the present evaluation does not isolate the causal contributions of difficulty classification, policy routing, and post-cleanup BO.
Hardware Architecture.comment: 21 pages, 3 figures, 7 tables. Accepted for publication in ACM Transactions on Design Automation of Electronic Systems (TODAES)

Hardware Architecture.title: When Is RTL Better? Auditing Evaluation Stability with Tool-Grounded Requirement Profiles
Hardware Architecture.summary: RTL-generation studies increasingly report functional correctness and post-synthesis quality, yet the evaluator itself is rarely treated as an experimental variable. A candidate can appear better when a security rule, protocol obligation, target context, feasibility gate, uncertainty policy, or provenance constraint is omitted. We introduce tool-grounded requirement profiles: machine-readable contracts binding each requirement's meaning to its executable evidence and comparison rule, together with cross-requirement gates, uncertainty handling, and provenance. We audit evaluator stability by freezing candidate pairs and perturbing only their evaluation profile. In a preregistered controlled pilot with six designs, twelve pairs, three requirement families, six evaluator conditions, and 72 decisions, a generic cell-count evaluator reports unsupported improvement for 6/12 pairs (50%; Wilson 95% interval 25.4 to 74.6%; design-cluster bootstrap interval 25 to 75%). The matched evaluator detects all twelve injected regressions, whereas syntax, generic synthesis, context mismatch, and gate ablation each lose the required distinction for 12/12 pairs. In a separately frozen external validation of all 290 public RTLLM v1.1 text-only candidates, 81/215 evaluable comparisons (37.7%; task-cluster 95% interval 24.8 to 51.4%) yield unsupported scalar improvements, including 72 functional-gate reversals. Separately, 26 OpenROAD-flow-scripts runs show why timing context and activity qualification must be part of the contract. The study does not rank generators; it establishes evaluator configuration as a measurable, auditable source of conclusion instability.
Hardware Architecture.comment: 6 pages, 3 figures, and 6 tables

Hardware Architecture.title: LocalTrain: Integer-Only Local Learning for Energy-Efficient CNN Training on Edge FPGAs
Hardware Architecture.summary: Local learning reduces cross-layer training dependencies, but an efficient accelerator must still retain operands, accumulate gradients, and select quantization scales. We present an FPGA system that trains a CNN and its regional auxiliary classifiers using a shared integer matrix engine. Compact errors are expanded on chip, gradients are folded tile by tile, and historical scales permit direct output conversion. At 200 MHz, the KV260 prototype achieves 76.57% accuracy on CIFAR-10 and 91.85% on SVHN at approximately 4.20 W mean module power. Effective matrix throughput is 31.22 and 31.57 GMAC/s, respectively. Against the same integer method on Jetson Orin Nano, measured training energy is 40.4% and 42.1% lower, with $1.86\times$ and $1.82\times$ longer runtime; measurements use the respective platform power domains. Selected state checks and matching complete-run prediction counts support functional agreement with the software reference.
Hardware Architecture.comment: 7 pages, 2 figures, 5 tables

Hardware Architecture.title: FORGE: Procedural Weight Generation for Sparse MoE Inference
Hardware Architecture.summary: We introduce FORGE (Fast On-chip Rotor Generation for Experts), a procedural weight generation system for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) inference. Rather than storing and loading every expert weight tensor from HBM, we show how a compact accelerator inside each Streaming Multiprocessor can regenerate them on-the-fly from $O(\log^2 d)$ rotor parameters per projection. Per replaced layer, gigabytes of stored expert weights are approximated with under a megabyte of seeds. This addresses the dual memory bottleneck of autoregressive Sparse MoE decode, where per-expert FFN operations are HBM-bandwidth-bound at small routed-token counts and the aggregate expert footprint forces multi-node Expert Parallelism (EP) with all-to-all traffic. We realize the approach as the Rotor Generation Unit (RGU), a fixed-function datapath that generates FFN weight tiles without competing with Tensor Core execution. With 30% of the MoE FFN layers replaced across five Sparse MoE models, we estimate 1.3-2.8x higher system throughput at matched GPU count and 1.10-1.15x lower per-user decode latency at short context. In exchange, downstream accuracy on three model families falls below that of the same model fine-tuned without rotor replacement, and the replacement ratio controls this tradeoff. FORGE also expands KV cache capacity by 1.2-2.6x. It is agnostic to the bit width at which weights are stored, so it can compose with quantization. The RGU is fully implemented/verified in SystemVerilog at ~0.9% SM area overhead (0.032 mm^2/SM, 7nm).
Hardware Architecture.comment: 16 pages. Accepted to ASPLOS 2027

Hardware Architecture.title: FPGA-Based Neural Network Accelerators for Space Applications: A Survey
Hardware Architecture.summary: Space missions are becoming increasingly ambitious, necessitating high-performance onboard spacecraft computing systems. In response, field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs) have garnered significant interest due to their flexibility, cost-effectiveness, and radiation tolerance potential. Concurrently, neural networks (NNs) are being recognized for their capability to execute space mission tasks such as autonomous operations, sensor data analysis, and data compression. This survey serves as a valuable resource for researchers aiming to implement FPGA-based NN accelerators in space applications. By analyzing existing literature, identifying trends and gaps, and proposing future research directions, this work highlights the potential of these accelerators to enhance onboard computing systems.
Hardware Architecture.comment: 48 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables. Author's accepted manuscript, published online in ACM Computing Surveys on 7 October 2026. This version replaces the April 2025 preprint

Hardware Architecture.title: Resource-constrained Remote Attestation of Smart Meters Using Merkle Trees in a Trusted Execution Environment
Hardware Architecture.summary: Smart meters are pivotal to the functioning of smart grids, as they measure and transmit energy consumption data that includes sensitive information about household energy usage patterns. While this data offers significant financial benefits, it can also reveal detailed insights into residents' daily routines, making the security of smart meters a critical concern. This paper introduces a novel remote attestation method for smart meters that ensures the integrity and privacy of data exchanged between smart meters and central servers while detecting unauthorized tampering. Our approach structures the communication data into a Merkle Tree-a hash data structure that facilitates efficient data integrity and authenticity verification. All operations involved in constructing the Merkle root and hashing critical data are executed in the secure environment of a Trusted Execution Environment (TEE) using OP-TEE, thereby maintaining the integrity and security of the smart meter's data. Comparing our experimental results with the related works highlights the superiority of our method in terms of resource efficiency, security robustness, and the feasibility of implementation on smart meters and resource-constrained devices, thereby enhancing the overall security and reliability of smart grid systems.
Hardware Architecture.comment: 21 pages

Hardware Architecture.title: SafeDSE: Joint Exploration of Safety Architecture Patterns, Mapping, and Scheduling for Dataflow Applications With Safety Arguments (Extended Version)
Hardware Architecture.summary: Embedded platforms increasingly host safety-related streaming functions next to less critical ones. Whether a safety architecture pattern, such as a doer/checker pair, protects a function depends on the cores that run its components. Their schedule must meet the throughput requirement, and mixing safety integrity levels (SILs) on one core raises development cost. This report presents SafeDSE, a design space exploration framework for synchronous dataflow applications. One declarative constraint model decides the pattern of each actor, the placement that the fault model requires, the static-order schedule, and the platform, and prices SIL promotion. Guards activate the chosen patterns in a fixed graph that holds all of them, and node potentials encode throughput. An independent verifier re-checks every solution, and a generator turns its checks into evidence of a safety argument in Goal Structuring Notation. On 9 benchmark instances under period bounds, no rule that fixes patterns before mapping was both always feasible and never more expensive under conservative pricing, while joint exploration was. In the generated arguments, 49 to 62% of the leaves cite verifier checks; the rest are claims a mapping cannot discharge. Optimality within the model was proven for all synthetic graphs with up to 16 actors. This extended version adds the full model, the verifier and generator in detail, the complete catalog and parameters, and a proof of the potential characterization. It also reports every experiment per instance, a mutation analysis of the verifier, and the negative results of the development.
Hardware Architecture.comment: 38 pages, 12 figures, 29 tables. Extended version of a paper submitted for publication; tool and data at github.com/SBU-CPS-Lab/SafeDSE

Hardware Architecture.title: Agentic Architect: An Agentic AI Framework for Architecture Design Exploration and Optimization
Hardware Architecture.summary:
Computer Architecture research has traditionally required the exploration of vast, highly complex design spaces through manual human effort. Large Language Models (LLMs) offer an opportunity to accelerate this process by enabling fast and automated implementation and testing of different architectural mechanisms and their combinations. We introduce Agentic Architect, a framework for agentic CPU microarchitectural design-space exploration and optimization. The Agentic Architect combines LLM-driven code evolution with cycle-accurate simulation and hardware cost modeling to explore performance, area, and power tradeoffs. Starting from a seed design, the LLM is prompted to explore the design space by implementing changes, guided by prior evaluation feedback. Each new design is compiled, simulated on training workloads, evaluated against the optimization objective, and constrained by area and power budgets. Its score and diagnostics update the candidate population and guide subsequent iterations.
  We evaluate the Agentic Architect framework across prefetching, cache replacement, and branch prediction. On 213 traces spanning five benchmark suites, its evolved prefetchers lead the evaluated L1D and L2 designs, delivering up to 6.7% and 2.6% additional speedup, respectively, over the strongest state-of-the-art design, while the best evolved cache replacement design improves over Mockingjay by up to 1.7%. Moreover, across 191 branch-prediction traces, the evolved branch predictor achieves 97.62% of TAGE-SC-L's geometric mean IPC at 10.58% of its area. Our analysis highlights the importance of seed selection, hardware constraints, and training workloads in shaping search outcomes. Overall, Agentic Architect establishes the first end-to-end framework for agentic CPU microarchitectural design optimization, opening a new direction for architecture research.

Hardware Architecture.title: LizTail: Unifying Shape Adaptation and Spatial Parallelism with Segment-Reconfigurable Systolic Arrays
Hardware Architecture.summary: Systolic arrays are widely used to accelerate neural-network inference, yet fixed two-dimensional arrays struggle with the substantial diversity in both matrix geometry and available parallelism across CNNs and Transformer-based large language models. This mismatch is particularly severe for skinny matrices, small-batch autoregressive decoding, and operators containing multiple independent partitions, leading to low processing-element (PE) utilization and repeated spatial folding. Existing reconfigurable arrays typically improve either shape adaptation or distributed execution, whereas supporting both through fine-grained routing incurs considerable interconnect, buffering, and control overheads. We present LizTail (named after lizard tail autotomy, where predefined fracture planes allow segments to detach and remain independently active, analogous to LizTail's predefined reconfiguration boundaries), a multi-mode systolic array that enables constrained segment-level reconfiguration by partitioning a $128\times128$ array into 32 regular $128\times4$ segments and adding connectivity only at predefined endpoints. The resulting substrate supports trimming, long-path extension through $180^\circ$ turn-back connections, and distributed execution in which each subarray can itself be trimmed or extended. Differentiated PE datapaths and segment-aware CEB/SIB buffers provide the required compute and data-delivery flexibility without unrestricted PE-level routing. A hardware-constrained mapper selects the execution organization, dataflow, task partition, and tiling. Across representative workloads, LizTail achieves geometric-mean speedups of $5.02\times$ on CNN inference and $25.67\times$ on LLM decoding over a TPU-like array, while reducing EDP by up to $38.23\times$. LizTail is open-sourced at https://github.com/kmjbwxa/LizTail.

Hardware Architecture.title: Fixed-Capacity Causal Models with Parallel Recovery for GPU Lossless Compression
Hardware Architecture.summary: GPU compression needs both dense complete frames and inexpensive checked recovery. We compare three causal representations under the same 512-row model budget, select before encoding one payload, and align entropy states with causal byte banks. Same-lane and residual banks decode concurrently; high-first banks decode in causal order. On ten reused structured/electrophysiology inputs, split-bank execution lowers aggregate median encode-plus-recovery time 13.10% for 0.18% more frame bytes. A separate twelve-configuration GPU comparison places it on the measured median frontier: 5.75% and 7.11% smaller frames than transformed nvCOMP Zstd at 35.14/19.03% lower paired cost for 64/8 KiB requests. A matched native-CPU model control isolates a 44.16% reduction in complete encoding cost; a CUDA-free CPU receiver restores the same frames. Three whole EEG recordings retain a separate Zstd-1--16 curve, while fixed ECG fixtures expose transformed-Zstd counterexamples. Model overhead, concentrated gains, technical ranges and adverse outcomes bound these operating points. ANS interleaving and transforms are established; reused inputs, unequal resources and fixed controls do not establish codec optima or population superiority.
Hardware Architecture.comment: 10 pages, 2 figures, 1 table

Programming Languages.title: claimcheck: Measuring and Improving Specification Faithfulness
Programming Languages.summary: Formal verification proves that a program satisfies its specification, but says nothing about whether the specification captures what the author meant. As LLMs increasingly write both code and specifications, a gap between the author's natural-language requirement and the specification becomes a live risk. A machine-checked proof of a property narrower than the one requested is worthless but passes every check. Closing this gap is solving the spec formalization problem: given a natural-language requirement, produce a formal artifact whose meaning matches it. To measure the gap, we curate an end-to-end benchmark for spec formalization spanning four formal languages: Dafny contracts and Lean 4, Isabelle and Rocq theorem statements. Each of its 3,234 rows pairs a natural-language requirement with a formal artifact and a label established by execution, by proof, or by the benchmark it is drawn from. A third of the rows are meaning-preserving rewrites of the artifact that keep the faithful label, so a judge cannot score by detecting that a row was edited. We introduce claimcheck, a tool that detects incorrect formalizations: the formal artifact is translated back into plain English by a model that never sees the requirement, and a separate model, the judge, decides whether the informalization and the requirement express the same guarantee. On all four languages it gains 8.2 to 9.8 points of macro recall over a single call shown the requirement and the artifact, and 4.2 to 6.0 over that call handed the same list of meaning-preserving rewrites. Showing the judge the artifact as well costs 1.4 to 4.5 points. Across four judges that also see the artifact, the gain shrinks as the judge gets stronger, to within a point of the informed single call for the strongest.

Programming Languages.title: Semantics for 2D Rasterization
Programming Languages.summary:
Rasterization is the process of determining the color of every pixel drawn by an application. Powerful rasterization libraries like Skia, CoreGraphics, and Direct2D put exceptional effort into drawing, blending, and rendering efficiently. Yet applications are still hindered by the inefficient sequences of instructions that they ask these libraries to perform. Even Google Chrome, a highly optimized web browser co-developed with the Skia rasterization library, still produces inefficient instruction sequences even on the top 100 most visited websites. The underlying reason for this inefficiency is that rasterization libraries have complex semantics and opaque and non-obvious execution models.
  To address this issue, we introduce $μ$Skia, a formal semantics for the Skia 2D graphics library, and mechanize this semantics in Lean. $μ$Skia covers language and graphics features like canvas state, the layer stack, blending, and color filters, and the semantics itself is split into three strata to separate concerns and enable extensibility. We then identify four patterns of sub-optimal Skia code produced by Google Chrome, and then write replacements for each pattern. $μ$Skia allows us to verify that the replacements are correct, including identifying numerous tricky side conditions. We then develop a high-performance Skia optimizer that applies these patterns to speed up rasterization. On 139 Skia programs gathered from the top 100 websites, this optimizer yields a speedup of 1.12$\times$ over Skia's most modern GPU backend, while taking just 0.03 ms for optimization. The speedups persist across a variety of websites, Skia backends, and GPUs. To provide true, end-to-end verification, optimization traces produced by the optimizer are loaded back into the $μ$Skia semantics and translation validated in Lean.

Programming Languages.title: Effect Systems as Abstract Interpretations
Programming Languages.summary:
Many forms of static reasoning about program behaviours are known in the literature, yet formal relationships are studied surprisingly infrequently. While most type systems are well-known to be captured by abstract interpretations, the situation for type-and-effect systems is, in the general case, unsettled despite strong hypotheses and occasional framing of effect systems as abstract interpretations.
  We develop a formal relationship between abstract interpretations and a general class of effect systems. First, we describe an embedding of effect quantales into abstract domains. Second, we recover the general form of an effect quantale as an abstract interpretation -- not on states or values, but on event occurrences.
Programming Languages.comment: Preprint of accepted NSAD 2026 paper. Corrected typo in equation on page 4

Programming Languages.title: Modeling Quantum Computing with $π$-calculus
Programming Languages.summary:
Quantum computing is a difficult concept to grasp for computer scientists because it is full of mathematical formulas that have no intuitive meaning related to the problem that the code solves. While these formulae define the way the system behaves, the operational semantics is very far from regular programming languages that reason with variables, assignments, and passing by value the results of computation. This article takes a step back to define a theoretical framework where quantum programs are not treated as sequential programs, but rather as concurrent programs where variables advertise their states through their own channels and code that uses them is reading that state (and possibly collapsing it).
  The PiQuant framework is a simple extension of the $π$-calculus that contains additional syntax and semantics for the handling of quantum variables.

Programming Languages.title: Stone Duality for Monads
Programming Languages.summary: We introduce a contravariant idempotent adjunction between (i) the category of ranked monads on $\mathsf{Set}$; and (ii) the category of internal categories and internal retrofunctors in the category of locales. The left adjoint takes a monad $T$-viewed as a notion of computation, following Moggi-to its localic behaviour category $\mathsf{LB}T$. This behaviour category is understood as "the universal transition system" for interacting with $T$: its "objects" are states and the "morphisms" are transitions. On the other hand, the right adjoint takes a localic category $\mathsf{LC}$-similarly understood as a transition system-to the monad $Γ\mathsf{LC}$ where $(Γ\mathsf{LC})A$ is the set of $A$-indexed families of local sections to the source map which jointly partition the locale of objects. The fixed points of this adjunction consist of (i) hyperaffine-unary monads, i.e., those monads where term $t$ admits a read-only operation $\bar{t}$ predicting the output of $t$; and (ii) ample localic categories, i.e., whose source maps are local homeomorphisms and whose locale of objects are strongly zero-dimensional. The hyperaffine-unary monads arise in earlier works by Johnstone and Garner as a syntactic characterization of those monads with Cartesian closed Eilenberg-Moore categories. This equivalence is the Stone duality for monads; so-called because it further restricts to the classical Stone duality by viewing a Boolean algebra $B$ as a monad of $B$-partitions and the corresponding Stone space as a localic category with only identity morphisms.
Programming Languages.comment: 19 pages without appendix, 35 pages total, to appear in final proceedings of MFPS2026

Programming Languages.title: Let Functions Speak: Lightweight Parametric Polymorphism via Domain and Range Types
Programming Languages.summary:
Subtyping provides polymorphism at a low cost: a concise type such as Int $\to$ Top covers every function that accepts an integer, whatever it returns, whereas the parametric alternative $\forall B.\,$ Int $\to$ B spends a quantifier and a type parameter to express the same. This cognitive overhead compounds as types nest. Subtyping, however, is not always enough: upcasting to Int $\to$ Top forgets the result type, so a program that needs the precise result must return to full parameterization.
