We present HADES, a programmable processing-near-memory engine built around one shared 32x32-bit 2R1W register-file macro that holds both data and program. Twelve 16-bit opcodes, three working registers and a 32-slot program express ten search workloads in 8 to 19 slots, and SCANP and SCANSEL shorten dual-row and selected scans. A post-layout 2x2 Tiny Tapeout implementation closes timing at 40 MHz with 26,968 square microns of standard cells beside a 15,744 square microns macro. All HADES results come from RTL or gate-level simulation of this implementation, and HADES energy is estimated. Against ESP8266 and ESP32 microcontrollers running plain C, and with an ideal host, HADES answers a resident query 10x to 32x and 2.2x to 11x faster, respectively. End to end, it wins at the evaluated batch sizes of B = 16 and B = 256 against both boards and loses the single-query (B = 1) runs to the ESP32. An Arduino Nano runs a restricted subset. Kernel power stays within about 2% of a spin loop on all three boards. These results hold for plain-C baselines under the evaluated conditions. At this scale the control and instruction storage fit around a shared memory macro, while the byte-wide interface and the loading path remain significant costs.
Hardware Architecture.comment: 16 pages, 4 TikZ figures

Hardware Architecture.title: Beyond LLM Serving: Characterizing Vision-Language-Action Workloads for Embodied AI System Design
Hardware Architecture.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models translate multimodal observations into low-level robot actions. During robot operation, each control period sets an inference deadline, and overruns leave the robot acting on stale observations, reducing task success. Meeting this deadline motivates on-device or nearby edge execution, where a single robot requires batch-1 inference outside the design point of LLM serving systems. Although VLA architectures combine familiar vision-language, autoregressive, and diffusion-style components, their runtime behavior in this batch-1 control setting remains uncharacterized. We characterize four representative VLA models on an edge GPU server and two onboard SoCs, using single-inference profiling and 43,200 closed-loop episodes. Action tensor dimensionality determines whether a stage is memory- or compute-bound, platform balance can shift that bottleneck, and GPU frequency scaling yields a platform-dependent energy-latency sweet spot. In closed-loop operation, overlapping inference with action execution creates an accuracy-speed-energy tradeoff, and no configuration is Pareto-dominant across deployment SLOs. These results guide joint design of VLA model architectures, hardware, and runtime policies.
Hardware Architecture.comment: To appear in the Proceedings of the 32nd ACM International Conference on Architectural Support for Programming Languages and Operating Systems (ASPLOS '27). 17 pages, 14 figures

Programming Languages.title: Bidirectional Elaborators à la Carte
Programming Languages.summary:
Surface syntax in proof assistants like Rocq, Lean, Agda, and Idris is highly implicit, lacking many details that are needed for user-written code to denote precisely defined mathematical objects. Elaboration is an algorithm that accounts for these details by translating surface syntax to an explicit enough core syntax. The reliability and predictability of elaboration relies on several critical properties of the core type system, including decidability of judgemental equality and the injectivity of type constructors; these dependencies are witnessed in a concrete system by explicit calls to conversion checking and weak-head reduction subroutines.
  We introduce a dependently typed monadic domain specific language for the executable specification of correct-by-construction elaboration algorithms that is abstracted from any particular representation of normal forms or algorithm for conversion checking. In particular, we represent a bidirectionally typed surface language for Martin-Löf type theory by shallow embedding in this DSL so that the translation of surface terms into core terms amounts to elementary equational calculation. This translation is correct by construction in the sense that it cannot produce ill-typed terms, and is automatically stable under judgemental equality of core terms and even under substitution; from the latter property, we obtain a new denotational interpretation of the suspension of elaboration problems. Finally, a concrete elaboration algorithm is extracted by algebraic means from a presheaf model of the DSL built out of the bi-initial natural model of Martin-Löf type theory.
Programming Languages.comment: We have corrected a mistake in the formulation of η-conversion, and added several more proofs

Programming Languages.title: Contravariant Universe Subtyping, Formalized, Mechanized
Programming Languages.summary:
In a type theory with a cumulative universe hierarchy, \emph{subtyping} is often incorporated to lift lower universe levels to higher ones. In practice, kernels of proof assistants typically implement universe subtyping conservatively: subtyping only propagates covariantly into the output types of $Π$ types, while input types must be equivalent. A full-blown subtyping relation also compares the input types contravariantly. However, contravariant subtyping is not justified by the existing set-theoretic model, and poses challenges in the development of a complete subtyping algorithm.
  We present \mclttsub, a complete mechanized study of contravariant universe subtyping for a core Martin-Löf type theory (MLTT), built as an extension of the verified McTT kernel in Rocq. We re-establish the syntactic meta-theory and the soundness and completeness properties of the normalization-by-evaluation (NbE) algorithm. To complete the verified pipeline for a type-checker, we give two complete and sound subtyping algorithms. The first one \emph{renormalizes} output types in every $Π$ iteration. Despite a simple completeness proof, this algorithm incurs additional computational cost. The second algorithm hence circumvents this cost by avoiding the renormalization at all. It simply recursively compares two already normalized types structurally. Nevertheless, a completeness proof of this algorithm in a semantic approach requires to reason about normalization in sub-contexts, a capability beyond what the current semantic gadget offers. Instead, we conduct a program equivalence proof through bisimulation relations. Using this technique, we prove that the NbE algorithm returns equal normal forms in sub-contexts up to universe levels, and successfully conclude the completeness of the subtyping algorithm.

Programming Languages.title: Mechanising Denotational Semantics in Agda
Programming Languages.summary:
Mechanisation of a mathematical definition (also referred to as formalisation) has many benefits. Here, we focus on mechanising denotational semantic definitions of programming languages by embedding them in the Agda language. The Agda type-checker detects and reports any issues with the wellformedness and type correctness of the embedded definitions.
  To minimise the effort required, and to facilitate correlation of the original definition with its Agda embedding, mechanisation should not involve significant reformulation or extension. Here, we show how to embed conventional Scott-Strachey denotational definitions in Agda with almost no changes to $λ$-notation or domain equations.
  Agda notation for definitions of types and functions corresponds closely to the conventional meta-notation of denotational semantics. We have developed a collection of Agda modules with postulated types for commonly used domain constructors and their associated operations.
  We illustrate our approach with mechanisations of three denotational definitions: a model of the untyped $λ$-calculus, Plotkin's denotational semantics of PCF, and a semantics of a sublanguage of Scheme. In previous work, similar mechanisations in Agda have revealed several unsuspected wellformedness issues in published denotational definitions.
  Some of the postulated properties of our definitions are inconsistent with a classical set-theoretic interpretation of Agda. We conjecture that they would be consistent with an interpretation of Agda in a higher-order intuititionistic logic, such as that used by Simpson in his work on synthetic domain theory. After recalling previous work on mechanising domain theory, we consider the possibility of mechanising synthetic domain theory in Agda.
Programming Languages.comment: 23 pages, excl. references. To be published in Proceedings of MFPS 2026

Programming Languages.title: (Implicitly) Characterizing Probabilistic Polynomial Time as Used in Cryptography
Programming Languages.summary: In this paper, we show how a recently introduced $λ$-calculus for randomized computation, called $λ\mathbf{BLL}$, can accurately capture the notions of first- and second-order polytime computations used in cryptographic definitions and proofs. These results, spelled out in the style of so-called \emph{implicit computational complexity}, imply that $λ\mathbf{BLL}$ is sufficiently powerful to express experiments and adversaries as used in cryptography, and that reductions, when formulated within the calculus, are guaranteed to be complexity-preserving. Remarkably, while polynomial-time soundness holds for the full calculus, polynomial-time completeness already follows in presence of a minimal finite set of basic functions.
Programming Languages.comment: Extended version of a paper to appear in the proceedings of FSTTCS 2026

Programming Languages.title: sGLP: Specifying Stochastic Agents that Simulate People
Programming Languages.summary:
Grassroots platforms are designed to be owned, operated and governed by their participants, and thus are constituted from person-to-person smartphone apps that run on participants' smartphones. A grassroots app is specified using a grassroots social contract, which is compiled through an abstraction cascade into a volition-guarded Grassroots Logic Program (vGLP), a multiagent concurrent logic programming language. A vGLP program in turn specifies a smartphone UI via which people express their volitions and thus control the app. Prudence dictates large-scale evaluation and testing of grassroots platforms prior to deployment, but using the many people needed to do that is a contradiction in terms. Hence another solution is needed.
  Here, we present stochastic GLP (sGLP), designed to allow grassroots platforms to be simulated at scale from the vGLP programs that deploy them, with stochastic agents in place of people. sGLP is GLP with a rate extension for specifying stochastic behaviour. A stochastic agent is an sGLP program replacing both the vGLP UI and the person behind it. It is typed by the dual of the interactive type of the UI and specifies a stochastic profile of a person's behaviour.
  We demonstrate sGLP on the grassroots social graph, with a population of men and women drawn from four stochastic profiles --- homophile or indifferent, wary or sociable --- and on grassroots currencies, with four profiles --- spenders or savers, cautious or generous --- and report what the mix of profiles does to the social graph that forms and to the currencies that circulate.
  We prove that every run of a vGLP program in which sGLP agents replace the UI and the people behind it is a vGLP run. We implemented sGLP in GLP by Gillespie's method, and ran reproducible simulations with it.

Programming Languages.title: Kaizen: Metamorphic Fuzzing and Differential Testing for LLM-Translated HPC Applications
Programming Languages.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to port scientific codes across heterogeneous high-performance computing (HPC) programming models, such as translating CUDA to OpenMP, OpenACC, Kokkos or SYCL. However, current evaluations use compilation success, token-level similarity, or developer-written tests from static benchmarks, which cannot reliably ensure behavioral correctness. We present Kaizen, a metamorphic fuzzing and differential testing framework for evaluating the correctness of LLM-translated HPC code. Kaizen uses metamorphic fuzzing via source-code mutation to generate semantically equivalent programs, grammar-based input fuzzing to explore behavioral diversity, and differential testing to expose semantic divergences between original and translated applications that compile and pass developer-written tests yet produce incorrect scientific results. We evaluate Kaizen on CUDA-to-OpenMP translation of 16 scientific applications from seven domains using three fine-tuned LLMs at kernel-level and full-program granularity. Our evaluation reveals that (1) compilation success is a poor proxy for correctness; (2) LLM-translated programs exhibit systematic compile-time error patterns, with nine categories for kernel-level translation and 27 for full-program translation; (3) semantic errors that survive compilation are often input-dependent and require differential testing to expose; and (4) full-program translation is substantially harder than kernel-level translation. These findings highlight the need for correctness-oriented evaluation of LLM-assisted HPC code translations.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: A Fast Greedy Algorithm with a 0.45 Approximation Guarantee for the Airplane Refueling Problem
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We study a natural greedy algorithm for the Airplane Refueling Problem (ARP), based on a well-known priority rule. We show that this algorithm achieves an approximation guarantee of $9/20$, noticeably improving the previously known $1/12$ guarantee for a fast algorithm. We also show that the same priority rule can be implemented in $O(n\log n)$ time and $O(n)$ space using a dynamic convex-hull data structure. These results provide a worst-case approximation guarantee for an existing greedy priority rule and establish an efficient implementation. In the real-RAM model, the running-time bound is independent of the magnitude of the processing times. The resulting method is also suitable as a fast primal routine inside more complex exact and approximation algorithms for large instances. These results narrow the gap between theoretically strong but complex approximation schemes and lightweight algorithms that can be used directly in computational pipelines. The algorithm combines a simple selection rule with a provable performance bound, making it a useful baseline for further algorithmic studies of ARP.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: nanoflann: A Header-Only KD-Tree Library for Exact Nearest-Neighbor Search on Compile-Time Product Manifolds
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Nearest-neighbor (NN) search underlies countless robotics algorithms, but many state spaces are not Euclidean: orientations live on $SO(2)$ or $SO(3)$ and poses on $SE(2)$ or $SE(3)$, and a Euclidean KD-tree on their raw coordinates returns wrong neighbors. We present a header-only, dependency-free C++ KD-tree library for exact NN search on user-defined product manifolds declared at compile time: the space is composed from base manifolds ($\mathbb{R}^n$, $SO(2)$, $SO(3)$, $S^n$; products $SE(2)$, $SE(3)$, tori) with a single type alias, and the library synthesizes a metric whose pruning is provably admissible, wrap-aware for circular coordinates and double-cover-aware for unit quaternions. Experiments confirm exactness (recall $1.0$ vs an exhaustive scan under the same product metric), where the Euclidean-on-raw shortcut collapses to recall $\approx 0.5^{m}$ for $m$ rotation blocks, with up to three orders of magnitude speedup over brute force. We further contribute an incremental, self-balancing single-tree index for points under heavy churn (e.g. sliding-window LiDAR maps) or $SE(3)$ trajectories: bounded memory and faster updates than prior work, with an optional asynchronous tail-latency-bounding mode. The implementation is open source: https://github.com/jlblancoc/nanoflann
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: 8 pages, 4 figures, accepted for publication in the IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (IEEE RA-L)

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: A Fixed Parameter Sublinear Time Approximation Scheme for Metric Min-Sum Clustering
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
Metric $k$-minsum clustering is a simple, natural, appealing density-based clustering criterion whose computational complexity remains poorly understood, despite the progress achieved fornother clustering criteria in the past three decades. In this paper we give an efficient approximation scheme for this problem that runs in sublinear time for mildly increasing $k$, and thus is fixed parameter tractable with respect to the parameter $k$. We complement this result by showing that similar algorithms are unlikely to exist for the closely related problems $k$-median and balanced $k$-median, assuming popular fine-grained complexity conjectures. Specifically, we show that no sublinear time algorithm with small approximation factors can exist even for $2$-median and balanced $2$-median.
  It was previously known that no efficient PTAS can exist for $k$-median and our results show a strong and perhaps surprising separation between the $k$-minsum clustering problem and $k$-median even in the sublinear regime. Our upper bounds improve qualitatively upon decades old results. Our lower bounds establish the first use of the Distributed PCP framework to clustering problems.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Parameterized Capacitated Vertex Cover Revisited
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
Capacitated Vertex Cover is a generalization of Vertex Cover where we seek a set of $k$ vertices covering all edges, but with the added constraint that for each vertex we are given a capacity, that is, a maximum number of incident edges the vertex can cover if selected. This problem is well-studied in parameterized complexity and is known to be in XP but W[1]-hard parameterized by treewidth. Natural dynamic programs lead to complexities of the form $C^{\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{tw})}n^{\mathcal{O}(1)}$, $Δ^{\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{tw})}n^{\mathcal{O}(1)}$, or $k^{\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{tw})}n^{\mathcal{O}(1)}$, where $C, Δ$ are respectively the maximum capacity and maximum degree. These results imply an FPT algorithm for parameter $k$ with complexity $k^{\mathcal{O}(k)}n^{\mathcal{O}(1)}$, as $\mathrm{tw}\le k$.
  These simple dynamic programming algorithms essentially constitute the state of the art. Our main question is therefore whether these algorithms can be improved. We address this question from numerous angles...
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: Abstract cropped to meet arXiv's requirements

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Approximating the Rural Postman Problem below 3/2
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We give an approximation algorithm for the rural postman problem with approximation ratio strictly smaller than $3/2$. We obtain this result by adapting to the rural postman problem the technique of sampling from maximum entropy distributions for the metric traveling salesman problem of Karlin, Klein, and Oveis Gharan. We also observe that, for every fixed $\varepsilon>0$, any $α$-approximation algorithm for the metric traveling salesman problem yields an $(α+\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithm for the rural postman problem; this implication is already implicit in the treatment of edges that must be traversed in the work of Lampis on the inapproximability of the traveling salesman problem.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: The Cost of Changing Edges for Diameter Computation and More
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
The sensitivity setting is a restricted setting for dynamic algorithms, particularly practical for scenarios where extensive preprocessing is feasible but responses to real-time modifications must be near-instantaneous before the data structure is eventually rebuilt. For graph problems, a sensitivity data structure is constructed with a preprocessing time P so that the following queries can be answered quickly, preferably in $O(1)$ time: given an edge $e$, return the answer to the problem on either $G \setminus e$ (decremental) or $G \cup e$ (incremental).
  We almost entirely settle the decremental setting for the diameter and eccentricities problems in a variety of approximation regimes by matching P to the static runtime while supporting $O(1)$-time queries, thereby improving upon all previous single-failure results [Biló, Cohen, Friedrich, Schirneck, MFCS 2021; Biló, Choudhary, Cohen, Friedrich, Krogmann, Schirneck, ICALP 2023, Algorithmica 2026]. More precisely: (1) We provide a tight reduction demonstrating that any exact distance sensitivity oracle can be used to efficiently solve decremental exact diameter and all-node eccentricities; (2) For the approximate setting, we match the runtime of all known static diameter algorithms across all sparsity settings, up to an additional $1+o(1)$ factor in approximation.
  Conversely, for the previously unexplored incremental setting of these problems: (3) We develop new lower bounds, demonstrating that no incremental algorithm can efficiently approximate diameter, radius, or eccentricity beyond a $5/3$ factor in undirected graphs or a $2$ factor in directed graphs; (4) We introduce two new instructive techniques and demonstrate how to utilize them to construct several new algorithms. Most notably, we develop incremental single-node eccentricity approximations for both directed and undirected graphs that match our new lower bounds.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: Corrected some errors and added an appendix with some (slight) improvement found by ChatGPT Astra for the reduction from decremental (exact) eccentries to DSOs. To appear at SODA 2027

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Toward Optimal Time-Space Tradeoffs for Set Reconciliation
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Set reconciliation, where two parties each holding a large set of elements aim to identify their set difference, is a fundamental task in many areas. Time (computation cost) and space (communication cost) are two important metrics in this problem, and much existing work optimizes one at the expense of the other, creating a clear trade-off. We study this trade-off through algorithmic upper bounds and matching space lower bounds. On one side, we propose XYZ-Sketch. For sufficiently large $d$, XYZ-Sketch achieves high-probability reconciliation for sets whose differing elements are uniformly random, using only $(1+\varepsilon)d$ elements for communication, while achieving $O(\log(1/\varepsilon))$ insertion time and expected $O(d\log V\log^{3/2}(1/\varepsilon))$ decoding time, where $d$ and $V$ denote the size of the difference between two sets and the universe size, respectively. On the other side, we establish a broad fixed-support canonical model and prove a matching space lower bound, establishing the asymptotic optimality of XYZ-Sketch. Our proof also establishes an extremality theorem resolving Walzer's conjecture. Experiments demonstrate the practical advantages of XYZ-Sketch, and the source code is available at https://github.com/djwj233/XYZ-Sketch.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: A Simple Algorithm for the Directed Multiple Source Replacement Paths Problem
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
In the replacement paths (RP) problem, we are given a graph $G = (V, E)$ with $n = |V|$ and $m = |E|$, together with two vertices $s, t \in V$, and are asked to compute the shortest-path distance from $s$ to $t$ in $G \setminus e$ for every failed edge $e \in E$. The multiple source replacement paths (MSRP) problem is its natural generalization: given a set $S \subseteq V$ of $σ$ sources, compute the replacement path distances for all pairs in $S \times V$.
  In this paper, we present a randomized combinatorial algorithm that solves MSRP on unweighted directed graphs in $\tilde{O}(m\sqrt{σn} + σn^2)$ time, with all the output distances correct with high probability. This improves the best known bound $\tilde{O}(m\min\{σ\sqrt{n}, n\} + σn^2)$ for directed graphs, which is obtained either by running the single source RP algorithm of Chechik and Magen [ICALP'20] from each source separately or by constructing and querying the all-pairs distance sensitivity oracle of Bernstein and Karger [STOC'09]. Our running time is essentially tight among combinatorial algorithms because Gupta, Jain, and Modi [PODC'20] proved a lower bound of $m{(σn)}^{1/2-o(1)}$ for such algorithms, which holds even on undirected graphs, and the additive term $σn^2$ is proportional to the time needed to write down the $Θ(σn^2)$ output distances. The algorithm is also remarkably simple.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: 15 pages, 1 figure. To appear in SOSA 2027

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Random Fourier Features in Near-Linear Time
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Random Fourier features approximate a shift-invariant kernel in $\mathbb{R}^d$, such as the Gaussian kernel $\exp(-\tfrac12\|x-y\|_2^2)$, using independent samples from its spectral measure to construct an unbiased estimator for the kernel value with subgaussian concentration. However, generating $m$ such features requires $O(md)$ time. A long line of work on structured random features has accelerated this computation for the Gaussian kernel and other radial kernels, albeit with weaker concentration guarantees. We close this gap by showing a random feature map that can be computed in near-linear time $O((d+m)\log d)$ and yields near-subgaussian concentration. We obtain it through a new and tighter analysis of the Fastfood feature map of Le, Sarlós and Smola (ICML 2013), using Brascamp-Lieb inequalities and the Schoenberg representation of radial kernels.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: The Matching Number Characterizes the Query Complexity of Edge Counting and Degree Moment Estimation
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Consider an unknown graph $G = (V,E)$ with vertex degrees $d_v$, accessed only by sampling uniformly random edges and querying the degrees of their endpoints. We study the query complexity of estimating the number of edges $m$ and the degree moments $M_s = \sum_{v \in V} (d_v)^s$ for fixed integers $s \ge 2$. In this model, [Beretta and Tětek, TALG 2024] estimate $m$ within relative error $\varepsilon$ using $O(\log n/\varepsilon^2+\sqrt n/\varepsilon)$ expected queries without knowing the number of vertices $n$, and [Bhattacharya and Pradhan, CIAC 2025] estimate $M_s$ using $O(n^{1-1/s}/\varepsilon^2)$ queries when $n$ is given. We show that the query complexity of both problems is governed by the matching number $ν$ of $G$ (the maximum number of pairwise disjoint edges) rather than the number of vertices $n$, and that the dependence on $\varepsilon$ for degree moments can be polynomially improved. Our algorithms rest on a simple observation: the endpoints of a maximum matching cover every edge, so a random endpoint of a random edge falls on this set of $2ν$ vertices with probability at least $1/2$. For every $\varepsilon\in(0,1]$, we give advice-free algorithms that estimate $m$ and $M_s$ within relative error $\varepsilon$ with probability at least $2/3$, without knowledge of $n$, $ν$, or other graph parameters. Specifically, our algorithms use $O(\min\{ν/\varepsilon, 1/\varepsilon^2+\sqrtν/\varepsilon\})$ expected queries for $m$ and $O(\min\{ν^{1-1/s}/\varepsilon^{2/s}, ν^{1-1/(2s-1)}/\varepsilon^{2/(2s-1)}\})$ for $M_s$. Finally, our lower bounds show that for every $k \ge 2$ and sufficiently small $\varepsilon$, these query complexities are optimal up to constant factors over graphs with matching number at most $k$.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Faster Deterministic Approximation for Counting Knapsack
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
Given $n$ nonnegative integer weights $w_1, \ldots, w_n$ and an integer knapsack capacity $T$, the $\#$Knapsack problem asks to count the number of subsets $I \subseteq \{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ such that $\sum_{i \in I} w_i \le T$. A long line of research has been devoted to designing faster $(1 \pm \varepsilon)$-approximation algorithms for this \#P-hard problem. Until very recently, the best-known time complexity was $\tilde{O}\bigl(n^{2.5}/\mathrm{poly}(\varepsilon)\bigr)$, achieved by the randomized algorithm of [Dyer, STOC 2003] and the deterministic algorithm of [Gawrychowski, Markin, and Weimann, ICALP 2018]. The recent work by [Feng and Jin, SODA 2025] improved the randomized complexity to $\tilde{O}\bigl(n^{1.5}/\mathrm{poly}(\varepsilon)\bigr)$, leaving open the question whether this $n^{2.5}$ barrier could also be broken by a \emph{deterministic} algorithm.
  In this work, we answer this question in the affirmative by presenting a deterministic $(1 + \varepsilon)$-approximation algorithm for \#Knapsack in $\tilde{O}\bigl(n^{2.4}/\mathrm{poly}(\varepsilon)\bigr)$ time. Our key technical innovation is to deterministically simulate the balancing technique, which was previously used in the literature of knapsack-type problems via random partitions and seemed to require randomization.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: String Representation Based on Substring Equation Systems
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Repetitiveness measures quantify how much repetitive structure a string contains and serve as parameters for compressed representations and indexing data structures. Many compression schemes represent strings by recording equalities between identical substrings. We study string compression based on substring equation systems (SESs), which represent strings as unique solutions to substring-equality and character-assignment constraints. We show that every string $w$ has an SES of size $O(χ(w))$, where $χ(w)$ is the size of a smallest suffixient set for $w$ with a unique terminal symbol appended. This result establishes the reachability of $χ$, which had been an open problem. We also prove that computing the size $s(w)$ of the smallest SES that represents $w$ is NP-hard and $(1 + \varepsilon)$-inapproximable for some fixed constant $\varepsilon > 0$. Finally, we prove that the size $b(w)$ of the smallest bidirectional macro scheme (BMS) representing $w$ satisfies $s(w) \leq b(w) \leq 4s(w)$. Hence, SES and BMS are equivalent up to a constant factor, and this equivalence gives the new bound $b(w) \in O(χ(w))$.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: W[1]-Hardness of Upper Clique Transversal
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: A clique transversal of a graph is a set of vertices intersecting every maximal clique. We prove that deciding whether a graph has an inclusion-wise minimal clique transversal of size at least $k$ is W[1]-hard when parameterized by $k$.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Publishing Below-Threshold Triangle Counts under Local Weight Differential Privacy
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We propose an algorithm for counting below-threshold triangles in weighted graphs under local weight differential privacy. While prior work has largely focused on unweighted graphs, edge weights are intrinsic to many real-world networks. We consider the setting in which the graph topology is publicly known and privacy is required only for the contribution of an individual to incident edge weights, capturing practical scenarios such as road and telecommunication networks. Our method uses two rounds of communication. In the first round, each node releases privatized information about its incident edge weights under local weight differential privacy. In the second round, nodes locally count below-threshold triangles using this privatized information; we introduce both biased and unbiased variants of the estimator. We further develop two refinements: (i) a pre-computation step that reduces covariance and thus lowers expected error, and (ii) an efficient procedure for computing smooth sensitivity, which substantially reduces running time relative to a straightforward implementation. Finally, we present experimental results that quantify the trade-offs between the biased and unbiased variants and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed improvements.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Asymptotically Faster Algorithms for Recognizing $(k,\ell)$-Sparse Graphs
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: For fixed integers $k,\ell$ with $0\leq\ell<3k$, we study the problem of deciding whether a graph is $(k,\ell)$-sparse, a notion arising in combinatorial optimization and rigidity theory. Standard pebble-game algorithms take $O(n^2)$ time for $0\leq\ell<2k$ and $O(n^3)$ time for $2k\leq\ell<3k$, although faster algorithms were known for some parameter choices. We develop efficient recognition algorithms using bounded-indegree orientations, reductions to rooted arc-connectivity, augmenting paths, and centroid decomposition. For $0\leq\ell<2k$, they run in $O(n^{1+o(1)})$ time, yielding the first subquadratic bound valid throughout the entire range. Purely combinatorial implementations run in $O(n\sqrt n)$ time throughout this range. For graphs with $O(n)$ edges, we also improve the purely combinatorial running time for decomposing the edge set into a fixed number of forests, or certifying that no such decomposition exists, from $O(n\sqrt{n\log n})$ to $O(n\sqrt n)$. For simple graphs with $2k\leq\ell<3k$, the general recognition algorithm runs in $O(n^2)$ time when $\ell\leq2k+2$ and in $O(n^2\log n)$ time otherwise. When $\ell=2k$ and $k\leq3$, a specialized algorithm improves this to $O(n^{1+o(1)})$ and admits a purely combinatorial $O(n\sqrt n)$ implementation. Whenever the input graph is not $(k,\ell)$-sparse, our recognition algorithms return an explicit violating vertex set.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Dense Weak Hiding: Closing Complexity Gaps in Nonconvex and PL Finite-Sum Optimization under Individual Smoothness
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
Under individual smoothness, known algorithms for nonconvex finite-sum optimization use $O(n+\sqrt nΔL_{\max}/\varepsilon^2)$ incremental first-order oracle (IFO) calls, while existing lower bounds miss the factor $\sqrt n$ in the second term. We prove the matching lower bound $Ω(n+\sqrt nΔL_{\max}/\varepsilon^2)$ for randomized IFO algorithms, allowing component indices and query points to depend on the complete preceding history. Thus PAGE and SPIDER are minimax optimal up to universal constants under individual and mean-squared smoothness.
  Under the global Polyak-Lojasiewicz (PL) condition, prior lower bounds did not capture the correct dependence on $n$ under individual smoothness, and the regime of small $κ$ remained open for randomized IFO algorithms. We prove an $Ω(n+κ_{\max}\sqrt n\log(Δ/\varepsilon))$ lower bound for $κ_{\max}\ge\sqrt n$, and an $Ω(n+n\log(Δ/\varepsilon)/(1+\log(\sqrt n/κ_{\max})))$ lower bound for $3\leκ_{\max}\le\sqrt n$. Restarted PAGE attains matching upper bounds under mean-squared smoothness in terms of $κ_{\rm ms}=L_{\rm ms}/μ$.
  Our lower bounds use dense weak hiding. Each hidden direction is spread across all components, making individual queries weakly informative while preserving the direction in the average. A sufficiently large dimension makes premature activation of future stages unlikely within the query budget. Balancing the cost of revealing a stage against the number of stages permitted by individual smoothness yields the missing $\sqrt n$ factor.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Revenue Maximization in Choice-Based Matching Markets
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: The primary contribution of this paper resides in devising constant-factor approximation guarantees for revenue maximization in two-sided matching markets with general pairwise rewards. A major distinction between our work and state-of-the-art results in this context (Ashlagi et al., 2022; Torrico et al., 2023) is that, for the first time, we are able to address reward maximization, reflected by assigning each customer-supplier pair an arbitrarily-valued reward. Our performance guarantees apply to two different settings: the customized model and the inclusive model. The fundamental difference between these settings lies in whether the platform should display to each supplier all selecting customers, as in the inclusive model, or whether the platform can further personalize this set, as in the customized model. Technically speaking, our algorithmic approaches and their analysis revolve around presenting a closely related combinatorial problem, a novel linear relaxation, and developing tailor-made analytical ideas. In both models considered, these ingredients allow us to overcome the lack of submodularity and subadditivity that stems from pairwise rewards, plaguing the applicability of existing methods. We complement our theoretical results with an extensive computational study under different classes of instances where we analyze the empirical reward and running time performance of our proposed methods.

Graphics.title: Lambda-Hold Control: Human-Like Movement Emerges from a Minimal Task Reward in Predictive Musculoskeletal Simulation
Graphics.summary: The massive overactuation in the human musculoskeletal system makes it challenging to train musculoskeletal models to generate human-like motion via reinforcement learning, primarily because exploration in the resulting high-dimensional and redundant action space is extremely inefficient. To address this problem, we propose the $λ$-hold controller, inspired by the equilibrium-point (EP) hypothesis, which has been widely supported by extensive evidence from human motor control studies. The policy's control variable is the per-muscle EP threshold length $λ$, from which a stretch-reflex recruitment law computes the muscle excitations automatically. Holding each $λ$ over an interval of the gait phase also sharply reduces the frequency at which the policy must be queried. Consequently, the controller, to our knowledge for the first time, enables a muscle-actuated skeletal model to learn human-like sprinting using only a minimal reward within an hour of training. The efficient exploration through the proposed $λ$-hold controller is not merely an engineering trick but an approach grounded in physiology, bringing together the EP hypothesis, intermittent control, and optimal feedback control. Beyond encapsulating human-like behavior in predictive simulation, this achievement contributes to developing a learnable model of the human motor controller.
Graphics.comment: 20 pages, 8 figures, 1 table. Project page and video demos: https://lee-jun-hyuk-37.github.io/projects/lambda-hold/. Code: https://github.com/Lee-Jun-Hyuk-37/Lambda-Hold (archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23265020)

Graphics.title: Learning Dynamic Grasping
Graphics.summary: Synthesizing believable 4D hand-object grasping sequences is important for character animation, extended reality, and embodied agents. Grasping requires a hand to approach, contact, and lift or manipulate an object coherently. Existing synthesis methods often model only the final static grasp or rely on additional conditions, such as language, target grasps, or object trajectories, to specify the interaction. We instead study the underconstrained problem of generating a complete grasping motion from a single initial hand-object state. Our framework decouples hand-motion generation from object-motion recovery. Given an object point cloud in the initial wrist frame and the initial parameterized hand configuration, conditional flow matching predicts a sequence-level contact map and a hand pose at each normalized sequence time. This time-indexed formulation avoids the error accumulation of autoregressive rollout while representing the complete motion. We then infer an attachment frame and recover rigid-object motion through training-free, contact-guided weighted registration. We evaluate on held-out DexYCB objects and unseen object geometries reconstructed from in-the-wild videos by Open-CHOIR. Compared with LatentHOI, our method produces smoother hand and object motion in every setting, matches or improves on its contact and penetration metrics in the wild under a shared initialization, and is about 30x faster per generated frame. In a 15-participant study, our motions were preferred in roughly two thirds of (forced-choice pairwise) comparisons. Precise contact closure on novel geometry, however, remains a key open challenge.

Graphics.title: Feed-Forward 3D Scene Modeling: A Problem-Driven Perspective
Graphics.summary: Reconstructing 3D representations from 2D inputs is a fundamental task in computer vision and graphics, serving as a cornerstone for understanding and interacting with the physical world. While traditional methods achieve high fidelity, they are limited by slow per-scene optimization or category-specific training, which hinders their practical deployment and scalability. Hence, generalizable feed-forward 3D reconstruction has witnessed rapid development in recent years. By learning a model that maps images directly to 3D representations in a single forward pass, these methods enable efficient reconstruction and robust cross-scene generalization. Our survey is motivated by a critical observation: despite the diverse geometric output representations, ranging from implicit fields to explicit primitives, existing feed-forward approaches share similar high-level architectural patterns, such as image feature extraction backbones, multi-view information fusion mechanisms, and geometry-aware design principles. Consequently, we abstract away from these representation differences and instead focus on model design, proposing a novel taxonomy centered on model design strategies that are agnostic to the output format. Our proposed taxonomy organizes the research directions into five key problems that drive recent research development: feature enhancement, geometry awareness, model efficiency, augmentation strategies and temporal-aware models. To support this taxonomy with empirical grounding and standardized evaluation, we further comprehensively review related benchmarks and datasets, and extensively discuss and categorize real-world applications based on feed-forward 3D models. Finally, we outline future directions to address open challenges such as scalability, evaluation standards, and world modeling.
Graphics.comment: 67 pages, 395 references. Project page: https://ff3d-survey.github.io. Code: https://github.com/ziplab/Awesome-Feed-Forward-3D. This work has been submitted to Springer for possible publication

Graphics.title: Automatic assembly modeling through attention-based assembly feature mate prediction and assembly feature pattern recognition
Graphics.summary:
Assembly modeling plays an important role in constructing product models, yet it is still mainly performed via interactive operations that are experience-dependent and labor-intensive. Data-driven strategies hold promise for automating this process; however, existing approaches either predict poses that cannot directly generate editable B-Rep assembly constraints or require prescribed part pairs or predefined assembly faces.
  To reduce the large candidate space of constraint prediction without predefined assembly faces, we propose a data-driven framework based on assembly feature mate prediction. The framework performs automatic assembly modeling from unassembled B-Rep parts, using assembly features to group the geometric entities of local mating interfaces and restrict candidate formation. Given the lack of suitable assembly feature annotations in existing datasets, we construct a large-scale dataset through an automatic annotation pipeline. Using the annotated dataset, we train an attention-based network to predict assembly feature mates, with Engineering Compatibility Fusion (ECF) incorporating explicit engineering compatibility into learned matching scores. To improve the accuracy of automatic assembly modeling, we use assembly feature patterns (AFPs) to guide the matching process. Finally, a post-processing search selects assembly feature mate and AFP mate candidates, whose associated constraints are generated and solved to complete assembly modeling.
  Experimental results show that the framework achieves assembly constraint accuracies of 74.79% on the six-assembly comparison set and 64.09% on the extended test set of 16 assemblies, which includes the comparison set. With ground-truth face labels supplied as additional input, the corresponding accuracies increase to 81.78% and 80.93%, respectively.

Graphics.title: Reels-RSI: Program-Level Self-Improvement for Code-Rendered Explainer Videos
Graphics.summary: Explainer videos -- a worked geometry problem, why the sky is blue, how a dynasty fell -- are usually one more target for pixel video generation. We argue they are a different kind of artifact: a program (script, storyboard and per-frame animation code) that a deterministic renderer turns into frames. A program can be read, diffed, tested and audited; pixels can only be watched. Reels-RSI is an open-source reel director for any agent harness; its self-improvement happens at the program level rather than in weights or prompts. Every revision pass is logged with a code snapshot; a retrospective pairs each check finding with the diff that fixed it and proposes lessons; a lesson that a static check can catch is compiled into a rule with a must-fail and a must-pass example, so the memory is unit-tested; and a rule learned today runs over everything made before it. A bounded, benchmark-gated step lets an agent rewrite the director's playbook, kept only when blind pairwise judgments on held-out topics prefer it; nothing enters memory without a human decision. Across 111 reels -- a field study, two playbook evolutions, a 2x2 memory ablation, a weaker director, a 48-reel learning curve and a judge-reliability study -- we find that the rule learned in the field caught four latent defects in frames authored before it existed and none after; that rules are an audit for a strong director (eight unguarded reels, no violation) and a guard for a weaker one (thirty violations unguarded versus five); that lessons shorten revision loops but do not compound or move the judge; and that the first rewrite's 11--1 verdict was a position bias in our vote design (judges pick the second-shown reel 62--81% of the time), masking scripts that traded thirteen facts for craft. We document four failure modes of the preference signal, which check caught each, and the fixes. Code, rules, lessons and data are public.
Graphics.comment: 19 pages, 4 figures, 9 tables. Code, rules, lessons, data and evolve reports: https://github.com/agentic-loops-x/Reels-RSI

Hardware Architecture.title: STISA: A 0.16 GOPS/W/PE Single-Shot Inference FPGA-based SNN Accelerator with Algorithm and Hardware Co-Design
Hardware Architecture.summary: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) offer great potential for low-power intelligent computing owing to their event-driven nature, yet their deployment is limited by high inference latency and inefficient hardware utilization caused by temporal dependencies. Existing accelerators struggle to balance timesteps, accuracy, and energy efficiency, while hardware-oriented timestep compression remains underexplored. To address these challenges, this work presents STISA, a unified algorithm-hardware co-design framework featuring: (i) a Temporal Splitter Compression (TSC) technique with a Temporal Split Structure (TSS) to reduce temporal redundancy while preserving network dynamics; (ii) a hardware-efficient spatiotemporal parallelism scheme, which co-optimizes dataflow and architecture through a Temporal-Prioritized Output-Stationary (TPOS) mapping and a flexible Block-Mux Streaming (BMS) architecture; and (iii) a joint TSC-TPOS-BMS co-optimization framework featuring a bandwidth-aware resource allocation strategy to achieve balanced accuracy, latency, and energy efficiency across diverse network architectures. On the algorithmic side, TSC reduces synaptic operations by 24.44%-51.71% while achieving competitive accuracies of 96.38%, 81.10%, 68.51%, and 82.40% on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet, and DVS-CIFAR10, respectively. On the hardware side, FPGA prototypes deliver up to 7.99 speedup, 30.4% power reduction, and 30.1% LUT reduction. Compared with state-of-the-art SNN accelerators, STISA achieves 0.16 GOPS/W/PE, demonstrating its scalability and superior energy efficiency for real-time SNN inference under constrained hardware resources.
Hardware Architecture.comment: Author accepted manuscript. Published in IEEE Transactions on Circuits and Systems I: Regular Papers

Hardware Architecture.title: CAFE: Conducting-Cell-Aware Adaptive Differential Encoding for Robust DNN Inference in FeFET-Based Compute-in-Memory
Hardware Architecture.summary: Ferroelectric field-effect transistor (FeFET)-based compute-in-memory (CIM) promises energy-efficient deep neural network (DNN) inference, but device variation can severely degrade bit-sliced CIM accuracy. Prior works either rely on hardware modifications or treat such variation as generic noise, overlooking a key FeFET asymmetry: negligible off-state leakage makes errors dominated by conducting on-state cells. This asymmetry is amplified by two's-complement sign extension, which maps small negative values to high-significance bit slices and magnifies their errors during shift-and-add reconstruction. In this paper, we propose CAFE, a conducting-cell-aware adaptive differential encoding framework built upon this FeFET-specific asymmetry. CAFE introduces C$^2$AM, a bit-significance-weighted conducting-cell activity metric that predicts output deviation and inference accuracy degradation under FeFET device variation. Guided by C$^2$AM, CAFE applies differential weight and activation encoding to eliminate sign-extension-induced conducting-cell amplification. To balance robustness and cost, CAFE performs type-wise encoding enumeration, layer-wise NSGA-II search, and post-GA pruning to allocate robust encodings where the robustness-cost trade-off is favorable. Across representative vision and language workloads, CAFE reduces C$^2$AM by up to $28.6\times$; in the main deployment study, it improves accuracy over two's-complement CIM by more than 87 percentage points and approaches full-differential robustness at $1.86$-$2.78\times$ normalized cost, compared with $3.06\times$ for uniform full-differential encoding.
Hardware Architecture.comment: Full version of the paper accepted to the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Computer Design (ICCD). 16 figures, 1 table

Hardware Architecture.title: ESL-former: Event Sparse Linear Transformer for FPGA-Accelerated Malware Detection
Hardware Architecture.summary: Transformer based intrusion detection has shown strong potential for identifying unknown malware variants, but its deployment on resource constrained edge devices remains difficult due to the high computational and memory cost of self attention. This paper presents an event sparse Linear Transformer framework for malware detection on FPGA edge platforms. Instead of relying on an explicit attention matrix, the proposed method derives token and channel importance directly from the accumulated key value state of Linear Transformer. A contribution aware scoring function is introduced to measure the perturbation of each token or kernel channel to the linear attention state, allowing redundant tokens and low contribution channels to be removed without constructing quadratic attention maps. To translate sparsity into practical hardware acceleration, the proposed design further replaces conventional binary mask based execution with a Top K active token buffer and a hardware compaction unit. The selected active tokens and channels are reorganized into dense fixed length data streams, enabling downstream processing elements to execute regular multiply accumulate operations with reduced redundant memory access and control overhead. This design is suitable for low power FPGA based malware detection, where both latency and on chip resource usage are critical. Experimental evaluation demonstrates that the proposed sparse Linear Transformer can reduce hardware cost while preserving malware classification accuracy.
Hardware Architecture.comment: Accepted at ICA3PP 2026. 19 pages, 5 figures

Hardware Architecture.title: MFSA: A Multi-Format Systolic Array with Native Micro Scaling Support
Hardware Architecture.summary: AI workloads increasingly employ low-precision formats such as BF16 / FP16, FP8 variants, FP4, Micro Scaling (MX), and INT modes across models, layers, and execution stages to balance accuracy, memory footprint, and throughput, which in turn requires hardware to support these formats in a flexible and efficient way. We present MFSA, a weight-stationary multi-format systolic array that achieves area efficiency through two architectural choices. At the PE level, MFSA uses dot-product-accumulator-based processing elements extended from an existing open-source trans-precision FPU to support reduced-precision formats (FP32/FP16/BF16/CFP8/FP4/INT16/INT8/INT4) with a shared datapath and proportional throughput scaling. At the array level, MFSA employs Online Block-Scale Rebasing (OBSR) for block-scaled formats, which folds each block scale into the running FP32 partial sum at block boundaries without adding a second cross-block accumulator, thereby reducing the additional overhead of block-scaling support. In TSMC 28 nm at 1 GHz, matched-throughput BF16/FP8/FP4 cascaded FMA-PE baselines are 1.5x/2.5x/4.5x larger than the single-format DPA-PE, the gap growing with subword parallelism. A routed 16x16 MFSA reaches a peak 0.5/1/2/4 TOPS of FP32/BF16/FP8/FP4, and OBSR cuts the incremental MX overhead by 64.2% in area and 67.5% in energy versus a naive MX implementation baseline, without hurting the numerical stability on real LLM traces. Adding support for all other formats based on a BF16+CFP8 systolic array costs 25.7% additional area. OBSR also extends to non-power-of-two block scales: folding the fractional part of an E4M3 scale into the MFPE dot product supports NVFP4 alongside OCP MX for 11.8% area and 7.3% power over a CFP8+FP4 base, less than half the cost of a naive implementation.
Hardware Architecture.comment: Accepted to the 44th IEEE International Conference on Computer Design (ICCD 2026)

Hardware Architecture.title: PAGE404: Breaking GPU Isolation Through Hardware-assisted Page Migration
Hardware Architecture.summary: NVIDIA's Grace Hopper (GH200) superchip represents a new generation of heterogeneous computing, tightly integrating a 72-core Arm-based CPU with a Hopper GPU on a single module via a high-bandwidth, cache-coherent interconnect. By eliminating the conventional PCIe bottleneck for CPU-GPU data movement, this design establishes a unified memory domain that scales to the capacities demanded by generative AI and high-performance computing (HPC) workloads. The architecture also introduces hardware-assisted page migration: driven by access counters, the system dynamically promotes frequently accessed pages from host CPU memory to GPU DRAM to improve memory locality. We study the security of this emerging architecture against new side- and covert-channel attacks targeting its page migration support. We analyze counter-driven migration across both the hardware mechanisms and the UVM driver's interrupt-handling pipeline, and identify two side-channel vulnerabilities: one rooted in the shared structure of access counters, and the other in the driver's response to migration interrupts. We further show that both channels are exploitable across Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) partitions, a feature intended to provide strong, hardware-enforced isolation between co-located tenants. Using proof-of-concept attacks, we build covert channels that reach roughly 8,500 bits per second through eviction-based signaling and 8,100 bits per second through migration-delay-based signaling across MIG instances. The interrupt-based channel also fingerprints inference workloads across distinct large language models (LLMs) and CPU SPEC2017 benchmarks, and estimates the prompt length processed during LLM inference with high accuracy. These results expose a security gap in hardware-managed heterogeneous memory systems and call into question the isolation guarantees of current MIG-enabled multi-tenant GPU deployments.

Hardware Architecture.title: Foundations of Hardware-Software Leakage Contracts
Hardware Architecture.summary:
Microarchitectural attacks such as Spectre and Meltdown undermine security by exploiting software-visible side effects of microarchitectural optimizations like caches and speculative execution. To use modern hardware securely, programmers must take into account the security implications of these optimizations. Yet instruction set architectures (ISAs)---the conventional abstraction layer between hardware and software---are ill-suited for secure programming: by design, they abstract from microarchitectural details and therefore fail to reflect their security consequences.
  A new security abstraction is emerging to fill this void: hardware-software leakage contracts. To support the principled development of secure software on modern hardware such contracts characterize side-channel leakage at the ISA level. Thereby they enable programmers and compilers to generate code that is provably resistant to side-channel attacks---without having to explicitly reason about the microarchitecture. On the other hand, they provide a specification for hardware designers to ensure that microarchitectures do not introduce unintended and undocumented side channels. This paper introduces the foundations of this emerging topic, discussing recent contributions and unresolved challenges along the way.
Hardware Architecture.comment: Author's manuscript. Final publication is available at Springer via https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-981-95-8617-2_4

Hardware Architecture.title: Arcalís: Accelerating Remote Procedure Calls Using a Líghtweight Near-Cache Solution
Hardware Architecture.summary: Modern microservices increasingly depend on high-performance remote procedure calls (RPCs) to coordinate fine-grained, distributed computation. As network bandwidths continue to scale, the CPU overhead associated with RPC processing, particularly serialization, deserialization, and protocol handling, has become a critical bottleneck. This challenge is exacerbated by fast user-space networking stacks such as DPDK, which expose RPC processing as the dominant performance limiter. While prior hardware accelerators have explored NIC-attached and FPGA-based offload, these approaches remain farther from the cache hierarchy, so the frequent data accesses during RPC processing each pay an extra interconnect traversal cost that inflates RPC time. Therefore, RPC handling should occur as close as possible to the cache; however, a near-cache solution must be small, hence practical and deployable. Our key insight to enable such a solution is taking advantage of a reconfigurable accelerator that can be configured specifically for the services currently running on the CPUs. We present Arcalís, a near-cache RPC accelerator that positions a lightweight hardware engine adjacent to the last-level cache (LLC). Arcalís offloads RPC processing to dedicated microengines that operate with cache-line latency while preserving programmability. By decoupling RPC processing logic, enabling microservice-specific execution, and positioning itself near the LLC, Arcalís achieves a 1.72-4.91$\times$ end-to-end speedup compared to the CPU baseline, significantly reduces microarchitectural overhead by up to 88\%, and achieves up to a 1.67$\times$ higher throughput than prior solutions. These results highlight the potential of near-cache RPC acceleration as a practical solution for high-performance microservice deployment.
Hardware Architecture.comment: 14 pages, 26 figures

Hardware Architecture.title: A LoRa-Compatible Receiver with Programmable Noise-Power Trade-Off and Integrated Wake-Up Mode
Hardware Architecture.summary: Programmable receivers allow an optimal performance in the variable conditions of the wireless channel. An extensive analysis of their noise-power trade-off enables the development of a main receiver with embedded wake-up circuitry. This makes the seamless integration of wake-up receivers (WuRXs) in RF receivers possible, avoiding power, area, complexity, and cost overheads in the system. In this paper, we propose the first LoRa-compatible receiver with an integrated wake-up mode and a programmable noise-power trade-off. In main-receiver mode, it consumes 4.57 mW for a sensitivity of -138 dBm, but it can save up to 62.6% of power consumption at the cost of an 8.3-dB sensitivity degradation. In wake-up mode, sensitivity down to -126 dBm is achieved for a 32-ms latency and 1.5 mW of power consumption. The power consumption remains relatively high due to a sub-optimal design of the the phase-locked loop (PLL). In the end, the wake-up mode consumes 3X less than the lowest-noise configuration in main-receiver mode.
Hardware Architecture.comment: 13 pages, 19 figures, submitted to TCAS-I journal

Programming Languages.title: Explorable Proofs: Making Written Proofs Explorable by Grounding Them in Formal Representations
Programming Languages.summary: LLM-generated explanations can make technical content more accessible, but there is a ceiling on what they can support interactively. Because LLM outputs are static text, they cannot be executed or stepped through. We argue that grounding explanations in a formalized representation enables interactive affordances beyond what static text supports. We instantiate this idea for mathematical proof comprehension with explorable theorems, a system that uses LLMs to translate a theorem and its written proof into Lean, a programming language for machine-checked proofs, and links the written proof with the Lean code. Readers can work through the proof at a step-level granularity, test custom examples or counterexamples, and trace the logical dependencies bridging each step. Each worked-out step is produced by executing the Lean proof on that example and extracting its intermediate state. A user study ($n = 16$) shows potential advantages of this approach: in a proof-reading task, participants who had access to the provided explorability features gave better, more correct, and more detailed answers to comprehension questions, demonstrating a stronger overall understanding of the underlying mathematics.

Programming Languages.title: Open-Source AI-Powered Optimization in Scalene: Advancing Python Performance Profiling with DeepSeek-R1 and LLaMA 3.2
Programming Languages.summary: Python's flexibility and ease of use come at the cost of performance inefficiencies, requiring developers to rely on profilers to optimize execution. SCALENE, a high-performance CPU, GPU, and memory profiler, provides fine-grained insights into Python applications while running significantly faster than traditional profilers. Originally, SCALENE integrated OpenAI's API to generate AI-powered optimization suggestions, but its reliance on a proprietary API limited accessibility. This study explores the feasibility of using opensource large language models (LLMs), such as DeepSeek-R1 and Llama 3.2, to generate optimization recommendations within SCALENE. Our evaluation reveals that DeepSeek-R1 provides effective code optimizations comparable to proprietary models. We integrate DeepSeek-R1 into SCALENE to automatically analyze performance bottlenecks and suggest improvements, enhancing SCALENE's utility while maintaining its open-source nature. This study demonstrates that open-source LLMs can be viable alternatives for AI-driven code optimization, paving the way for more accessible and cost-effective performance analysis tools.

Programming Languages.title: MolLean: A Process-Verifiable Language for Chemical Reasoning
Programming Languages.summary: Chemical chain-of-thought can contain hallucinated structural and property claims. We thereby introduce MolLean, a process-verifiable language that grounds chemical reasoning in an explicit molecular state. A layered Lean-based kernel checks state transitions and assertions over molecular readouts, from primitive graph edits to compound transformations. Meanwhile, a typed witness protocol separates native structural checks from externally supplied measurements. We further introduce MolLean-MCP, a stateful tool interface that exposes these transitions, checks, and readouts during generation: the model receives feedback to decide its next action, and rejected actions leave the state unchanged. MolLean supports one-pass trace execution, whole-trace refinement, and interactive reasoning through MolLean-MCP. We evaluate these three modes with direct chain-of-thought on 8,800 matched examples across 12 tasks spanning molecular generation, editing, optimization, and reactions. With Qwen3.6-27B, whole-trace refinement outperforms direct chain-of-thought on all 12 tasks. MolLean-MCP complements whole-trace refinement with stepwise verification feedback, reaching better performance in reaction tasks. Together, these results highlight an executable foundation for chemical reasoning, in which explicit chemical commitments can be checked and revised rather than remaining solely in free-form explanations.

Programming Languages.title: Cover Semantics for Intuitionistic Modalities
Programming Languages.summary: Intuitionistic modal logic (IML) has inspired several developments in programming languages including modal type systems for staging, computational effects and language-based security. IMLs are typically studied using Kripke-style relational semantics, which simplifies proofs of meta-theoretic properties, such as completeness and consistency, by making it easy to construct models. Kripke-style relational semantics, however, relies upon classical reasoning principles, which makes it unappealing from a computational perspective and unsuitable for formalization in a constructive type theory. Goldblatt provides an alternative semantics for IMLs by extending Beth-Kripke-Joyal-style "cover" semantics for intuitionistic propositional logic with relations to support modalities. Goldblatt's "relational cover" semantics overcomes classical reasoning but introduces a new limitation: it relies upon a "modal localization" condition that restricts the class of models and complicates model construction. Goldblatt bypasses this restriction by using intricate order-theoretic completion arguments to prove completeness. In this article, we present a conservative extension of relational cover semantics that alleviates this restriction and is amenable to simpler and standard model construction techniques. We formalize our semantics in Agda and prove completeness constructively in the style of Normalization by Evaluation for a variety of IMLs featuring independent box and diamond modalities.

Programming Languages.title: Typechecking without Minimum Types: Finite Bases and Backward Checking for $F_{<:}^{\top}$
Programming Languages.summary:
System $F_{<:}^{\top}$ has decidable subtyping but lacks minimum types. We prove that typechecking is decidable for arbitrary explicitly annotated terms with unrestricted subsumption. The difficulty is that type abstraction uses a variable's declared bound to type its body, while quantified subtyping forgets that bound. We construct finite covers that preserve all required subtype comparisons across this change of context. These covers yield a compositional finite typing basis and a decision procedure.
  We then derive a backward checker that propagates acceptable targets without constructing the complete typing basis. Rectangularity of typing families gives a uniform elimination domain while retaining every result type, even when the canonical type is not least. Finite inverse families transport targets through type substitution. The same inverse specification recovers bound forgetting and yields finite type-avoidance families. Both typechecking procedures are total Rocq functions proved equivalent to the original typing judgment. For a separate symbolic word-RAM realization, we prove a quartic worst-case work bound. We measure family representation sizes and comparison storage in independent OCaml prototypes on synthetic checking judgments.

Programming Languages.title: sGLP: Simulating People with Stochastic Agents
Programming Languages.summary:
Grassroots platforms are designed to be owned, operated and governed by their participants, and thus are constituted from person-to-person smartphone apps that are run by the participants. A grassroots app is specified using a grassroots social contract, which is compiled through an abstraction cascade into a volition-guarded Grassroots Logic Program (vGLP), a multiagent concurrent logic programming language. A vGLP program in turn specifies a smartphone UI via which people express their volitions and thus control the app. Prudence dictates large-scale evaluation and testing of grassroots platforms prior to deployment, but using the many people needed to do that is a contradiction in terms. Hence another solution is needed.
  Here, we present stochastic GLP (sGLP), designed to allow grassroots platforms to be simulated at scale from the vGLP programs that deploy them, with stochastic agents in place of people. sGLP is GLP with a rate extension for specifying stochastic behaviour. A stochastic agent is an sGLP program replacing both the vGLP UI and the person behind it. It is typed by the dual of the interactive type of the UI and specifies a stochastic profile of a person's behaviour.
  We demonstrate sGLP on the grassroots social graph, with a population of men and women drawn from four stochastic profiles --- homophile or indifferent, wary or sociable --- and on grassroots currencies, with four profiles --- spenders or savers, cautious or generous --- and report what the mix of profiles does to the social graph that forms and to the currencies that circulate.
  We prove that every run of a vGLP program in which sGLP agents replace the UI and the people behind it is a vGLP run. We implemented sGLP in GLP by Gillespie's method, and ran reproducible simulations with it.

Programming Languages.title: Formalizing Flag Algebras in Lean
Programming Languages.summary:
Razborov's flag algebra method is one of the most successful tools for proving asymptotic density inequalities in extremal graph theory. It reduces an inequality about all large graphs avoiding a forbidden pattern to finitely many algebraic conditions, and a certificate satisfying them can be found by semidefinite programming. We formalize the method for finite simple graphs in Lean 4, building on Mathlib. The formalization covers flags and their densities, the flag algebra as a quotient vector space, positive homomorphisms as limits of graph sequences, Razborov's random extensions, and the downward operator that averages out labels. On top of this theory, we build verified computation of flag densities and a tactic that turns certificates found by semidefinite programming into Lean proofs. The certificate serves only as candidate data; Lean checks every fact the proof uses.
  With this development we verify seven Turán-type upper bounds. Adding lower-bound constructions proved in Lean yields the asymptotic form of Mantel's theorem and the asymptotic Erdős pentagon theorem $π(C_5;K_3)=24/625$; to our knowledge, the latter has not previously been formalized in a proof assistant. We also prove two inequalities of Goodman. All density theorems reported here depend only on the standard axioms of Lean's logic.
  Formalization also led us to treat forbidden subgraphs with a different semantics. Instead of building a separate flag algebra for each forbidden family, we keep a single algebra of all graphs and impose the constraint only when interpreting an inequality, through randomly labeled limits of graphs satisfying it. We prove that this ensemble semantics yields the intended density bounds, and that a condition we call root-plantability characterizes when it agrees with the standard semantics.

Programming Languages.title: Verifying deployed bytecode against executable EVM semantics, with exact gas and no added axioms
Programming Languages.summary: Much of Ethereum's most consequential code is immutable bytecode: old output of unverified compilers, and protocol logic run as contract code. We show that such bytecode can be verified as it is, without trusting what produced it, without simplifying the machine it runs on, and with no axioms beyond Lean's own. Blanc, a Lean 4 verification stack, reads fixed runtime bytes via kernel-checked certificates and states every theorem against Jaune, an executable semantics of the EVM and block processing that passes all 34,205 blockchain-test cases of Ethereum's fixture release v20.0.2 that involve only forks that have governed mainnet since May 2025. Eight artifacts, deployed from 2017 to 2026, come from seven compiler versions and an assembler. For the EIP-7002 contract, we prove that the end-of-block call to it, whose failure would invalidate the block, succeeds whatever its storage holds, and that each block's withdrawal requests are exactly the oldest pending submissions; mainnet met these theorems' starting premises when Prague began. For a Uniswap V2 pair, we prove that after any valid history whose hashed slots stay apart, from any checkpoint representing its Solidity model's state, the storage represents that model replayed over exactly the committed calls, a balanced liquidity ledger stays balanced, and, under a premise on token answers, geometric-mean reserves per share fall only through the protocol fee. Exact gas makes liveness provable: a tracked WETH9 holder without code can withdraw by a transaction whose gas has a closed form, matching all 3,748 comparable mainnet receipts of its shape in 30,000 blocks. On Curve pool bytes compiled with the lock bug exploited in 2023, Jaune executes such a reentrancy from deployment; for bytes from a fixed compiler, we prove the lock excludes it. AI agents wrote the proofs in fifteen days under one author's direction, atop an existing stack.
Programming Languages.comment: 37 pages, 5 tables, 4 figures. Verification package: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23351349

Programming Languages.title: Recursive Formation and First-Class Reuse of Compositional Capabilities
Programming Languages.summary: We introduce FormCraft, a framework for representing acquired operations as first-class capabilities that can be recursively composed, directly invoked, and selectively retained in a persistent library through domain-specific verification. The framework separates capability well-formedness and public callability from later admission to persistent storage while preserving formation provenance and operational identity. We formalize recursive compositional closure over a uniform capability space and show that formed composites can be reused through the same public interface without re-forming their historical derivation. Experiments across continuous, discrete, propositional, and sequence domains demonstrate instance-independent reuse, independent checking, persistent acquisition, and reduced reuse-time search work under first-class exposure.

Programming Languages.title: DataKernelBench: Can LLMs Optimize Database Queries on GPUs?
Programming Languages.summary:
GPUs increasingly accelerate database systems, but query-specific peak performance still often relies on hand-written kernels. Existing LLM kernel benchmarks focus on machine learning operators, leaving irregular, heterogeneous, data-movement-heavy database-style operators untested. We introduce DataKernelBench, which translates SQL into validated PyTorch TorchPlan programs and evaluates LLMs that optimize either the core tensor-bounded snippet or the full query in CUDA or Triton through execution-guided repair. Across ten proprietary and open-weight models on TPC-H SF10 with an H100 GPU, the strongest full-query CUDA configuration achieves $2.11\times$ speedup over the TorchPlan baseline at full pass rate. We find that higher-performing implementations commonly use kernel fusion and execution-strategy changes, stronger models benefit most from full-query specialization, and workload context matters more than hardware context. To handle data larger than GPU memory, we extend TorchPlan with Dask-cuDF for on-demand partition loading on TPC-H SF100 with four H100 GPUs, achieving $2.54\times$ speedup.
  Project page: https://kerneldf.github.io/datakernelbench

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Fast Forgiving Base64 Decoding with SIMD Instructions
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: On the Internet, we use the Base64 format to represent binary data (e.g., images or cryptographic keys) as text. The ES2026 JavaScript standard, following the WHATWG forgiving-base64 rules, requires decoders to ignore ASCII whitespace while rejecting other non-alphabet characters. Prior SIMD Base64 decoders assume whitespace-free input. We present a block-oriented decoding algorithm that removes whitespace inside the SIMD loop: clean 64-character blocks are decoded directly, while blocks with ignorable characters are compacted into a small stack buffer. We provide implementations for x64 (SSSE3 through AVX-512 VBMI2), ARM NEON, and LoongArch. Our C++ decoder reaches up to 94 GB/s on recent AMD Zen 5 processors. In Node 25, integration of our decoder raises Uint8Array.fromBase64 throughput by up to 6x compared with Node 19. The implementation has been adopted by major browsers and JavaScript runtimes.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Claw-Free and Line Graph Edge Deletion on Block Graphs
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Edge deletion problems ask for the fewest edges whose deletion gives a graph with a specified property. We study two such problems on block graphs. First making the graph claw-free, and second making it a line graph. Since every line graph is claw-free, the second problem is at least as difficult as the first. We show that on block graphs the two optimum values are always equal, and both are attained by the line graph of a forest. The main step is a completion argument, in which starting from any claw-free solution, we put back edges to get some nice structure inside each block still maintaining the claw-free property. This reduces both edge-deletion problems to the same problem of selecting vertices within the blocks of the input graph. We solve it by dynamic programming in $O(n+m)$ time, which also produces an optimal deletion set and a forest whose line graph is what remains after the completion argument. We also extend the method to $K_{1,r+1}$-free edge deletion for every fixed $r$.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Bounded-Density Vertex Deletion Beyond Vertex Cover
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We study \textsc{Bounded-Density Vertex Deletion} (BDVD), where one asks whether at most \(k\) vertices can be deleted so that every remaining subgraph has density at most a rational input threshold \(τ_ρ\).
  We address the twin-cover and distance-to-cluster cases left open by Raupach, Breitkopf, Herrmann, and Nichterlein (MFCS 2026). We prove fixed-parameter tractability parameterized solely by the twin-cover number, for unrestricted input density.
