For distance to cluster, we establish fixed-parameter tractability parameterized by \(\operatorname{dc}(G)+\lfloor2τ_ρ+1\rfloor\), and complement this with \(\mathsf{W[1]}\)-hardness parameterized by \(\operatorname{dc}(G)\) alone when the target density is part of the input, even for integral targets.
  Thus distance to cluster alone is fixed-parameter tractable throughout \(τ_ρ<1\), while it is insufficient for unrestricted input density.
  Finally, we settle the combined parameter treewidth plus solution size, an open problem posed by Bazgan, Nichterlein, and Vazquez Alferez (JCSS 2025). We prove that BDVD is \(\mathsf{W[1]}\)-hard parameterized by \(\operatorname{td}(G)+k\), and hence also by \(\operatorname{tw}(G)+k\), already for targets strictly between \(1\) and \(2\).

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Sparse universal graphs for planarity
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We show that for every integer $n\geq 1$ there exists a graph $G_n$ with $(1+o(1))n$ vertices and $n^{1 + o(1)}$ edges such that every $n$-vertex planar graph is isomorphic to a subgraph of $G_n$. The best previous bound on the number of edges was $O(n^{3/2})$, proved by Babai, Chung, Erdős, Graham, and Spencer in 1982. We then show that for every integer $n\geq 1$ there is a graph $U_n$ with $n^{1 + o(1)}$ vertices and edges that contains induced copies of every $n$-vertex planar graph. This significantly reduces the number of edges in a recent construction of the authors with Dujmović, Gavoille, and Micek.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: v5: corrects an error in the proof of Lemma 20

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Hypothesis Selection via Weighted Medians
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Given $n$ distributions (hypotheses) $\mathcal H=\{H_1,\ldots,H_n\}$ and samples from an unknown target distribution $P$, proper hypothesis selection seeks a distribution whose total variation distance to $P$ is close to the best achievable within the known distributions. We give an algorithm that, using $O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log(n/δ))$ target samples, running in $O(n\varepsilon^{-2}\log(n/δ))$ time, with probability at least $1-δ$, returns $H_{\hat i}$ satisfying $d_\mathrm{TV}(P,H_{\hat i})\leq 3\min_{i\in[n]}d_\mathrm{TV}(P,H_i)+\varepsilon.$ The algorithm achieves the optimal approximation factor and sample complexity. The running time improves the dependence on the failure probability from polynomial to logarithmic in the state-of-the-art bound $\tilde{O}(n\varepsilon^{-2}δ^{-1})$ of Aamand, Aliakbarpour, Chen, and Silwal (COLT 2026), thereby answering their Question~2.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Improved lower bounds of the time complexity of shellsort
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: In this paper we develop the framework of using a parametrized mapping $[σ(1), σ(2), \cdots, σ(n)] \mapsto σ(1)z + σ(2)z^2 + \cdots σ(n)z^n$ to perform runtime analysis on Shellsort. In particular, we show that the worst-case time complexity of Shellsort using Tokuda's gap sequence proposed in 1992 is at least $Ω(N^{1.26})$ with a generalisation of this result to any strictly decreasing gap sequence where each term at most a fixed distance away from a geometric sequence with rational common ratio, and we also show that strictly decreasing gap sequences giving worst-case Shellsort time complexities of $O(N \log^c N)$ must have $Ω(\log N / \log \log N)$ terms of order $Ω(N / (\log N)^c)$.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: Fixed proof of lemma 1 and a made few other amendments

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Simple, Faster (min, +) Matrix Multiplication and APSP
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: In this note, we provide a deterministic algorithm that computes the $(\min, +)$-Matrix Product $C = A * B$ of two $N \times N$ matrices $A$ and $B$ with polynomially bounded integer entries in $\tilde{O}(N^{2.9964})$ time, improving upon the exponent of $O(N^{2.9995})$ time obtained in the recent breakthrough by Anthropic (Alman and Vassilevska Williams, 2026). Our algorithm uses a phased approach first proposed by Bringmann, Grandoni, Saha, and Vassilevska Williams in 2016. The phased approach produces an approximation $\tilde{C}$ of $C$ in truly subcubic time such that the number of remaining triples $(i,k,j): A_{i,k}+B_{k,j} < \tilde{C}(i,j)$ is truly subcubic. This provided strong evidence that a truly subcubic $(\min, +)$-Matrix Product and therefore, a truly subcubic algorithm for All Pairs Shortest Paths (APSP) may exist. However, to find the remaining triples in subcubic time, a sparse certificate is needed whose construction was not known. We use the thin matrix product theorem of the recent breakthrough to provide such a certificate. This gives a simple modular subcubic algorithm for APSP.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Subexponential Parameterized Approximation for Group-Fair Euclidean $k$-Center
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
Clustering is a basic tool for grouping data into meaningful classes, but in many applications the resulting clusters must also respect the fairness conditions among different groups. We study this direction for the group-fair Euclidean $k$-center problem in fixed dimension, where the input points are partitioned into disjoint color classes, and every cluster must satisfy given lower and upper bounds on the fraction of each color.
  We give a separator-based recursive approximation algorithm for the continuous-center setting. The main idea is to first reduce the continuous search space to a finite candidate center set and then use the geometric sphere separators to break the instance into smaller subproblems.
  Our algorithm gives a bicriteria approximation: the clustering radius is within a factor of $(1+ε)$ of the optimum exactly fair solution, while the fairness bounds are relaxed only by a multiplicative factor. For fixed dimension, number of colors, and approximation parameters, the running time is polynomial in input size and subexponential in $k$. A recent IJCAI-ECAI2026 result gives a $(1+ε)$-approximation for group-fair $k$-center in bounded doubling metrics with running time $(k/ε)^{\mathcal{O}(k)}n^{\mathcal{O}(1)}$. In the fixed-dimensional Euclidean setting considered here, we improve the dependence on $k$ to subexponential, while allowing continuous centers. The fairness guarantees of the two results are different: the previous work allows an additive fairness violation, whereas our algorithm uses a controlled multiplicative relaxation.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: FPTAS for Polygonal Multi-Robot Motion Planning
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We study multi-robot motion planning in a polygonal environment with polygonal robots. The setting of the problem consists of a polygonal domain $\mathcal{W}$ with $n$ vertices and $k$ robots $R_1,\dots,R_k$ translating in $\mathcal{W}$ each of which is represented by a polygon of constant complexity. Given a source configuration $\mathbf{s}$ and a target configuration $\mathbf{t}$ of the robots in $\mathcal{W}$, the goal of the problem is to find a collision-free motion plan from $\mathbf{s}$ to $\mathbf{t}$ that is shortest with respect to some cost function. We present the first fully polynomial-time approximation schemes (FPTAS) for motion planning with any fixed number $k$ of robots, under the min-sum objective, the min-max objective, and the min-makespan objective. Here, the min-sum variant aims to minimize the total traveling distance of all robots, the min-max variant aims to minimize the maximum traveling distance of a single robot, and the min-makespan variant aims to minimize the total time cost under the assumption that all robots move with a maximum speed $1$. The algorithm directly generalizes to the problem in any fixed dimension $d$, with a polytope environment and polytope robots. Our result settles an open question of Agarwal, Halperin, Sharir, Steiger [SODA'24] and Agarwal, Holmgren, Steiger [SODA'26], who gave an FPTAS for $k=2$ unit-square robots and a bicriteria-approximation algorithm for a fixed number $k$ of unit-square or unit-disk robots, respectively. Compared to the previous results, our algorithm is substantially simpler.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Entrywise Low-Rank Approximation and Matrix $p \rightarrow q$ Norms via Global Correlation Rounding
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
Given a matrix $A$, the goal of the entrywise low-rank approximation problem is to find $\operatorname{argmin} \|A-B\|_p$ over all rank-$k$ matrices $B$, where $\| \cdot \|_p$ is the entrywise $\ell_p$ norm. When $p = 2$ this well-studied problem is solved by the singular value decomposition, but for $p \neq 2$ the problem becomes computationally challenging. For every even $p > 2$ and every fixed $k$, we give the first polynomial-time approximation scheme for this problem, improving on the $(3 + \varepsilon)$ approximation of Ban, Bhattiprolu, Bringmann, Kolev, Lee, and Woodruff, the bi-criteria approximation of Woodruff and Yasuda, and the additive approximation scheme of Anderson, Bakshi, and Hopkins. Prior algorithmic approaches based on sketching and column selection, which yielded a polynomial-time approximation scheme in the $p < 2$ setting, face concrete barriers when $p > 2$. Instead, we use the Sherali-Adams hierarchy of convex programs, and in so doing suggest a methodology for how to use convex hierarchies to design polynomial-time approximation schemes for continuous optimization problems.
  We use the same algorithmic strategy to give a new family of additive approximation algorithms for matrix $p \rightarrow q$ norms, which are intimately related to small-set expansion and quantum information. In particular, we give the first nontrivial additive approximation algorithms in the regime $p < 2 < q$.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: An Analytic 0.48-Approximation for Non-Monotone k-Submodular Maximization under a Matroid Constraint
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We give a randomized polynomial-time $0.48$-approximation for maximizing a nonnegative non-monotone $k$-submodular function under a matroid constraint, for every $k\ge2$. The algorithm combines a top-two label rule with a nested-chain potential and maximum-weight matroid bases. Its analysis reduces the approximation guarantee to a one-dimensional time allocation: a uniform local lower bound leads to a linear differential equation, concavity closes the remaining interval, and two elementary budgets complete the proof. A strict saving in the time budget absorbs sampling and discretization errors, yielding the exact $0.48$ guarantee in the value-oracle model.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Undirected Network Coding and Faster External-Memory Integer Sorting
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
Network coding allows intermediate nodes to combine messages, whereas routing only forwards them. The Li-Li conjecture asserts that network coding and fractional routing have the same capacity region in undirected multiple-unicast networks. We give a counterexample to this conjecture and apply it to external-memory integer sorting. Since Aggarwal and Vitter posed the question in 1988, whether integer sorting can beat the external-memory comparison bound has remained a central and extensively studied open problem.
  We give a deterministic sorting algorithm: for $N$ integers of $Θ(\log N)$ bits, a memory holding $M$ integers, and block transfers of $B$ integers, where $2B\le M\le N$, the number of block transfers is $O\left(\frac{N}{B}\left[1+\frac{\log N}{(\log(M/B))^{1-\varepsilon}(\log M)^\varepsilon}\right]\right)$, where $\varepsilon>0$ is an absolute constant. In a range of parameter regimes, this bound is asymptotically smaller than the classical comparison-sorting bound. We also use Lean 4 to verify the sorting algorithm's correctness and complexity bounds, and the strict advantage of coding over routing.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Towards Dynamic Top-$k$ Simple Shortest Paths
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: Computing the top-$k$ \textit{simple} shortest paths between two vertices of a graph, i.e., solving the P-KSSP problem, is a fundamental primitive in graph analytics. In modern scenarios, however, queries are rarely one-shot: parameters change as applications adapt their information needs, and recomputing a solution from scratch at every request quickly becomes a bottleneck. We study P-KSSP in a dynamic setting, focusing on changes of the parameter $k$: given a top-$k$ solution for a pair of vertices and a new value $k'$, the goal is to compute a top-$k'$ solution reusing the previously computed paths. Our approach rests on the \textit{pseudo-tree}, a compact representation of a collection of simple $s$--$t$ paths: we show that building it from an arbitrary, unstructured solution amounts to trie construction, and give two constructions running in time linear in the size of the collection. On top of it, we design UPD, a dynamic algorithm that updates a solution upon a change of $k$; we prove its correctness, analyze its complexity, and show that it is a general, solver-agnostic scheme, which starts from the paths alone, is parametric in the routine that generates candidate paths and combinable with known preprocessing techniques, as well as with an online pruning rule that we formalize. While a worst-case update is asymptotically comparable to recomputing from scratch, an extensive experimental evaluation shows that a variant of UPD is the fastest method in the large majority of tested configurations, often by a wide margin (with speedups over recomputation that grow with $k$ and $k'$ and exceed $60\times$), yielding a practical recipe for the configuration to deploy.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Temporal Path Covers: Dilworth Properties and Parameterized Complexity
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
The Temporal Path Cover (TPC) and Temporally Disjoint Path Cover (TDPC) problems were introduced by [Chakraborty, Dailly, Foucaud, Klasing, MFCS '24] as the natural temporal analogues of Path Cover and Path Partition, and were shown to be NP-hard on temporal DAGs. All tractable graph classes for T(D)PC established in that paper satisfy a temporal Dilworth property, namely that the size of a respective minimum temporal path cover is equal to the size of a maximum temporal antichain. This raises a natural question: is T(D)PC guaranteed to be polynomial-time solvable under the promise that the respective Dilworth property holds? For both problems, we answer this question in the affirmative for their decision version and in the negative for their search version (under P $\neq$ NP).
  In another direction, we present parameterized algorithms and hardness results for TPC and TDPC. Our main result is that TPC is W[1]-hard parameterized by the deletion distance to linear forest even for temporal graphs with two time-steps, answering in the negative an open question by Chakraborty et al. about whether an XP algorithm parameterized by the treewidth plus the number of time-steps can be improved to an FPT one. On the other hand, we prove that an FPT algorithm does exist if the vertex cover number is used as parameter instead of the treewidth in the above parameterization. We complement this with a proof that including the number of time-steps in the parameter is necessary to yield tractability, as, otherwise, both TPC and TDPC remain NP-hard even for constant vertex cover size. Along the way, we establish several additional para-NP-hardness results involving structural parameters such as the pathwidth and the maximum degree of the underlying graph.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Biclique decompositions from Welzl orders
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: A biclique decomposition of a graph is a partition of its edges into complete bipartite subgraphs. We consider graphs whose vertices can be ordered such that the neighborhood of every vertex is the union of a sublinear number of intervals. We observe that these graphs admit compact representations in the form of biclique decompositions of small size. Here, the size of a decomposition is measured as the sum of the number of vertices of its bicliques. Combining this result with the existence of suitable vertex orderings for graphs of low neighborhood complexity, as proven by Welzl in 1988, we recover and extend several known results up to logarithmic factors. These results include upper bounds on the Zarankiewicz problem, matrix multiplication, quantum circuit complexity, and shortest path algorithms in "well-structured" instances.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: 17 pages, 5 figures. Accepted for presentation at the 10th SIAM Symposium on Simplicity in Algorithms (SOSA 2027)

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Optimal Online Stochastic Matching
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We resolve the problem of unweighted online stochastic matching with a known arrival law by establishing its optimal competitive ratio. For Poisson arrivals, we achieve $1-e/e^e\approx0.8206$, matching the upper bound of Chierichetti, Giacchini, Panconesi, and Vattani [ICALP 2025]. For exactly $n$ i.i.d.~arrivals, we obtain the same guarantee up to an additive $O(n^{-1/2})$ loss.
  Our key technical contribution is an exact correspondence between Poisson matching and exponential scheduling, preserving both online performance and the expected offline optimum. To prove the latter, we show that the distribution of the maximum of a random supermodular set function is determined by its joint distributions along chains of nested sets, a result of independent interest. This reduces the analysis to chains, where classical Poisson--exponential duality applies. The offline equivalence extends to arbitrary nonnegative edge weights. We then design a posterior allocation policy for exponential scheduling and use the correspondence to transfer its optimal competitive guarantee to online matching.
  Additionally, we show that the optimal competitive ratio under an unknown arrival law is strictly lower than $1-e/e^e$, establishing a strict separation between the known and unknown arrival models.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: A proximal gradient algorithm for composite log-concave sampling
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We propose an algorithm to sample from composite log-concave distributions over $\mathbb{R}^d$, i.e., densities of the form $π\propto e^{-f-g}$, assuming access to gradient evaluations of $α_f$-convex $f$ and a restricted Gaussian oracle (RGO) for $α_g$-convex $g$, where $α_g \ge 0$. The latter requirement means that we can easily sample from the density $\text{RGO}_{g,h,y}(x) \propto \exp(-g(x) -\frac{1}{2h}||y-x||^2)$, which is the sampling analogue of the proximal operator for $g$. If $f + g$ is $α$-convex and $f$ is $β$-smooth, our sampler achieves $\varepsilon$ error in total variation distance using $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(κ\sqrt d \log^4(1/\varepsilon))$ oracle calls where $κ:= 1 \vee β/α$, with $0\le α_g \le β$ and $α:= α_f + α_g > 0$, which matches prior state-of-the-art results for the case $g=0$. We further extend our results to cases where (1) $π$ is non-log-concave but satisfies a Poincaré or log-Sobolev inequality, and (2) $f$ is non-smooth but Lipschitz.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Output-linear time enumeration of potential maximal cliques
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
First defined by Bouchitté and Todinca, Potential Maximal Cliques (PMC) are a well studied notion in graph theory due to its numerous applications. The PMCs of an undirected graph $G$ are defined as the maximal cliques of the minimal triangulations of $G$. Their number can be exponential in the size of the graph. PMCs were crucial in the design of a polynomial-time algorithm which solves Maximum Weight Independent Set on $P_6$-free graphs (Grzesik, Klimošová, Pilipczuk, Pilipczuk, 2020). They also play a central role in the proposal of a polynomial-time algorithm to solve Largest Induced Subgraph of treewidth $\le t$ (Fomin, Todinca, Villanger, 2013).
  Last but not least, certainly one of the main application of PMCs is the existence of an exact dynamic-programming algorithm to determine the treewidth of a graph (Fomin, Kratsch, Todinca, Villanger, 2008) which uses its list of PMCs as an input. In fact, the enumeration of PMCs stands as the bottleneck for the computation of treewidth with this method: the PMC-enumeration step takes output-quadratic time (Bouchitté, Todinca, 2002) while the dynamic-programming one takes a time linear in the number of PMCs. This two-step procedure was proven to be among the most performing approaches in practice to determine treewidth.
  Answering a longstanding open question, we propose an algorithm to enumerate PMCs in output-linear time, {\em i.e.} a running time linear in the number of PMCs. This offers nice perspectives not only from the theoretical viewpoint - better running time for the PMC-based methods determining treewidth, for Minimum Fill-In and Largest Induced Subgraph of treewidth $\le t$ - but also from the practical side, with the possibility to propose top-performance implementation.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: This paper was accepted at SODA 2027. 54 pages, 18 figures

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Gray Codes With Constant Delay and Constant Auxiliary Space
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We give the first two algorithms to enumerate all binary words of $\{0,1\}^\ell$ (like Gray codes) while ensuring that the delay and the auxiliary space is independent from $\ell$, i.e., constant time for each word, and constant memory in addition to the $\ell$ bits storing the current word. Our algorithms are given in two new computational models: tape machines and deque machines. We also study more restricted models, queue machines and stack machines, and show that they cannot enumerate all binary words with constant auxiliary space, even with unrestricted delay.
  A tape machine is a Turing machine that stores the current binary word on a single working tape of length $\ell$ (which never increases), using no other tape. The machine has a single head and must edit its tape to reach all possible words of $\{0,1\}^\ell$, and output them (in unit time, by entering special output states), with no duplicates. Hence a tape machine uses constant auxiliary space by definition (up to the head position). We construct a tape machine that achieves this task with constant delay between consecutive outputs, so that the machine implements a so-called skew-tolerant quasi-Gray code. We then construct a more involved tape machine that implements a Gray code.
  A deque machine stores the current binary word on a double-ended queue of length $\ell$, and stores a constant-size internal state. It works as a tape machine, except that it modifies the content of the deque by performing push and pop operations on the endpoints. Hence again a deque machine uses constant auxiliary space by definition. We construct deque machines that enumerate all words of $\{0,1\}^\ell$ with constant-delay. The main technical challenge in this model is to correctly detect when enumeration has finished.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: 30 pages. This is the authors' version (will full proofs) of the corresponding ICALP'2026 article

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Exact Cut Complexity of Equal-Length Proportional Cake Cutting
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We study proportional cake cutting under an equal-length constraint, where each of $n$ agents must receive a bundle of length exactly $1/n$ that is worth at least $1/n$ to that agent. Our main result determines the exact worst-case number of cuts needed to guarantee such an allocation, namely $2n-2$ for every $n$. This improves on the previously known quadratic upper bound. The proof combines the constrained necklace-splitting theorem with a recursive assignment argument based on Hall's theorem. The same bound extends to the stronger requirement of envy-freeness when $n$ is a prime power, and an $O(n^{1.525})$ upper bound holds for arbitrary $n$. We then ask whether such allocations can be computed. We first show that no deterministic protocol in the Robertson--Webb model terminates after finitely many queries on every instance and always returns an exact equal-length proportional allocation, even for two agents with identical valuations. For every $\varepsilon>0$, however, $O(n^2/\varepsilon)$ queries suffice to produce an allocation in which every agent receives a bundle of length exactly $1/n$ and value at least $1/n-\varepsilon$, again using at most $2n-2$ cuts. Finally, we augment the Robertson--Webb model with two-knife queries. We show that recursive balanced halving attains the optimal bound of $2n-2$ cuts when $n$ is a power of two. For arbitrary $n$, we give a procedure using $O(n\log n)$ cuts.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: A preliminary version of this paper appeared in the proceedings of the 51st International Symposium on Mathematical Foundations of Computer Science (MFCS 2026)

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Dynamic 3-Coloring of Bipartite Graphs with Optimal Locality
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We give a dynamic graph algorithm which maintains a 3-coloring in bipartite graphs under edge insertions such that the coloring only changes within a radius of $O(\log n)$ around an inserted edge. In the context of locality theory in distributed graph algorithms, this gives an upper bound on the locality under the dynamic-LOCAL model. Our bound on the locality is tight, as the problem admits a matching $Ω(\log n)$ lower bound in the stronger online-LOCAL model, by a result of Chang et al. [PODC 2024]. Thus, our result closes the gap between dynamic and online locality of this problem.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Revisiting Non-Adaptive Set Membership Schemes: Removing the Logarithmic Factor
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We study non-adaptive bit-probe schemes for static set membership. Each query reads a fixed number of bits and answers by strict majority. We revisit the random bipartite-graph construction of Garg and Radhakrishnan [STACS, 2017]. The main observation is that a slightly stronger expansion property already bounds the number of exceptional elements. This makes a separate probabilistic estimate for exceptional elements unnecessary. A detailed union-bound calculation then gives, for every fixed $t\ge5$, a logarithm-free existence bound of $O_t(m^{1/c}n^{1-1/c})$, where $c=\lfloor(t-1)/2\rfloor$. For odd $t$, this removes the logarithmic factor from the general upper bound of Garg and Radhakrishnan [STACS, 2017].

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Fair Allocation with Dichotomous Preferences over Item Complements
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We study the problem of fair allocation when agents have dichotomous submodular preferences over groups of, rather than individual, items. These preferences naturally extend existing models, and have a natural interpretation in settings such as course allocation. We show that this seemingly minor extension results in computational intractability barriers: computing a utilitarian or Nash-optimal allocation with item complements is NP-hard. However, when agents' complementary bundles have size at most $k$, there exist poly-time algorithms that compute $\frac1k$-$\texttt{maxUSW}$ allocations and approximate Nash-welfare-maximizing allocations. While PO+EF-1 allocations may not exist in the complementary preference setting, it is possible to compute $\frac1{k+1}$-approximately $\texttt{maxUSW}$ EF-X allocations in polynomial time; furthermore, these allocations offer each agent $i$ a utility of at least $\frac{\texttt{MMS}_i - k}{k+1 + \frac1n}$, where $\texttt{MMS}_i$ is agent $i$'s maximin share guarantee.
  While the standard dichotomous binary submodular setting admits simple sequential techniques for computing fair and efficient allocations, our results for the complements setting require more complex tools from combinatorial optimization.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: PHastR: Faster Minimal Perfect Hashing with Rotated Layouts
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We present PHastR, a minimal perfect hash function of the PHast family. Like PHast+, the fast-to-build variant of PHast, PHastR finds feasible seeds with bit-parallel operations: its seeds move keys along rings of slots, and to evaluate the seeds of a bucket it cyclically shifts, for each key, a word recording which slots of its ring are used. Unlike PHast+, however, it is almost immune to self-collisions, which make two keys of a bucket collide for (almost) all its seeds: more than a third of the buckets bumped by PHast+ with wrapping and multiplier 3 contain one. With 8-bit seeds, PHastR uses $1.94$ bits per key, essentially the same space as the best variant of PHast+ with wrapping, but it is built in $37\%$ of the time, and its queries are $28\%$ faster on $10^9$ keys, as it bumps $0.5\%$ of the keys instead of $3.9\%$; they are faster also than those of PHast, which takes twelve times as long to build, and about as fast as those of PtrHash, which uses more than one bit per key more. With a larger expected bucket size PHastR comes within $0.02$ bits per key of the space of PHast, using $1.90$ bits per key, and still has faster queries. Its construction also scales better with the number of threads: with all the threads of a 48-core machine it is almost three times faster than that of PHast+. Finally, we argue that when each key can be placed only within a range of $W$ slots, every placement of $n$ random keys on $n$ slots, however found, must bump on large key sets a constant fraction of the keys: we derive a lower bound of about $0.1/W$ on this fraction, and we estimate that the best placement bumps about $1/2W$ of the keys, which is about one tenth of the keys bumped by PHastR.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: O(1) Expected Insertion for Random Walk d-ary Cuckoo Hashing up to the Load Threshold
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: The random walk $d$-ary cuckoo hashing algorithm was defined by Fotakis, Pagh, Sanders, and Spirakis to generalize and improve upon the standard cuckoo hashing algorithm of Pagh and Rodler. Random walk $d$-ary cuckoo hashing has low space overhead, guaranteed fast access, and fast in practice insertion time. In this paper, we give a theoretical insertion time bound for this algorithm. More precisely, for every $d\ge 3$ random hashes, let $c_d^*$ be the sharp threshold for the load factor at which a valid assignment of $cm$ objects to a hash table of size $m$ exists with high probability. We show that for any $d\ge 3$ hashes and load factor $c<c_d^*$, the expectation of the random walk insertion time is $O(1)$, that is, a constant depending only on $d$ and $c$ but not $m$.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: A preliminary version of this paper appeared in FOCS 2024. Major update from v4 to v6 to fix errors in the previous version and include the $d=3$ case. Minor update to v7. 34 pages

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Approximation Algorithms for Emergency Vertex Cover with Few Stations and Fault-Tolerant Coverage
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: The Emergency Vertex Cover problem (Em-VC) assigns budgets to stations at graph vertices to cover every edge while minimizing the total budget. The cost of covering an edge from a station is the shortest-path distance from the station to the nearer endpoint plus the edge length. We study how restricting the number of stations affects the cost of ordinary and fault-tolerant coverage. In ordinary Em-VC, we prove that the optimal solution using at most two stations costs at most $5/4$ times the unrestricted optimum, improving the known $4/3$ guarantee for a single station. A recurrence extends this bound to larger station limits, giving approximation factors that converge to $\sqrt{5}-1$. Budget-threshold enumeration computes the restricted optimum in polynomial time for every fixed station limit. Under $k$-fold coverage, every edge must be covered by at least $k$ distinct stations, ensuring coverage after any $k-1$ station failures. We prove that selecting the $k$ vertices with the smallest full-coverage costs yields a $2$-approximation relative to the unrestricted optimum for $k$-fold coverage. When $k=2$, we combine upper bounds derived from the structure of the covering balls to improve the approximation guarantee to $5/3$.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Learning-Augmented Streaming Algorithms for Approximating Boolean Max-CSPs
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We study learning-augmented streaming algorithms for estimating the value of Boolean Maximum Constraint Satisfaction Problems (Max-CSPs). Specifically, we consider streaming algorithms equipped with an $\varepsilon$-accurate oracle: for each variable, the oracle outputs a label in $\{-1,1\}$ that agrees with a fixed optimal assignment with probability $1/2+\varepsilon$, and disagrees otherwise. Prior work by Dong, Peng, and Vakilian [ITCS 2025] showed that, for the special case of Max-Cut, such an oracle enables a $(1/2+Ω(\varepsilon^2))$-approximation using $\operatorname{poly}(1/\varepsilon)$ words of space in insertion-only streams, and $\operatorname{poly}(1/\varepsilon,\log n)$ words of space in dynamic streams. We substantially generalize and strengthen their result, provided that a highly accurate estimate of $\varepsilon$ is available. For any Boolean Max-$2$CSP and any $η>0$ independent of $\varepsilon$, we obtain, with high constant probability, a single-pass $(1-η)$-approximation using $\operatorname{poly}(1/\varepsilon,1/η)$ words of space in insertion-only streams, and $\operatorname{poly}(1/\varepsilon,1/η,\log n)$ words of space in dynamic streams, where $n$ is the number of variables. We further extend our techniques to general Boolean Max-$k$CSPs for $k\ge 3$, with slightly worse space complexity.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Approximating Unsplittable Capacitated Vehicle Routing: Analysis via Factor-Revealing LPs
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: The capacitated vehicle routing problem (CVRP) is one of the most extensively studied problems in combinatorial optimization. Given a depot and a set of customers with demands in a metric space, the objective is to find a set of tours, each starting and ending at the depot, operated by a capacitated vehicle located at the depot, such that all customers are served and the total travel cost is minimized. We consider the unsplittable variant, where the demand of each customer must be served entirely by a single tour. The previous best approximation ratio was about $α+1.694$, where $α$ is the approximation ratio for the traveling salesman problem. We propose improved approximation algorithms. First, we introduce a unified algorithmic framework that generalizes and integrates known linear programming (LP) rounding and matching-based approaches. We show that these techniques are complementary and can be combined to yield improved approximation ratios. Second, we develop a novel analytical framework based on customer demand discretization, which yields new structural bounds and, through factor-revealing LPs, achieves expected approximation ratios of about $α+1.647$ for the general-capacity case and $α+1.548$ for the fixed-capacity case. Finally, we derandomize our algorithms using a priori 2-tour sets and the method of conditional expectations while maintaining nearly the same approximation ratios.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Near-Optimal Online Metric Matching on $Δ$-ary HST
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
In the online metric matching problem, we have $n$ servers with known locations in some metric space. Requests arrive one-by-one at certain locations, and upon arrival a request must be matched to a server that was not matched to a previous request. The goal is to minimize the matching cost. For randomized algorithms with an oblivious adversary, the best known competitive ratio is obtained by embedding the metric space into an HST, and then solving the problem in the setting where the metric space is defined by the HST.
  Bansal et al. (Algorithmica, 2014) introduced a framework for online metric matching where one develops an algorithm in a restricted reassignment model, and then transforms this into a true online algorithm. Using this framework, they obtained an expected competitive ratio of $O(\log n)$ for HSTs; this also gives the best known competitive ratio of $O(\log^2 n)$ for general metrics. In this paper, we revisit this framework with the aim of developing new algorithms. For HSTs where each node has at most $Δ$ children, we develop an algorithm via this framework with an expected competitive ratio of $O((\log\log Δ) \cdot \log Δ)$. In particular, this ratio is independent of $n$, the number of servers/requests. It is near-optimal, as the expected competitive ratio of any algorithm is $Ω(\log Δ)$.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: The Komlós Problem in Matrix-Multiplication Time
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We give a randomized algorithm that, for an $m\times n$ matrix whose columns have Euclidean norm at most one, finds a signing with discrepancy below $99$ in expected $\widetilde O(L_{\mathrm{in}}+n^ω)$ bit operations, where $L_{\mathrm{in}}$ is the input encoding length and $ω$ is the exponent of matrix multiplication. The previous fastest algorithm with a constant discrepancy bound, due to Li, is deterministic and uses $O(mn+n^{ω+2}\log^3 n)$ arithmetic operations. We build on the spectral signing framework of Guo, Fang, and Lu and of Li, which rounds a single fractional coloring while one spectral potential controls every row. Li's potential tracks a top eigenvalue, and the gap below that eigenvalue, which can be of order $1/n$, limits the length of every step. We replace it with a resolvent potential that is smooth without any gap condition, and we draw step signs at random, so that the potential only needs to be concave while progress is measured separately. Our key insight is to reuse a single subspace of directions throughout a batch of steps, thereby using only one spectral computation, so that the more expensive linear algebraic operations are paid for only polylogarithmically often at each scale. Within a batch, we sample directions from a Gaussian completion matrix whose inverse we maintain under rank-one row replacements. Finally, we use a finite-precision analysis to prove stability of the algorithm and attain the bit-complexity bound.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Near-Linear Preprocessing for Range Weighted Longest Increasing Subsequence Queries
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary: We give a deterministic data structure for range weighted longest increasing subsequence (LIS) queries on $n$ values with positive weights. Preprocessing takes $O(n\log^2 n)$ time and space. Value queries take $O(\log n)$ time, and an optimal subsequence of $k$ elements can be reported in $O(k + \log n)$ time. This resolves an open question on truly subquadratic preprocessing with polylogarithmic query time. The key is a single-crossing property of envelopes for value-separated endpoint sets, enabling $O(\log n)$-time persistent merges. The bounds assume constant-time exact addition and comparison of weights.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Computational and Statistical Hardness of Calibration Distance
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
The distance from calibration, introduced by Błasiok, Gopalan, Hu, and Nakkiran (STOC 2023), has recently emerged as a central measure of miscalibration for probabilistic predictors. We study the fundamental problems of computing and estimating this quantity, given either an exact description of the data distribution or only sample access to it.
  We give an efficient algorithm that exactly computes the calibration distance when the distribution has a uniform marginal and noiseless labels, which improves the $O(1/\sqrt{|\mathcal{X}|})$ additive approximation of Qiao and Zheng (COLT 2024) for this special case. Perhaps surprisingly, the problem becomes $\mathsf{NP}$-hard when either of the two assumptions is removed. We extend our algorithm to a polynomial-time approximation scheme for the general case.
  For the estimation problem, we show that $Θ(1/ε^3)$ samples are sufficient and necessary for the empirical calibration distance to be upper bounded by the true distance plus $ε$. In contrast, a polynomial dependence on the domain size -- incurred by the learning-based baseline -- is unavoidable for two-sided estimation.
  Our positive results are based on simple sparsifications of both the distribution and the target predictor, which significantly reduce the search space for computation and lead to stronger concentration for the estimation problem. To prove the hardness results, we introduce new techniques for certifying lower bounds on the calibration distance -- a problem that is hard in general due to its $\textsf{co-NP}$-completeness.
Data Structures and Algorithms.comment: To appear at SODA 2027. v2 added figures for visualizing the NP-hardness reduction

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Tolerant Testers for Subgraph-Freeness
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
In this paper we study the problem of tolerantly testing the property of being $H$-free (which also implies distance approximation from being $H$-free). In the general-graphs model, we show that tolerant $K_k$-freeness testing can be achieved with query complexity that is polynomial in the arboricity of the input graph $G$, $arb(G)$, and independent of the size of $G$ (for graphs in which the average degree is $Ω(1))$.
  Specifically for triangles, our algorithm distinguishes graphs which are $ε$-close to being triangle-free from graphs that are $3ε(1+η)$-far from being triangle-free with expected query complexity which is $\tilde{O}(arb^3(G))$ (for constant $η$ and $ε$). For general $k$-cliques our algorithm distinguishes graphs which are $ε$-close to being $K_k$-free from graphs which are ${k \choose 2}ε(1+η)$-far from being $K_k$-free with expected query complexity which is polynomial in $k$, $1/ε$, $1/η$ and $arb(G)$. We then generalize our result and provide a similar result for any motif $H$ which is $2$-connected and has radius $1$. This includes for example the wheel graph.
  Finally, we show that our tester can be applied to the bounded-degree model for tolerantly testing $H$-freeness for any motif $H$. The query complexity of the algorithm is polynomial in the degree bound, $d$, improving the previous state-of-the-art by Marko and Ron (TALG 2009) that obtained quasi-polynomial query complexity in $d$.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Eccentricity Shortest Path: the structural parameter landscape
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
The Eccentricity Shortest Path problem asks, given a connected graph and a nonnegative integer $R$, whether some shortest path is within distance $R$ of every vertex. We study its structural parameterized complexity. We give fixed-parameter algorithms for vertex-deletion distance to cographs, vertex-deletion distance to interval graphs, and bandwidth. The interval-deletion result answers a question of Bhyravarapu et al. (IWOCA 2023). We obtain XP algorithms for vertex-deletion distance to chordal graphs, clique-width, and rank-width, without requiring expressions or decompositions for the latter two. Consequently, the problem is polynomial-time solvable for every fixed treewidth, answering a question of Chakraborty et al. (2026). We also derive fixed-parameter tractability for treedepth and XP membership for diameter from earlier algorithms.
  We prove $\mathsf{W}[3]$-hardness for cutwidth, and hence pathwidth and treewidth, even on graphs of maximum degree at most five; $\mathsf{W}[2]$-hardness for vertex clique-cover number; and NP-hardness on graphs of tree-independence number at most two. For maximum leaf number $\ell$, we obtain an $O(\ell^4)$-bit compression and a polynomial kernel. Finally, unless $\mathsf{NP}\subseteq\mathrm{coNP}/\mathrm{poly}$, we exclude polynomial kernels for bandwidth, feedback edge number, vertex-deletion distance to a clique, and vertex cover number. The last bound also excludes polynomial kernels for vertex-deletion distance to proper interval graphs.

Data Structures and Algorithms.title: Subset Sum in Almost-Linear Time
Data Structures and Algorithms.summary:
We give a deterministic algorithm for finding a subset of the input integers $1\le a_1,\ldots,a_n \le Δ$ that sums to the target $t$ in $\mathcal{O}(n+Δ^{1+o(1)})$ time. This improves upon the previous $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(n + Δ^{1.5})$-time algorithm by Chen, Lian, Mao, and Zhang (SODA 2024), and achieves almost tight dependence on $Δ$ assuming SETH.
  We use an inverse theorem for subset sums due to Conlon, Fox, and Pham (2023), and develop a quotient variant of economic cap covering from the polytope approximation literature.

Graphics.title: SliderEdit++: Improved Slider Trajectories in Instruction-Based Image Editing
Graphics.summary: Slider-based control aims to give users continuous, fine-grained control over the intensity of individual edits in instruction-based image editing. However, existing approaches fail to deliver reliable continuous controllability: traversing a slider can produce abrupt visual jumps and non-monotonic changes, while jointly controlled sliders can interfere with one another. To systematically study these limitations, we introduce SlideBench, a comprehensive benchmark for continuous image editing spanning diverse editing categories and equipped with a unified suite of metrics quantifying monotonic progression, perceptual continuity, and inter-slider disentanglement. Building on these observations, we propose SliderEdit++, which explicitly regularizes the intermediate editing trajectory rather than supervising only its endpoints. Our method combines velocity- and semantic-space trajectory regularization with spectral control to encourage smooth, predictable slider traversal, together with a disentanglement objective that reduces interference between independently controlled edits. On SlideBench, SliderEdit++ achieves state-of-the-art performance, improving the overall score by 18.5% relative to the strongest baseline. At the same time, using a few-step editing backbone makes our method approximately 3x to 20x faster than existing slider-based approaches, enabling substantially more responsive interactive editing.

Graphics.title: RoboSimStudio: An Interactive Toolkit for Human and Agent Rapid Real2Sim of Robot Manipulation Tasks
Graphics.summary: It has been difficult to accurately model the physics of the interaction between a robot and the objects it manipulates, including contact mechanics, coupled contact dynamics, deformations, stiffness and friction. We present RoboSimStudio (RSS), an interactive toolkit that makes choices of solver, contact model, and physical parameters explicit and editable, allowing both humans and coding agents to quickly create and iteratively refine simulations based on observed physical behavior. We implement RSS with the open Newton physics simulation system and describe experiments with human-guided real2sim using (1) visual evaluation, (2) force-feedback and (3) agentic Real2Sim2Real. Code, video and additional information can be found on the project website: https://robosimstudio.github.io
Graphics.comment: 13 pages, 7 figures, 1 table. Project website: https://robosimstudio.github.io

Graphics.title: GLoD-LVSM: Learning Geometry-Grounded Continuous-LoD Scene Representations for Large View Synthesis Models
Graphics.summary: Large view synthesis models (LVSMs) reconstruct scenes from sparse views and render novel views quickly, but they incur unnecessary storage and rendering costs due to token redundancy. We present GLoD-LVSM, a compact, geometry-grounded scene representation for LVSMs with continuous levels of detail. First, instead of learning a fixed set of scene anchor initializations, GLoD-LVSM learns a continuous field that initializes a flexible number of anchors to match the desired budget. A condenser then aggregates scene information into these anchors, with both the field and condenser trained end-to-end. Second, the condenser infers reference-token and anchor geometry to guide compression through geometry-grounded attention, improving rendering quality and enabling frustum culling during decoding. Compared with existing LVSM scene-compression baselines, GLoD-LVSM achieves the best trade-off between rendering quality and scene token count. Compared with the uncompressed base model, GLoD-LVSM reduces the scene-token count by 33.4% and accelerates rendering by $1.23\times$ with no quality loss. Under a relaxed quality-loss budget, the reduction increases to 85.5%, with $3.00\times$ rendering speedup. Further analysis reveals that view-synthesis supervision yields emergent scene depth and self-organized anchors that align with surfaces and adapt their density to local texture complexity. Beyond rendering, we further show that our scene representation also supports scene-semantic understanding, highlighting its potential for broader downstream tasks.

Graphics.title: VisibilitySplat: Ray-Traced Occlusion for Relighting with 3D Gaussian Splatting
Graphics.summary: We address inverse rendering with 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by introducing explicit visibility modeling for relighting as well as material and light decomposition. Our approach augments the standard rasterized 3DGS pipeline with a sparse visibility oracle that estimates transmittance-weighted occlusion for Gaussian primitives from sampled lighting directions. This oracle is implemented using a point-based ray tracer accelerated by a bounding volume hierarchy (BVH) and queried sparsely within the inverse-rendering objectives, while the original 3DGS loop is retained for training efficiency, interactive visualization, and tooling compatibility. Shading follows a physically based rendering (PBR) formulation with a principled microfacet bidirectional reflectance distribution function (BRDF) and low-resolution high-dynamic-range (HDR) environment maps. We evaluate our method on the TensoIR synthetic dataset against baselines based on neural radiance fields (NeRFs), tensor representations, and 3DGS. The results show competitive performance and improvements over several earlier baselines for novel-view synthesis (NVS), albedo reconstruction, and relighting. Ablations indicate that explicit visibility modeling is an important contributor to relighting and material-illumination disentanglement, while pure PBR supervision can favor appearance fitting in NVS. Overall, the findings suggest that sparse, point-based visibility queries effectively complement rasterized splatting for inverse rendering while preserving the practical advantages of the 3DGS ecosystem.
Graphics.comment: 10 pages, 5 figures, 3 tables. Published at WSCG 2026

Graphics.title: Q-MAGIC: Quad-only Mesh Autoregressive Generation via Singularity-Aware Circular Relative Offset Tokenization
Graphics.summary: Autoregressive models have proven effective for triangular mesh generation by transforming it into predicting the next face, converting the non-differentiable connectivity prediction into a sequence of token predictions. However, generating quad-only meshes remains challenging because quad faces impose stricter topological constraints than triangles. The model must not only serialize quad faces into a valid token sequence, but also support unambiguous connectivity reconstruction during de-serialization. To address this, we propose Q-MAGIC, a novel autoregressive model for quad mesh generation. We first introduce a tailored serialization scheme for quad meshes, which requires at least two new vertices for the next face and is less flexible than triangles due to strict wiring constraints. To meet these requirements and reduce serialization length, we propose a singularity-aware serialization that prioritizes wiring from singular points, leading to more coherent traversals. Additionally, we propose a circular relative offset tokenization that encodes geometry mainly via local relative offsets. Built upon this representation, an autoregressive Transformer learns the underlying distribution of quad meshes via next-token prediction, enabling effective quad mesh generation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Q-MAGIC produces more compact sequences while consistently improving geometric fidelity and mesh quality compared to state-of-the-art methods.

Graphics.title: Efficient Geometry Representation Strategies for the Shape Optimization of Profile Extrusion Dies
Graphics.summary: The design of profile extrusion dies remains a challenging task due to the complex rheological behavior of polymer melts and the geometric intricacies of flow channels. Traditional manual optimization approaches, which rely heavily on human experience, are inefficient and often employ unvalidated heuristics. To address these challenges, we present a deterministic and explainable framework for automatic die design based on adjoint-based shape optimization. This approach enables the computation of sensitivities that directly indicate beneficial modifications to the flow channel geometry. A major difficulty in such optimization processes lies in generating boundary-conforming meshes that evolve consistently with changing geometries. To overcome this issue, we employ non-boundary conforming geometry representation methods that eliminate the need for an explicit surface representation along physical boundaries. A dedicated reconstruction technique is developed to recover accurate sensitivity information at the virtual interface between fluid and solid regions. The proposed algorithm is demonstrated on 3D geometries with varying complexity, including realistic extrusion die flow channels. Several objective functionals relevant to industrial applications, such as flow balance at the outflow, are considered. The results highlight significant improvements in performance metrics while maintaining numerical robustness. This work showcases the potential of adjoint-based techniques for automated die design in a domain still largely governed by manual trial-and-error procedures, establishing a foundation for data-efficient, sustainable manufacturing workflows using computational rheology.

Graphics.title: Spectral World Renderer: Unified 3D Hyperspectral Unmixing
Graphics.summary: Cameras and the foundation models built on them recognize what a 3D scene contains, but not what it is made of: surfaces of the same colour can be different materials. Hyperspectral unmixing explains each spectrum as a mixture of material signatures, yet in 3D it is applied to rendered images after the views are composited, or tied to slow implicit fields, and no multi-view data with known composition exist to check the result. We present the Spectral World Renderer (SWR), which unifies world generation and unmixing. A coding agent builds executable 3D worlds that are rendered with measured spectra, so every hyperspectral image comes with exact labels and sub-pixel proportions; the resulting SWR-Bench provides eight indoor and outdoor worlds in which decompositions can be verified. SWR then unmixes inside rendering: each Gaussian of a compact 3D representation is decoded into material abundances before compositing, so one render yields spectra and material maps, and any surface can be queried by material name, a clicked pixel or a reference spectrum. Without material labels, SWR identifies materials best in all eight worlds, has the best mean PSNR on real captures, trains 3.7-12.9x faster than unmixing baselines, renders 34.9 labelled views/s and separates same-coloured materials.

Operating Systems.title: Characterizing Predictability-Latency Trade-offs of KV-Cache SSD Offloading in LMCache for LLM Serving Systems
Operating Systems.summary: KV-cache offload is widely used to stretch GPU memory for LLM serving, but its storage behavior has not been characterized at the block-device level. In this paper, we study LMCache through realworld multi-session workloads that span same/different context x same/different prompt, using over 100 stateless requests per workload. Our comparison is observational rather than factorial: it contrasts two realizable deployment snapshots -- LMCache 0.3.0 with buffered I/O and the kernel page cache, and LMCache 0.3.16 with prefix-aware deduplication and O_DIRECT. Key findings define the paper. First, the legacy stack appears almost read-free at the SSD layer in all four workloads, but a flush_ram experiment shows that this is conditional on page-cache warmth: once the cache is evicted, the same path issues about 1 GB of sequential reads in 683 ms. Second, deduplication delivers a dramatic write reduction only for the exact-repeat workload: one set collapses from 1.62 GB to 11.75 MB of writes, while the other three sets remain in the 2-5 GB range. Third, O_DIRECT converts a hidden and bimodal read cost into an explicit and stable one: on one set, warm TTFT rises from 27 ms to 93 ms because each of the 99 warm requests re-reads the same ~12 MB partial chunk from SSD. The main conclusion is therefore not "newer is better," but a system trade-off: predictability versus average-case latency.

Operating Systems.title: Range: Decoupling KV-Cache Reuse Granularity from Storage Work
Operating Systems.summary:
LLM serving reuses cached key-value (KV) state to skip prefill, and growing contexts push that state past GPU HBM and CPU DRAM onto NVMe SSDs, placing prefix restore on the critical path of time-to-first-token (TTFT). We find that on a well-configured host-issued path the SSD is not the bottleneck: restoring the same 6 GiB of KV takes 2.1 s as 192 objects but 3.0 s as 6,144 objects, and more under layerwise loading, because every layer of the storage stack - lookup, allocation, I/O submission, GPU delivery, store, index - charges per logical object while the bytes stay the same. This cost grows with the KV footprint: longer contexts, deeper models under layerwise loading, and tensor parallelism each multiply the object count. Prior systems move this per-object work from the CPU to the GPU; the work remains per object.
  This paper presents Range, a KV-cache storage engine for vLLM and LMCache built on one principle: every cost on the storage path scales with bytes or physical batches, never with logical objects. Range tickets replace per-key lookup and ownership with token metadata and physical leases; byte stripes make the on-media layout independent of reuse granularity; completion-owned GPU transfer banks batch delivery and extraction and release each layer to attention as it lands. Range keeps the kernel cuFile path and changes four lines of vLLM. On a fixed 6 GiB restore, Range's median TTFT stays at 1.79-1.80 s across a 32x range of object counts and under layerwise delivery, within 70 ms of the prefix already being resident in GPU memory, while tuned in-process LMCache rises from 2.12 s to 3.01 s. Range improves on the fastest multiprocess DRAM-bounced path by 0.44 s at coarse granularity while moving no payload through host memory, and holds layerwise reuse at the cost of coarse-grained reuse, where the best stock path takes 2.24 s.

Operating Systems.title: Apple Neural Engine: Architecture, Programming, and Performance
Operating Systems.summary: The Apple Neural Engine (ANE) is Apple's fixed-function matrix accelerator. It has shipped in every Apple system-on-chip since the A11 in iPhones and iPads and the M1 in Macs. Applications reach it only through Core ML, which documents almost nothing below its own surface. This work reverse-engineers the engine. We reach it directly, below Core ML, from an ordinary user process, and that access opens the rest to measurement. We measure on Apple silicon and decompile the private runtime, compiler, kernel driver, and firmware, checking each against the other. We give the datapath and the roofline that bounds throughput and energy. Below that are the compiler and the program format it emits, the weight-compression scheme, the kernel driver, the firmware, and the command protocol. We decode compiler targets for the A11 through A18 and M1 through M5 families, with per-chip tables and an operation-by-device matrix. We measured silicon on the M1 and M5 only, and we mark every claim measured, decompile-derived, or predicted. We record how we reached the engine and what we could not measure. The route is callable from user space, but Apple does not document or support it, and it breaks across operating-system updates. It serves measurement and on-device research. Core ML remains the path for shipped software.

Operating Systems.title: Where the SRAM Goes: Per-Symbol Attribution of Static Memory in FreeRTOS-C and Embassy-Rust IoT Firmware on a 64 KB RISC-V Microcontroller
Operating Systems.summary: Selecting a firmware stack for a memory-constrained microcontroller is usually guided by aggregate binary sizes, which report how much SRAM a build consumes but not where it goes or why. We address that gap with a per-symbol attribution method that decomposes static RAM into architectural categories - scheduler heap, network buffers and pools, task stacks, and linker-reserved regions - by bounding sized ELF symbols to the .data, .bss and .stack section ranges. The method is validated by reconciling every category sum exactly against the size-based totals for all sixteen builds. We apply it to eight cumulative firmware milestones, from a bare task scaffold to a full MQTT-over-Ethernet client, implemented twice, in FreeRTOS-C and in Embassy-Rust, on the CH32V203RBT6, a RISC-V microcontroller with 64 KB SRAM and an on-chip Ethernet MAC and PHY, with functional parity verified on hardware at every milestone. The decomposition shows that both stacks spend a nearly identical share of their RAM on networking (63.8% versus 63.9%), yet the absolute cost differs by 4.4 times: 40,719 bytes for lwIP against 9,316 bytes for smoltcp. FreeRTOS task stacks grow linearly at roughly 1 KB per task while Embassy async state grows with state-machine complexity. We also report that lwIP could not be integrated under an all-static discipline on this platform, requiring a 20 KB arena that smoltcp does not. The measurement harness, the attribution tool, and the sixteen firmware implementations are released as artefacts.
Operating Systems.comment: 13 pages, 5 figures, 10 tables. Submitted to SN Computer Science

Hardware Architecture.title: X-RIC: An Agentic RAN-Intelligent Controller Benchmark for Enhancing Reinforcement Learning
Hardware Architecture.summary: The O-RAN ALLIANCE introduces architectural flexibility through disaggregation and AI-driven control. While the RAN Intelligent Controller (RIC) enables centralized optimization, current AI approaches lack reasoning capabilities and explainability. We propose eXplainable RIC (X-RIC), a novel framework integrating agentic AI into O-RAN architectures. X-RIC combines reactive Reinforcement Learning (RL) with strategic agentic reasoning through: (i) automated Behavioral Cloning (BC) using domain heuristics for sample-efficient training, (ii) a Telecom Language Model (TLM), a transformer-based reasoning module providing contextual abstraction and interpretability, and (iii) closed-loop co-adaptation within the Near-RT RIC control loop enabling continuous policy refinement. To ensure deployment readiness, we introduce BARX (Benchmarking Agentic Reasoning for RAN), a domain-specific evaluation framework assessing agentic control across latency, compliance, and determinism metrics. We validate X-RIC on SLA-aware network slicing in simulation and O-RAN-compliant testbed deployments. X-RIC achieves 89% operational cost reduction while maintaining SLA compliance, converging 75% faster with 50% fewer training steps and 46% lower variance.
Hardware Architecture.comment: 9 pages, 10 figures. Accepted for publication in the proceedings of the IEEE International Conference on Mobile Ad-Hoc and Smart Systems (MASS), October 21-23, 2026, Hong Kong SAR, China

Hardware Architecture.title: Architecting for Hardware Diversity: Meta's End-to-End Co-Design for High-Performance AI Training on AMD GPUs
Hardware Architecture.summary: Meta deploys a heterogeneous fleet comprising NVIDIA GPUs, AMD GPUs, and proprietary MTIA accelerators to reduce costs and mitigate vendor lock-in. However, the extensive history of NVIDIA-specific optimizations hinders performance portability to other hardware. This paper presents our methods for optimizing alternative accelerators, using AMD Instinct MI350X versus NVIDIA B200 for recommendation model training as a case study. We propose three reusable principles. First, hardware-model co-design is essential: rather than directly porting models from NVIDIA GPUs, revising model structures and software recipes allows full exploitation of accelerator-specific strengths (e.g., MI350X's 1.6x HBM capacity relative to B200). Second, our analytical performance model enables zero-warmup optimal kernel selection across diverse datatypes and matrix shapes in production models, drastically simplifying tuning. Third, increasingly mature agentic workflows have lowered the barrier to porting from the CUDA ecosystem; we extend these workflows for microarchitecture-aware kernel optimizations and custom shim generation. Compared to the directly ported baseline, these methods deliver up to 1.5x improvement in end-to-end training throughput. To our knowledge, this is the first hyperscaler report on productionizing AMD GPUs for large-scale training. Our contributions have been upstreamed to the open-source PyTorch, Triton, and ROCm ecosystems.
Hardware Architecture.comment: 16 pages, 21 figures, 6 tables. To appear in the 59th IEEE/ACM International Symposium on Microarchitecture (MICRO 2026)

Hardware Architecture.title: FAME: An FPGA-Based Platform for Approximate Multipliers Evaluation with Pattern-Guided DNN Retraining
Hardware Architecture.summary: Approximate multipliers can reduce hardware area and energy consumption in Deep Neural Network (DNN) inference; however, they introduce computational errors. Assessing the accuracy of numerous approximate multiplier designs across diverse DNN models and large-scale datasets remains challenging due to prohibitive evaluation times. This overhead primarily stems from the slow emulation of approximate multiplier behavior using look-up tables (LUTs) on CPU and GPU platforms. Moreover, the resulting accuracy degradation must be carefully quantified and, if necessary, mitigated (e.g., through retraining), further increasing the overall evaluation cost. To address these challenges, we propose FAME, an FPGA-based platform for evaluating approximate multipliers. The platform exploits the reconfigurable logic of Field-Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs) to implement approximate multipliers directly in hardware, eliminating the need for LUT-based emulation on CPU/GPU platforms and thereby enabling efficient DNN inference while significantly reducing evaluation time on large datasets. Furthermore, we introduce a pattern-guided DNN retraining technique to mitigate accuracy degradation induced by approximate multipliers. Specifically, retraining is guided by multiplier-specific patterns to effectively recover potential accuracy losses. We evaluate FAME using two DNN models, ResNet-18 and MobileNetV2, on the ImageNet dataset across 27 approximate multipliers. During inference, our approach achieves up to a 3.47x speedup in approximate multiplier evaluation compared to prior LUT-based emulation methods. Furthermore, the proposed retraining technique improves accuracy by up to 65.5% over existing retraining approaches for the evaluated multipliers. The code is publicly available at: https://github.com/gicLAB/FAME
Hardware Architecture.comment: Accepted at the 38th IEEE/SBC International Symposium on Computer Architecture and High Performance Computing (SBAC-PAD) 2026

Hardware Architecture.title: Compiling Multi-Threshold Operators for Quantized Non-Monotonic and Fine-Granular Activations in Custom-Tailored DNN Accelerators
Hardware Architecture.summary: Aggressive quantization of neural networks can expose activation functions as bottlenecks for efficient hardware acceleration. Implementing quantized activations as multi-threshold operations has been shown to be a promising optimization, allowing for efficient hardware implementation of few-bit activations. However, current implementations are limited to monotonically increasing functions, quantization schemes with one-dimensional (per-channel) granularity and a small set of predefined activation-quantizer combinations. We formalize the multi-threshold representation to extend it to non-monotonic functions and fine-granular parameters, i.e., multi-dimensional thresholds. For automated conversion of quantized function compositions into threshold representation, we propose a systematic approach via algebraic rules integrated into the ONNX-based compiler infrastructure. We experimentally validate our solution on a selection of monotonic and non-monotonic functions by extending the binary search based multi-threshold operator that is integrated into the FINN framework for end-to-end synthesis of custom-tailored FPGA accelerators. The cost of hardware support for non-monotonicity and fine-granularity is characterized in comparison to an alternative approach utilizing existing operators via graph-level decomposition. We compare our method to prior work as well as the approach taken by the hls4ml framework. As an outlook, we demonstrate the prospects of using the multi-threshold representation during the training of a neural network as a form of quantization aware training.

Hardware Architecture.title: Wattlytics: A Web Platform for Co-Optimizing Performance, Energy, and TCO in HPC Clusters
Hardware Architecture.summary: The escalating computational demands and energy footprint of GPU-accelerated computing systems complicate informed design and operational decisions. We present the first release of Wattlytics (https://wattlytics.netlify.app), an interactive, browser-based decision-support system. Unlike existing procurement-oriented calculators, Wattlytics uniquely integrates benchmark-driven GPU performance scaling, dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS)-aware piecewise power modeling, and multi-year total cost of ownership (TCO) analysis within a single interactive environment. Users can configure heterogeneous systems across contemporary GPU architectures (GH200, H100, L40S, L40, A40, A100, and L4), select representative scientific workloads (e.g., GROMACS, AMBER), and explore deployment scenarios under constraints such as energy prices, system lifetime, and frequency scaling. Wattlytics computes multidimensional decision metrics (TCO breakdown, work-per-TCO, power-per-TCO, and work-per-watt-per-TCO) and supports design-space exploration, what-if scenarios, sensitivity metrics (elasticity, Sobol indices, Monte Carlo) and collaborative features to guide realistic cluster design and procurement under uncertainty. We validate the fitted power and performance models and compare four deployment modes: fixed budget, fixed GPU count, fixed performance, and fixed power. Our case studies show that, under budget or energy constraints, optimally deployed energy-efficient GPUs can outperform higher-performance alternatives in overall cost-effectiveness. Wattlytics helps users explore the design parameter space and distinguish between cost- and risk-driving factors, turning HPC design into a well-informed and explainable decision-making process.

Hardware Architecture.title: The Program Hypergraph: Multi-Way Relational Structure for Geometric Algebra, Spatial Compute, and Physics-Aware Compilation
Hardware Architecture.summary: Source code organizes a program as expressions and declarations, which a compiler can represent as an abstract syntax tree (AST). Some compilers introduce a further abstraction of the computation as a graph. Nodes represent operations, while connections record how values pass between them and how execution proceeds. Yet these connections can leave the full scope of conditions governing a computation implicit. Developers may then need defensive checks, rely on compiler hacks, pragmas, and implementation-specific code to maintain those conditions as the program evolves. Our thesis is that a hypergraph more faithfully represents complex computation across all targets by making joint constraints inherent to its structure, with an overall less burdensome design-time API. Our Program Hypergraph (PHG) extends our Semantic Graph with relations that connect across an operation's participants, their dependencies, and the invariants they must preserve. Joint resolution in the graph guides lowering into standard Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR). Satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) checks intrinsic to the graph discharge applicable proof obligations. Supporting information remains available until the decisions that require it are complete. As a primary benefit, verification follows from the rules used to construct and transform the graph. For properties established this way before execution, the generated program needs no added runtime checks, no 'boxing' or 'tagging' or other managed runtime support. We develop this account through geometric algebra, shared-memory capacity, and spatial placement, distinguishing structural guarantees from numerical and resource obligations that require further evidence. The proposed integration makes the same information available at design-time, so engineers can inspect the consequences of a choice before it becomes an implementation constraint.
Hardware Architecture.comment: 27 pages, 0 figures, 4 tables. Updated for contributions from Karwowski et al

Hardware Architecture.title: Independent Data-Integrity Verification for LLM-Driven Functional Coverage Closure in Hardware Design
Hardware Architecture.summary: LLM agents can write directed tests that close functional coverage, but coverage only shows that a state was reached, not that the data on the way there was correct. This is a long-known point in verification and we do not claim it as new. We describe a small coverage-closure agent that applies it to an LLM loop: coverage is read from the report that the simulation itself exports (cocotb-coverage YAML) and never taken from the model's account, and data integrity is checked by scoreboards that are separate from the model. On three architecturally distinct RTL designs (an asynchronous FIFO, a UART transmitter and an AHB2APB bridge) the agent raised coverage from 91.7%, 88.9% and 67.4% to 100% within its 8-iteration budget in every logged run, using one design-agnostic agent. A reactive scoreboard monitor attached to the FIFO's base testbench also found a clock-domain-crossing bug in the author's own stimulus code. The monitor is not yet attached to the LLM-generated tests, so their data integrity is not independently checked; one manual check on a single FIFO test is reported as preliminary. We list the weaknesses of this evidence: three designs, no baseline, no ablation, and logged runs that come from several agent checkpoints.

Hardware Architecture.title: Minimum RISC-V: Maximum FPGA Efficiency
Hardware Architecture.summary: RISC-V processors are now widely available for FPGAs, with most FPGA vendors replacing their proprietary soft-CPU architectures with this instruction-set architecture (ISA). Although contemporary FPGAs are increasingly resource- and feature-rich, a soft processor system---including memory---often occupies a disproportionately large footprint and delivers only modest performance relative to the potential of the target device. In this work we first design a lightweight but deeply pipelined RISC-V core that can run above 700 MHz in a mid-range device and that is capable of retiring one instruction per clock under ideal conditions. We then develop and demonstrate a new optimization method that compiles the final application binary and a specialized processor instance contemporaneously. The method expands each instruction into an application-specific encoding, removes unused datapath and decode logic during synthesis, and yields cores that remain assembler-compatible with the original program while no longer being binary-compatible with a general-purpose RISC-V. We implement example designs on RV32I (base integer), RV32M (integer multiply), and RV32F (single-precision floating-point) configurations. Our optimized RISC-V is as small as 170 ALMs and closes timing at 775 MHz in an Altera Agilex-5 device. Finally, we show that these processors can be packed into a deterministic area and stepped-and-repeated continuously without material impact on performance, enabling predictable multi-core density planning.

Hardware Architecture.title: A Black-Box Positioning Solution for Effortless Integration in Wearable Navigation
Hardware Architecture.summary: Accurate localization is critical for a wide range of applications, including navigation, augmented reality, safety management, and healthcare. However, achieving accurate positioning remains challenging, especially in GPS-degraded environments. Pedestrian Dead Reckoning (PDR), which estimates position based on inertial sensor data, offers a promising alternative but typically demands substantial effort in algorithm design and system integration. This complexity often leads to prolonged development timelines and elevated costs. To address these challenges, we present the PDR Sensor (PDRS), a plug-and-play, black-box PDR module optimized for seamless integration into wearable and IoT platforms. PDRS integrates a microprocessor and an inertial measurement unit (IMU) within a compact, low-power module. It executes real-time sensor fusion onboard, providing position updates via standard interfaces (I2C, SPI, UART). Experimental evaluations demonstrate its high robustness, achieving a step detection error of just 0.16% over 1250 steps and a traveled distance error of 1.87% under diverse conditions. The system further exhibits low latency (2.5 ms) and modest power consumption (52.35 mA). Unlike conventional studies, the PDRS leverages a holistic co-design of hardware and software to enhance performance and integration aspects, simplifying adoption without requiring deep expertise. By lowering technical barriers, PDRS enables developers and researchers to prioritize innovation in IoT and wearable technologies, accelerating prototyping, reducing development time, and advancing industry progress. Future work aims to enhance accuracy, reduce power usage and module size, and integrate AI-driven techniques to better mitigate drift.
Hardware Architecture.comment: 8 pages

Hardware Architecture.title: PSA: A Pruning-Friendly Sparse-Aware Accelerator for Efficient Sparse Convolution in SNNs
Hardware Architecture.summary: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) are promising for energy-efficient artificial intelligence due to their event-driven sparse computation, and neuron pruning can further reduce redundant operations. However, in practical hardware accelerators, spike sparsity and pruning-induced sparsity produce highly irregular sparse workloads that are difficult to execute efficiently.
